Chapter-1 Introduction to Accounting Standards

PART A Question 1. “Accounting Standards standardize diverse accounting policies with a view to eliminate the non- comparability of financial statements and improve the reliability of financial statements.” Discuss and explain the benefits of Accounting Standards.

[5 Marks I 6 Minutes I ICAI FAV I (MTP Nov ’21 & April ‘23) (PYP Nov’18,) High Chance]

Answer 1. Accounting Standards standardize diverse accounting policies with a view to eliminate the non- comparability of financial statements and improve the reliability of financial statements. Accounting Standards provide a set of standard accounting policies, valuation norms and disclosure requirements. Accounting standards aim at improving the quality of financial reporting by promoting comparability, consistency and transparency, in the interests of users of financial statements. The following are the benefits of Accounting Standards:

(i) Standardization of alternative accounting treatments: Accounting Standards reduce to a reasonable extent confusing variations in the accounting treatment followed for the purpose of preparation of financial statements.

(ii) Requirements for additional disclosures: There are certain areas where important is not statutorily required to be disclosed. Standards may call for disclosure beyond that required by law.

(iii) Comparability of financial statements: The application of accounting standards would facilitate comparison of financial statements of different companies situated in India and facilitate comparison, to a limited extent, of financial statements of companies situated in different parts of the world. However, it should be noted in this respect that differences in the institutions, traditions and legal systems from one country to another give rise to differences in Accounting Standards adopted in different countries.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Begin with the meaning/objective of Accounting Standards and then explain the benefits point-wise. Use keywords like comparability, reliability, transparency, and consistency. Conclude with how standards improve financial reporting quality. Time-Saving Tips: Remember the 3 core benefits: standardization, disclosure, and comparability. Write answers in bullet points with short explanations instead of long paragraphs. Revise ICAI language for direct presentation.

Examiner Observation Students often write only the definition and forget proper explanation of benefits. Lack of headings and ICAI keywords reduces marks. Structured point-wise answers score better.

Question 2. Explain the objective of ‘Accounting Standards’ in brief. State the advantages of setting Accounting Standards.

[5 Marks I 6 Minutes I ICAI FAV I (PYP Nov ’22, Old & New SM) High Chance]

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 3

Answer 2. Accounting Standards are the written policy documents issued by Government relating to various aspects of measurement, treatment, presentation and disclosure of accounting transactions and events. Following are the objectives of Accounting Standards: a. Accounting Standards harmonize the diverse accounting policies and practices followed by different companies in India. b. Accounting Standards facilitates the preparation of financial statements and make them comparable. c. Accounting Standards give a sense of faith and reliability to the users.

The main advantage of setting accounting standards are as follows: a. Accounting Standards makes the financial statements of different companies comparable which helps investors in decision making. b. Accounting Standards prevent any misleading accounting treatment. c. Accounting Standards prevent manipulation of data by the management.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: First explain the objective briefly, then separately write the advantages in numbered points. Maintain proper headings for “Objective” and “Advantages” to improve presentation. Time-Saving Tips: Use keywords like standardization, reliability, comparability, and useful information. Learn advantages in sequence for quick recall during exams.

Examiner Observation Students commonly mix objectives with advantages in one paragraph. Avoid unnecessary theory and focus on concise ICAI-oriented points for better scoring.

Question 3. Briefly explain the process of issuance of Indian Accounting Standards.

[4 Marks I 5 Minutes I ICAI FAV I (Study Material), Medium to High Chance]

Answer 3. Due to the recent stream of overseas acquisitions by Indian companies, there is need for adoption of high- quality standards to convince foreign enterprises about the financial standing as also the disclosure and governance standards of Indian acquirers. The Government of India in consultation with the ICAI decided to converge and not to adopt IFRSs issued by the IASB. The decision of convergence rather than adoption was taken after the detailed analysis of IFRSs requirements and extensive discussion with various stakeholders. The ICAI has worked towards convergence of global accounting standards by considering the application of IFRS in Indian corporate environment. Recognising the growing need of full convergence of Ind AS with IFRS, ICAI constituted a Task Force to examine various issues involved Ind AS are issued by the Central Government of India under the supervision and control of ASB of ICAI and in consultation with NFRA. NFRA recommends these standards to the MCA and MCA has to spell out the accounting standards applicable for companies in India.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Explain the process step-by-step starting from IFRS convergence to issuance by the Central Government. Mention ICAI, ASB, NFRA, and MCA clearly. Time-Saving Tips: Memorize the sequence: IFRS → ICAI Task Force → ASB → NFRA → MCA. Writing the answer in flow format saves time and improves clarity.

Examiner Observation

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 4

Many students forget the role of NFRA and MCA. Incomplete process explanation and missing sequence lead to loss of marks.

Question 4. Explain the significance of emergence of IFRS as Global Standards.

[4 Marks I 4 Minutes I ICAI FAV I (Study Material), Medium]

Answer 4. Global Standards facilitate cross border flow of money, global listing in different bourses and comparability of financial statements. Global Standards improve the ability of investors to compare investments on a global basis and thus lowers their risk of errors of judgment. It facilitates accounting and reporting for companies with global operations and eliminates some costly requirements sayre in statement of financial statements.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Start with the concept of global standards and explain their significance in international business and reporting. Focus on comparability, transparency, and investor confidence. Time-Saving Tips: Remember 3 important points: cross-border flow, global comparability, and uniform reporting. Use short bullet points instead of detailed explanations.

Examiner Observation Students often write generic advantages without linking them specifically to IFRS. Answers should focus on international reporting benefits.

Question 5. What do you mean by Carve outs/ins in Ind AS? Explain.

[4 Marks I 4 Minutes (MTP Jan 2025), High Chance]

Answer 5. Certain changes have been made in Ind AS considering the economic environment of the country, which is different as compared to the economic environment presumed to be in existence by IFRS. These differences are due to differences in economic conditions prevailing in India. These differences which are in deviation to the accounting principles and practices stated in IFRS, are commonly known as ‘Carve-outs’. Additional guidance given in Ind AS over and above what is given in IFRS, is termed as ‘Carve in’.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: First define Carve-outs and Carve-ins separately and then explain their relevance in Indian economic conditions. Use simple comparative language. Time-Saving Tips: Remember: deviation from IFRS = Carve-out; additional guidance = Carve-in. A comparison table format can help save time.

Examiner Observation Students usually confuse carve-outs with carve-ins. Clear definitions with proper distinction are necessary to secure full marks.

Question 6. Write a short note on International Accounting Standard Board.

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes | ICAI Fav. | RTP, High Chance] © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 5

Answer 6. With a view of achieving the objective of setting global standards, the London based group namely the International Accounting Standards Committee (IASC), responsible for developing International Accounting Standards (IAS), was established in June, 1973.  It is presently known as International Accounting Standards Board (IASB).  Between 1973 and 2001, the IASC released IASs. Between 1997 and 1999, the IASC restructured their organisation, which resulted in formation of IASB. These changes came into effect on 1st April, 2001. Subsequently, IASB issued statements about current and future standards.  IASB publishes its Standards in a series of pronouncements called International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS).  The standards issued by IASC till 31.03.2001 are known as IASs and the standards issued by IASB since 01.04.2001 are known as IFRSs.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Start with the establishment of IASC in 1973 and mention its transformation into IASB in 2001. Highlight the difference between IAS and IFRS in separate bullet points. Write the timeline (1973–2001 and post-2001) clearly to secure full marks. Use keywords like global standards, IAS, IFRS, and IASB for quick scoring.

Examiner’s Observation Students often confuse IASC with IASB and miss the restructuring year (2001). Many fail to distinguish between IASs and IFRSs. Answers lacking chronological presentation lose marks. Proper use of dates and standard names helps fetch full marks.

### PART B

### Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. Accounting Standards a) Harmonies accounting policies and eliminate the non-comparability of financial statements. b) Improve the reliability of financial statements. c) Both (a) and (b). d) Manipulate the data for the management.

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason:  Accounting Standards are designed to harmonize accounting policies across different entities, improving the comparability of financial statements (eliminating non-comparability).  They also aim to improve the reliability of financial statements by ensuring consistency and transparency in reporting. Thus, accounting standards help achieve both (a) and (b), making (c) the correct answer.

Question 2. It is essential to standardize the accounting principles and policies in order to ensure a) Transparency b) Consistency. c) Comparability d) All the above

(Study Material)

Ans: (d) Reason: Standardizing accounting principles and policies is essential to ensure: o Transparency: Clear and understandable financial statements that reflect the true financial position of the company. o Consistency: Consistent application of accounting policies over time, which allows stakeholders to understand trends and patterns. o Comparability: Ensures that financial statements of different companies can be compared, making it easier to assess performance across companies and industries. Thus, all the above are achieved by standardizing accounting principles and policies.

Question 3. Accounting Standards for non-corporate entities in India are issued by a) Central Govt. b) State Govt. c) Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. d) MCA

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason:

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 7

In India, the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) is responsible for issuing Accounting Standards (AS) for non-corporate entities, including individuals, partnerships, and firms. ICAI develops these standards to ensure uniformity and consistency in the preparation of financial statements for non-corporate entities. Thus, the correct answer is (c).

Question 4. Which committee is responsible for approval of accounting standards and their modification for the purpose of applicability to companies? a) NFRA. b) MCA. c) Central Government Advisory Committee. d) IASB

(Study Material)

Ans: (b) Reason: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) is responsible for the approval of accounting standards and their modifications for applicability to companies in India. The MCA plays a key role in the regulation of accounting standards under the Companies Act, 2013, and ensures that these standards align with the broader regulatory framework. Thus, the correct answer is (b) MCA.

Question 5. Global Standards facilitate a) Cross border flow of money. b) Comparability of financial statements c) Uniformity and Transparency of financial statements d) All the three

(Study Material)

Ans: (d) Reason: (i) Global Standards facilitate: (ii) Cross-border flow of money: By standardizing accounting practices globally, investors and companies can engage in international trade and investments more easily. (iii) Comparability of financial statements: Standardized accounting practices ensure that financial statements from different countries are comparable. (iv) Uniformity and Transparency: Global standards ensure that financial reporting is consistent and transparent, making it easier for stakeholders to understand the financial health of businesses. Thus, the correct answer is (d) All the three.

Chapter-2

Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements

PART A Question 1. Explain in brief, the alternative measurement bases, for determining the value at which an element can be recognized in the Balance Sheet or Statement of Profit and Loss.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes | ICAI Favourite| MTP March ’19 & April ‘19, March ’21, Oct ’23, (RTP Nov 18), High Chance]

Answer 1. The Framework for Recognition and Presentation of Financial statements recognizes four alternative measurement bases for the purpose of determining the value at which an element can be recognized in the balance sheet or statement of profit and loss. These bases are: (i) Historical Cost; (ii) Current cost (iii) Realizable (Settlement) Value and (iv) Present Value.

A brief explanation of each measurement basis is as follows:

1. Historical Cost: Historical cost means acquisition price. According to this, assets are recorded at an amount of

cash or cash equivalent paid or the fair value of the asset at the time of acquisition. Liabilities are generally recorded at the amount of proceeds received in exchange for the obligation.

2. Current Cost: Current cost gives an alternative measurement basis. Assets are carried out at the amount of

cash or cash equivalent that would have to be paid if the same or an equivalent asset was acquired currently. Liabilities are carried at the undiscounted amount of cash or cash equivalents that would be required to settle the obligation currently.

3. Realizable (Settlement) Value: As per realizable value, assets are carried at the amount of cash or cash

equivalents that could currently be obtained by selling the assets in an orderly disposal. Liabilities are carried at their settlement values; i.e. the undiscounted amount of cash or cash equivalents paid to satisfy the liabilities in the normal course of business.

4. Present Value: Under present value convention, assets are carried at present value of future net cash flows

generated by the concerned assets in the normal course of business. Liabilities under this convention are carried at present value of future net cash flows that are expected to be required to settle the liability in the normal course of business.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Start by defining measurement bases and then explain all four bases separately: Historical Cost, Current Cost, Realizable Value, and Present Value. Use point-wise format with short definitions and examples if possible. Time-Saving Tips: Remember the sequence: Historical → Current → Realizable → Present Value. Write only keywords and one-line explanations to save time in theory questions.

Examiner Observation

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 9

Students often forget one measurement base or confuse current cost with realizable value. Proper headings and exact ICAI terminology help in scoring full marks.

Question 3. Explain how financial capital is maintained at historical cost? Kishore started a business on 1st April, 2019 with Rs.15,00,000 represented by 75,000 units of Rs.20 each. During the financial year ending on 31stMarch, 2020, he sold the entire stock for Rs.30 each. In order to maintain the capital intact, calculate the maximum amount, which can be withdrawn by Kishore in the year 2019-20 if Financial Capital is maintained at historical cost.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes | ICAI Favourite (PYP Jan 21), High Chance]

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 10

Answer 3. Financial capital maintenance at historical cost: Under this convention, opening and closing assets are stated at respective historical costs to ascertain opening and closing equity. If retained profit is greater than or equals to zero, the capital is said to be maintained at historical costs. This means the business will have enough funds to replace its assets at historical costs. This is quite right as long as prices do not rise. Maximum amount withdrawn by Kishore in year 2019-20 if financial capital is maintained at historical cost

Particulars Financial Capital Maintenance at Historical Cost

(Rs.)

Closing equity (Rs.30 x 75,000 units) 22,50,000 represented by cash

Opening equity 75,000 units x Rs. 20 = 15,00,000

Permissible drawings to keep Capital intact 7,50,000 (22,50,000 – 15,00,000)

Thus Rs.7,50,000 is the maximum amount that can be withdrawn by Kishore in year 2019-20 if financial capital is maintained at historical cost.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: First explain the concept theoretically, then solve the numerical by calculating opening equity, closing equity, and permissible drawings. Time-Saving Tips: Use a simple 3-step format: Opening Capital → Closing Capital → Drawings. Practice standard formats repeatedly for faster solving.

Examiner Observation Students often skip theory explanation and write only calculations. Both theory and practical portions carry importance.

Question 6. “One of the characteristics of financial statements is neutrality”- Do you agree with this statement? Comment.

[4 Marks | 4 Minutes | ICAI Favourite [MTP March ‘18, PYP Nov ’18, Old & New SM), Medium–High Chance]

Answer 6.Yes, one of the characteristics of financial statements is neutrality. To be reliable, the information contained in financial statement must be neutral, that is free from bias. Financial Statements are not neutral if by the selection or presentation of information, the focus of analysis could shift from one area of business to another thereby arriving at a totally different conclusion on the business results. For example, if the assets of a company primarily consist of trade receivables and insurance claims and the financial statements do not specify that the insurance claims have been lying unrealized for a number of years or that a few key trade receivables have not given balance confirmation certificates, an erroneous conclusion may be drawn on the liquidity of the company. Financial statements are said to depict the true and fair view of the business of the organization by virtue of neutrality.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Start with the meaning of neutrality and explain why financial statements should be free from bias. Include the given example briefly. Time-Saving Tips: Remember neutrality = unbiased information + true and fair view. Write concise explanation instead of lengthy theory.

Examiner Observation Students write general definitions of reliability without explaining neutrality specifically. Example-based explanation scores better.

Question 10. A Ltd. has entered into a binding agreement with Gamma Ltd. to buy a custom-made machine Rs.1,00,000. At the end of 20X1-X2, before delivery of the machine, A Ltd. had to change its method of production. The new method will not require the machine ordered and it will be scrapped after delivery. The expected scrap value is nil.

You are required to advise the accounting treatment and give necessary journal entry in the year 20X1- X2.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes| ICAI Favourite (RTP May’20, May’23 & Nov ‘23), High Chance]

Answer 10. A liability is recognized when outflow of economic resources in settlement of a present obligation can be anticipated and the value of outflow can be reliably measured. In the given case, A Ltd. should recognize a liability of Rs.1,00,000 to Gamma Ltd. When flow of economic benefit to the enterprise beyond the current accounting period is considered improbable, the expenditure incurred is recognized as an expense rather than as an asset. In the present case, flow of future economic benefit from the machine to the enterprise is improbable. The entire amount of purchase price of the machine should be recognized as an expense.

Journal entry

To Gamma Ltd. 1,00,000

(Loss due to change in production method)

Profit and loss A/c Dr. 1,00,000

To Loss on change in production method 1,00,000

(Loss transferred to profit and loss account)

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 16

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Identify whether liability and expense should be recognized based on the framework. Then pass journal entries properly. Time-Saving Tips: Focus on keywords: present obligation, future economic benefit, expense recognition. Learn journal entry format properly.

Question 11. With regard to financial statements name any four.

(i) Users (ii) Qualitative characteristics (iii) Elements

[5 Marks | 5 Minutes| ICAI Favourite (RTP Nov 20, RTP May 19, MTP Mar’23), Medium–High Chance]

Answer 11.

(i) Users of financial statements: Investors, Employees, Lenders, Supplies/Creditors, Customers, Government & Public

(ii) Qualitative Characteristics of Financial Statements: Understand ability, Relevance, Comparability, Reliability & Faithful Representation

(iii) Elements of Financial Statements: Asset, Liability, Equity, Income/Gain and Expense/Loss

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Write separate headings for users, characteristics, and elements. Present answers in bullet format. Time-Saving Tips: Learn standard ICAI lists in sequence for quick recall.

Examiner Observation Incomplete lists are common mistakes. Write at least four correct points under each heading.

Question 12. Explain main elements of Financial Statements.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes| ICAI Favourite (RTP May 18) (PYP May ’18) (MTP Jan 2025), High Chance]

Answer 12. Elements of Financial Statements

The Framework for preparation and Presentation of financial statements classifies items of financial statements can be classified in five broad groups depending on their economic characteristics: Asset, Liability, Equity, Income/Gain and Expense/Loss.

Asset Resource controlled by the enterprise as a result of past events from which future economic

benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 17

Liability Present obligation of the enterprise arising from past events, the settlement of which is

expected to result in an outflow of a resource embodying economic benefits.

Equity Residual interest in the assets of an enterprise after deducting all its liabilities.

Income/gain Increase in economic benefits during the accounting period in the form of inflows or

enhancement of assets or decreases in liabilities that result in increase in equity other than those relating to contributions from equity participants

Expense/loss Decrease in economic benefits during the accounting period in the form of outflows or

depletions of assets or incurrence of liabilities that result in decrease in equity other than those relating to distributions to equity participants

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Define each element separately: Asset, Liability, Equity, Income, and Expense. Use proper ICAI definitions. Time-Saving Tips: Remember elements in sequence and practice writing short definitions regularly.

Examiner Observation Students confuse income with equity and expense with liability. Definitions must be precise.

Question 13. A trader commenced business on April 1, 2020 with Rs.120,000, represented by 6000 units of a certain product at Rs.20 per unit. During the year 2020-21 he sold these units at Rs.30/- per unit and had withdrawn Rs.60,000. The price of the product at the end of financial year was Rs.25/- per unit. Compute retained profit of the trader under the concept of physical capital maintenance at current cost. Also, state, whether Answer would be different if the trader had not withdrawn any amount.

[5 Marks | 8 Minutes| ICAI Favourite (PYP July’21,) (MTP 5 Marks Sep ’23), High Chance]

Answer 13. Physical Capital Maintenance at Current cost in the given case, the specific price index applicable to the product is 125 (25/20X100). Current cost of opening stock = (Rs. 1, 20,000 / 100) x 125 Or 6,000 unit’s x Rs. 25 = Rs. 1, 50,000 Current cost of closing cash = Rs. 1, 20,000 (Rs. 1, 80,000 – Rs. 60,000) Opening equity at closing current costs = Rs. 1,50,000

Closing equity at closing current costs = Rs. 1, 20,000 Retained Profit = Rs. 1, 20,000 – Rs. 1, 50,000 = (-) Rs. 30,000 The negative retained profit indicates that the trader has failed to maintain his capital. The available fund of Rs. 1, 20,000 is not sufficient to buy 6,000 units again at increased price of Rs. 25 per unit. The drawings should have been restricted to Rs. 30,000 (Rs. 60,000 – Rs. 30,000). If the trader had not withdrawn any amount, then the Answer would have been as below: Current cost of opening stock = Rs. 1, 80,000 Opening equity at closing current costs = Rs. 1, 50,000 Retained Profit = Rs. 1, 80,000 – Rs. 1, 50,000 = Rs. 30,000 If the trader had not withdrawn any amount, then the retained profit would have been Rs. 30,000.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Calculate retained profit using current cost concept and then analyze the effect of drawings separately.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 18

Time-Saving Tips: Prepare calculations in step-wise format and focus on adjusted current cost figures.

Examiner Observation Students usually make errors in adjusted capital calculations. Interpretation of retained profit/loss is important.

Question 14. What is meant by ‘Measurement’? What are the bases of measurement of Elements of Financial Statements? Explain in brief.

[6 Marks | 7 Minutes| ICAI Favourite (RTP Nov 21, PYP Dec ’21), High Chance]

Answer 14. Measurement refers to the process of quantifying, in monetary terms, the elements (assets, liabilities, equity, income, and expenses) of the financial statements for recognition in the balance sheet and statement of profit and loss (or income statement).

As per the Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) (aligned with the IASB's 2018 Conceptual Framework, applicable in ICAI curriculum for periods relevant to 2026 exams), measurement involves selecting a measurements basis that provides relevant and faithfully representative information about the asset, liability, or related income/expenses.

The Framework primarily distinguishes between two broad categories of measurement bases:

1. Historical Cost: Historical cost measures are derived, at least in part, from the price of the transaction or other

event that gave rise to the asset or liability.

 Assets are recorded at the amount of cash or cash equivalents paid (or fair value of consideration given) at

acquisition.  Liabilities are recorded at the amount of proceeds received (or amounts expected to be paid) in exchange

for the obligation.

Changes in value are not reflected except for impairment (assets) or when a liability becomes onerous.

2. Current Value

Current value measures reflect conditions at the measurement date using updated information. They include:

 Fair value — The price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly

transaction between market participants at the measurement date (exit price).  Value in use (for assets) — The present value of estimated future cash flows expected from continuing use

and ultimate disposal of the asset.  Fulfilment value (for liabilities) — The present value of cash flows expected to be required to settle the

liability (including any risk adjustments).

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 19

 Current cost — The cost of an equivalent asset at the measurement date (amount that would have to be

paid to acquire the same or equivalent asset currently) or, for liabilities, the amount required to settle the obligation currently.

The Conceptual Framework emphasizes that the selection of a measurement basis (or combination) depends on which provides the most relevant information and faithful representation, considering factors like the nature of the item, contribution to future cash flows, and cost constraint. Different Ind AS standards apply specific bases (e.g., historical cost for many PPE items under Ind AS 16, fair value for certain financial instruments under Ind AS 109, etc.).

In preparing financial statements, a mix of these bases is often used in varying combinations for different elements to best achieve the objective of providing useful financial information.

(Note: The older 'Framework for the Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements' listed four bases— historical cost, current cost, realizable/settlement value, and present value—but under the current Ind AS Conceptual Framework applicable for CA Final exams in 2026, the emphasis is on historical cost vs. current value categories, with sub-bases like fair value, value in use, fulfilment value, and current cost.)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Define measurement first and then explain historical cost and current value categories clearly. Time-Saving Tips: Use headings and sub-headings for each basis to improve presentation and speed.

Examiner Observation Students often write outdated framework concepts without clarity. Updated ICAI terminology gives better marks.

### PART B

### Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. Two principal qualitative characteristics of financial statements are

a) Understand ability and materiality b) Relevance and reliability

c) Relevance and materiality d) Comparability and materiality.

(Study material)

Ans: (b)

Reason

The two principal qualitative characteristics of financial statements are Relevance and Reliability:

o Relevance: Information is relevant if it is capable of influencing decisions. It helps users make predictions and decisions about the company’s future performance.

o Reliability: Information is reliable when it is complete, free from bias, and faithfully represents what it is intended to depict.

These two characteristics are fundamental in ensuring that financial statements are useful to stakeholders.

Thus, the correct answer is (b).

Question 2. Value of equity may change due to

(a) Contribution from or Distribution to equity participants (b) Income earned

(c) Expenses incurred (d) All the three.

(Study material)

Ans: (d)

Question 3. An accounting policy can be changed if the change is required

a) By statute or accounting standard b) For more appropriate presentation of financial statements

c) Both (a) and (b) d) By statute as well as accounting standards.

(Study material)

Ans: (c)

Reason

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 29

 An accounting policy can be changed if the change is required:

o By statute or accounting standard: Legal or regulatory changes, such as amendments to accounting standards or statutory requirements, may necessitate a change in accounting policies.

o For more appropriate presentation of financial statements: If a change in accounting policy improves the presentation or provides more reliable and relevant information, it is considered appropriate.

Thus, both (a) and (b) are valid reasons for changing an accounting policy.

Hence, the correct answer is (c).

Questions 4. The ‘going concern’ concept assumes that

a) The business can continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future.

b) The business cannot continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future.

c) The business is continuing to be profitable.

d) The business cannot continue if it is not able to earn profits.

(Study material)

Ans: (a)

Reason

 The going concern concept assumes that a business will continue its operations for the foreseeable future, unless there is evidence to the contrary. This means the business is expected to remain in operation and not liquidate or significantly reduce its activities in the near future.

 This concept underpins the preparation of financial statements, as it assumes that the business will not be forced to stop its operations and sell off assets.

Thus, the correct answer is (a).

Question 5. All of the following are components of financial statements except

a) Balance sheet b) Statement of Profit and loss

c) Human responsibility report d) Social responsibility report.

(Study material)

Ans: (c)

Reason

The core components of financial statements typically include:

 Balance sheet: Shows the company's financial position at a specific point in time.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 30

 Statement of Profit and Loss: Reflects the company’s performance over a period, detailing revenues, expenses,

and profits.

 Social responsibility report: This may be included in corporate social responsibility (CSR) disclosures, but it is not

a standard component of financial statements.

However, a "Human responsibility report" is not a standard component of financial statements.

Thus, the correct answer is (c).

Chapter-3 Applicability of Accounting Standards

PART A Question 1. What are the issues, with which Accounting Standards deal?

[4 Marks | 4 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (RTP Nov 20) (Old & New SM), Medium–High]

Answer 1. Accounting Standards deal with the issues of (i) Recognition of events and transactions in the financial statements, (ii) Measurement of these transactions and events, (iii) Presentation of these transactions and events in the financial statements in a manner that is meaningful and understandable to the reader, and (iv) Disclosure requirements.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Start by stating that Accounting Standards govern the treatment of financial transactions. Then explain the four areas separately: recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure. Time-Saving Tips: Remember the keyword sequence: Recognition → Measurement → Presentation → Disclosure (RMPD). Write answers in point format instead of detailed paragraphs.

Examiner Observation Students often explain only disclosure and forget other areas. Proper sequence and ICAI terminology improve presentation and marks.

Question 2. (a) A company with a turnover of Rs. 225 crores and borrowings of Rs. 51 crore during the year

st ended 31 March, 2021, wants to avail the exemptions available in adoption of Accounting Standards applicable to companies for the year ended 31.3. 2021. Advise the management on the exemptions that are available as per the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes | ICAI Fav (RTP May ’22), High Chance]

Answer 2. (a) The question deals with the issue of Applicability of Accounting Standards for corporate entities. The companies can be classified under two categories viz SMCs and Non−SMCs under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021. As per the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, criteria for above classification as SMCs, are: “Small and Medium Sized Company” (SMC) means, a company− whose equity or debt securities are not listed or are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange, whether in India or outside India; (1) which is not a bank, financial institution or an insurance company; (2) whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed rupees two−fifty crores in the immediately preceding accounting year; (3) which does not have borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees fifty crores at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 32

(4) which is not a holding or subsidiary company of a company which is not a small and medium− sized company. Since, XYZ Ltd.’s turnover was Rs. 225 crores which does not exceed Rs. 250 crores but borrowings of Rs. 51 crore are more than Rs. 50 crores, it is not a small and medium sized company (SMC). The exemptions available to SMC are not available to this company.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: First identify whether the company qualifies as SMC by checking turnover and borrowing criteria separately. Then conclude whether exemptions are available. Time-Saving Tips: Memorize SMC limits: Turnover ≤ Rs.250 Cr and Borrowings ≤ Rs.50 Cr. Direct comparison format saves calculation and writing time.

Examiner’s Observation Students generally check only turnover and ignore borrowings. Final conclusion without proper reasoning leads to mark deduction.

Question 3. XYZ Ltd., with a turnover of Rs. 50 crores during previous year and borrowings of Rs. 1 crore during any time in the previous year, wants to avail the exemptions available in adoption of Accounting Standards applicable to companies for the year ended 31.3.20X1. Advise the management on the exemptions that are available as per the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes | ICAI Fav (Study material), High Chance]

Answer 3. The question deals with the issue of Applicability of Accounting Standards for corporate entities. The companies can be classified under two categories viz SMCs and Non SMCs under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021. As per the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, criteria for above classification as SMCs, are: “Small and Medium Sized Company” (SMC) means, a company

1. whose equity or debt securities are not listed or are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange, whether

in India or outside India;

2. which is not a bank, financial institution or an insurance company;
3. whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed rupees two- fifty crores in the immediately

preceding accounting year;

4. which does not have borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees fifty crores at any time during

the immediately preceding accounting year; and

5. which is not a holding or subsidiary company of a company which is not a small and medium- sized
6. company.

Since, XYZ Ltd.’s turnover was Rs. 50 crores which does not exceed Rs. 250 crores and borrowings of Rs. 1 crore are less than Rs. 50 crores, it is a small and medium sized company (SMC).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Check all SMC conditions one by one and conclude that the company qualifies as SMC. Mention that exemptions available to SMCs can be availed. Time-Saving Tips: Prepare a small checklist for SMC criteria to avoid missing any condition during exams.

Examiner’s Observation Students often forget to mention that securities should not be listed. Complete condition-wise analysis is expected by ICAI.

Question 4. A company was classified as Non-SMC in 20X1-X2. In 20X2-X3, it has been classified as SMC. The management desires to avail the exemptions or relaxations available for SMCs in 20X2-X3. However, the accountant of the company does not agree with the same. Comment.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes | ICAI Fav (Study material), Medium Chance]

Answer 4. As per Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, an existing company, which was previously not a SMC and subsequently becomes a SMC, should not be qualified for exemption or relaxation in respect of accounting standards available to a SMC until the company remains a SMC for two consecutive accounting periods. Therefore, the management of the company cannot avail the exemptions/ relaxations available to the SMCs for the FY 20X2-X3.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: State the ICAI rule regarding transition from Non-SMC to SMC and explain the requirement of two consecutive accounting periods. Time-Saving Tips: Remember the “2 consecutive years rule” for newly classified SMCs. Short conceptual explanation is sufficient.

Examiner’s Observation Students commonly conclude directly without mentioning the mandatory waiting period. ICAI expects exact rule-based answer.

Question 5. M/s X & Co. (a partnership firm) had a turnover of Rs. 5 crores (excluding other income) and borrowings of Rs. 1.5 crores in the previous year. It wants to avail the exemptions available in application of Accounting Standards to non-corporate entities for the year ended 31.3.2022. Advise the management of M/s X & Co in respect of the exemptions of provisions of Ass, as per the directive issued by the ICAI.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes | ICAI Fav (MTP Oct ’22 MTP Oct’18, Old & New SM), High Chance]

Answer 5. Advice to the management of M/s X & Co. (a partnership firm) regarding exemptions available in the application of Accounting Standards (AS) for the year ended 31.3.2022. M/s X & Co. is a non-corporate entity (partnership firm). The applicability of Accounting Standards to non- corporate entities is governed by the criteria laid down by the ICAI through its announcements and the relevant framework for non-company entities. For the accounting period ended 31.3.2022 (i.e., financial year 2021-22), the classification criteria for non- company entities (as applicable at that time, prior to later revisions effective from 2024 onwards) were as follows:  Level I entities (full compliance with all AS): Entities that are listed or in the process of listing,

banks/Fis/insurance companies, or commercial/industrial/business entities with turnover (excluding other income) exceeding Rs. 50 crores in the immediately preceding accounting year, or borrowings (including

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 34

public deposits) exceeding Rs. 10 crores at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year, or holding/subsidiary of the above.  Level II entities (SMCs – Small and Medium-sized Companies/enterprises, with partial exemptions):

Commercial/industrial/business entities with turnover (excluding other income) exceeding Rs. 40 lakhs but not exceeding Rs. 50 crores, and/or borrowings exceeding Rs. 10 lakhs but not exceeding Rs. 10 crores (with certain thresholds).  Level III and Level IV (further relaxations for smaller entities). Given the facts: o Turnover (excluding other income) = Rs. 5 crores (which is more than Rs. 40 lakhs but less than Rs. 50 crores). o Borrowings = Rs. 1.5 crores (which is more than Rs. 10 lakhs but less than Rs. 10 crores). M/s X & Co. falls under Level II non-company entity (SME/SMC category) for the year ended 31.3.2022, as it meets the turnover and borrowings criteria for this level and is not covered under Level I. Exemptions/relaxations available to Level II entities (as per ICAI directive applicable at the relevant time): Level II entities are entitled to certain exemptions/relaxations in the application of Accounting Standards, primarily related to disclosure requirements and some recognition/measurement aspects. The key exemptions are:

1. Accounting Standards not applicable in their entirety (full exemption):

 AS 3 – Cash Flow Statements  AS 17 – Segment Reporting  AS 18 – Related Party Disclosures (in certain cases, partial or full relaxations)  AS 24 – Discontinuing Operations  AS 28 – Impairment of Assets (not applicable in entirety to SMCs in many contexts) Partial exemptions/relaxations in other standards (e.g.):  AS 15 – Employee Benefits (relaxations in actuarial valuations and disclosures for certain employee benefits).  AS 16 – Borrowing Costs (certain simplifications).  AS 19 – Leases (disclosure relaxations).  AS 20 – Earnings Per Share (not applicable if not listed).  AS 22 – Accounting for Taxes on Income (deferred tax relaxations in some cases).  AS 25 – Interim Financial Reporting (not mandatory).  AS 29 – Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets (certain disclosure relaxations). Note: The entity must comply fully with the remaining Accounting Standards (e.g., AS 1 Disclosure of Accounting Policies, AS 2 Valuation of Inventories, AS 4 Contingencies and Events Occurring after the Balance Sheet Date, AS 5 Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies, AS 9 Revenue Recognition, AS 10 Property, Plant and Equipment, AS 11 The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates, AS 12 Accounting for Government Grants, AS 13 Accounting for Investments, AS 14 Accounting for Amalgamations (where applicable), etc.). The management should:  Ensure full compliance with applicable AS for Level II entities.  Avail the above exemptions/relaxations where eligible.  Make appropriate disclosures in the notes to accounts stating that the financial statements have been

prepared in accordance with the Accounting Standards applicable to non-corporate entities at Level II, along with the fact of availing exemptions.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 35

 If preparing financial statements for statutory purposes (e.g., under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act),

ensure the audit report reflects compliance accordingly. These relaxations aim to reduce the compliance burden on smaller non-corporate entities like partnership firms while ensuring the financial statements still present a true and fair view. (Note: The ICAI revised the classification criteria significantly in November 2024, effective for accounting periods commencing on or after April 1, 2024, merging into Large vs. MSME categories with higher thresholds (turnover up to Rs. 250 crores and borrowings up to Rs. 50 crores for MSMEs), but for the year ended 31.3.2022, the pre- revision criteria apply as stated above.)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: First classify the entity into the correct level based on turnover and borrowings. Then mention exemptions available to that level. Time-Saving Tips: Remember Level I, II, III, IV classification limits in summary format. Focus on AS fully exempted for Level II entities.

Examiner’s Observation Students usually confuse corporate SMC rules with non-corporate entity levels. Proper classification is the key scoring area.

Question 6. Based upon criteria for rating of non-corporate entity, categorize the following as Level I, Level II and Level III Level IV entities for the purpose of compliance of Accounting Standards in India. (a) Rama Textiles whose turnover (excluding other income) exceeds ten crore but does not exceed rupees fifty crore in the immediately preceding accounting year. (b) Star Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees two crore but not in excess of rupees ten crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year. (c) Newman Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) less than rupees fifty lakh at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year (d) SS Finance is a financial institution carrying its business in India since last 10 years. (e) DD Finance, holding company of SS Finance. (Entity mentioned at Point (v) above) (f) Reliable Co-op Bank, a co-operative bank, carrying banking operations since last 15 years.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes | ICAI Fav. | RTP MAY 2024, High Chance]

Answer 6. (a) Level III Entity – Rama textiles, whose turnover (excluding other income) exceeds rupees ten crore but does not exceed rupees fifty crore in the immediately preceding accounting year. (b) Level III Entity – Star industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees two crore but not in excess of rupees ten crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year. (c) Level IV Entity – Newman Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) of less than rupees fifty lakhs at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year. (d) Level I Entity – SS is a financial institution carrying its business in India since last 10 years. (e) Level I Entity – DD finance, holding company of SS finance (Entity mentioned in point (d) above).

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 36

(f) Level I Entity – Reliable co-operative banks carrying on banking business for the last 15 years.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips First identify special entities (Bank, FI, Insurance Co., Holding/Subsidiary of Level I) → directly Level I. For remaining entities, check Turnover and Borrowings limits. Memorize key limits: Rs.50 Cr turnover & Rs.10 Cr borrowings for Level III; below Rs.50 lakh borrowings generally indicates Level IV.

Examiner’s Observation Students often forget that Financial Institutions and Banks are automatically Level I entities. Holding/Subsidiary relationship is frequently ignored. Many candidates classify solely on turnover and miss the special category conditions. Read the entity type first, then apply monetary limits.

Question 7. As per the revised scheme effective from accounting periods commencing on or after April 1, 2024, classify non-company entities for the purpose of applicability of Accounting Standards. Briefly explain the criteria for each category.

[6 Marks | 7 Minutes | ICAI Fav. | RTP September 2025, Very High Chance]

Answer 7. The revised scheme for applicability of Accounting Standards to Non- company entities shall come into effect in respect of accounting periods commencing on or after April 1, 2024, which is as under:

1. For the purpose of applicability of Accounting Standards, Non- company entities are classified into two

categories, viz., Micro, Small and Medium Sized Entities (MSMEs) and large entities.

2. Micro, Small and Medium Sized Entity (MSME) means, a non- company entity:

(i) Whose equity or debt securities are not listed or are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange, whether in India or outside India; (ii) Which is not a bank, financial institution or an insurance company; (iii) Whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed two hundred and fifty crore rupees in the immediately preceding accounting year; (iv) Which does not have borrowings in excess of fifty crore rupees at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and (v) Which is not a holding or subsidiary of an entity which is not a micro, small and medium-sized entity.

Explanation- For the purposes of this clause, a non-company entity shall qualify as a Micro, Small and Medium Sized entity, if the conditions mentioned therein are satisfied as at the end of the relevant accounting period. Large entity is a non-company entity that is not an MSME. The terms ‘Small and Medium Enterprise‛ and ‘SME‛ used in Accounting Standards shall be read as ‘Micro, Small and Medium size entity‛ and ‘MSME‛, respectively. Further, the terms Level II, Level III and Level IV entities used in Accounting Standards shall be read as ‘Micro, Small and Medium Sized Entity‛ and Level I entity shall be read as a ‘Large‛ entity.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Memorize the 5 MSME conditions using the sequence: Listing → Nature → Turnover → Borrowings → Holding/Subsidiary. Remember only two figures: Rs. 250 Cr turnover and Rs. 50 Cr borrowings. Write points in the exact ICAI order.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 37

Examiner’s Observation Students confuse this revised scheme with the old Level I–IV classification. Monetary limits are often quoted incorrectly. Many forget the holding/subsidiary condition. ICAI expects clear distinction between MSME and Large Entity.

Question 8. Virat Traders, an unlisted partnership firm, had a turnover of Rs. 249.99 crore and borrowings of Rs. 25.01 crore during the financial year 2023-24. It is not a bank, financial institution, or insurance company, and also not a subsidiary of any other entity. The firm wishes to avail MSME exemptions for FY 2024—25. Is it eligible?

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes | ICAI Fav. | RTP MAY 2026, High Chance]

Answer 8. Company qualifies as an MSME if following conditions are satisfied: (a) whose equity or debt securities are not listed or are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange, whether in India or outside India; (b) which is not a bank, financial institution or an insurance company; (c) whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed 250 crore rupees in the immediately preceding accounting year; (d) which does not have borrowings in excess of 50 crore rupees at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and (e) which is not a holding or subsidiary of an entity which is not a MSME entity. Yes, Virat Traders qualifies as an MSME since it meets all five criteria. Further, it has been assumed that Virat Traders is not newly qualifying as an MSME in FY 2024-25 because a non-company entity that newly qualifies as an MSME can avail exemptions only after it remains as MSME for two consecutive years. Until then, full AS compliance is required.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Use the 5-condition checklist from Question 7. Tick each condition one by one and conclude. Always mention the two consecutive years rule if the question hints at first-time qualification.

Examiner’s Observation Students generally conclude MSME status correctly but forget the newly qualifying MSME rule. Missing the final assumption can result in loss of presentation marks. Numerical limits should be compared carefully (Rs.249.99 Cr and Rs.25.01 Cr are intentionally close to thresholds).

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 38

PART B Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. The following Accounting Standard is not applicable to Non-Corporate Entities falling in Level II in its entirety. a) AS 10 b) AS 17 c) AS 2 d) AS 13

(Study material)

Ans: (b) AS 17 Reason  AS 17 deals with Segment Reporting, which is generally not applicable to non-corporate entities, especially those falling in Level II (such as small and medium-sized businesses).  AS 10 (Accounting for Fixed Assets), AS 2 (Valuation of Inventories), and AS 13 (Accounting for Investments) are applicable to non-corporate entities, though some exemptions or modifications may apply depending on the level of the entity. Thus, the correct answer is (b) AS 17.

Question 2. “Small and Medium Sized Company” (SMC) means, a company a) Which may be a bank, financial institution or an insurance company. b) Whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed rupees two-fifty crores in the immediately preceding accounting year; c) Whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed rupees fifty crores in the immediately preceding accounting year; d) Whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed rupees five hundred crores in the immediately preceding accounting year.

(Study material)

Ans: (b) whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed rupees two-fifty crores in the immediately preceding accounting year; Reason As per the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, a Small and Medium-sized Company (SMC) is defined based on certain quantitative thresholds and qualitative exclusions. One of the key criteria for classifying a company as an SMC is: Its turnover (excluding other income) should not exceed Rs.250 crores in the immediately preceding accounting year.
