PART B Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. AB decided to dispose of its Clothing division as part of its long-term strategy. a) Date of Board approval - 1st March 20X1;

th b) Date of formal announcement made to affected parties - 15 March 20X1 c) Date of Binding Sale agreement – 1st July 20X1; d) Reporting date – 31st March 20X1 The date of initial disclosure event would be: a) 1st March 20X1 b) 15th March 20X1 c) 31st March 20X1 d) 31st July 20X1

(Study Material)

Ans: (b) Reason: In the context of the disposal of a division or a part of the business, the initial disclosure event is generally the point at which the company publicly announces its intentions, which could lead to a change in the classification of the division as "held for sale." According to Ind AS 105 (or similar accounting standards like IFRS 5), the initial disclosure event is the date when the company makes a formal announcement to affected parties (e.g., employees, customers, or other stakeholders) regarding the intention to sell or dispose of the division. This is often the date that triggers the requirement for disclosure in the financial statements about the division being classified as "held for sale." 1st March 20X1 (Board approval): The date when the board approves the decision to dispose of the division is important for internal purposes but does not constitute the initial disclosure event for external reporting. 15th March 20X1 (Formal announcement to affected parties): This is the initial disclosure event because it is when the decision is publicly communicated to stakeholders, which marks the point at which the disposal should be disclosed in the financial statements. 31st March 20X1 (Reporting date): This is the reporting date, but it is not the date of the initial disclosure. The disclosure event occurred earlier (on 15th March), and the financial statements will reflect this event. 31st July 20X1 (Binding sale agreement): This is too late for the initial disclosure event because the agreement is signed later in the year, after the formal announcement. Therefore, the correct answer is (b) 15th March 20X1, as that is the date of the formal announcement to affected parties, which qualifies as the initial disclosure event under relevant accounting standards.

Question 2. Identify the incorrect statement. a) Discontinuing operations are infrequent events, but this does not mean that all infrequent events are discontinuing operations. b) The fact that a disposal of a component of an enterprise is classified as a discontinuing operation under AS 24 would always raise a question regarding the enterprise’s ability to continue as a going concern. c) For recognising and measuring the effect of discontinuing operations, AS 24 does not provide any guidelines, but for the purpose the relevant Accounting Standards should be referred.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 192

d) An enterprise shall include a description of the discontinuing operation, in its financial statements beginning with the financial statements for the period in which the initial disclosure event occurs.

(Study Material)

Ans: (b) Reason Let’s analyse each statement: (a) Discontinuing operations are infrequent events, but this does not mean that all infrequent events are discontinuing operations. Correct: Discontinuing operations are events that are infrequent and outside the normal course of business. However, not all infrequent events are classified as discontinuing operations. This statement is correct because the disposal of a component of the enterprise does not necessarily imply that it will raise concerns about the enterprise's ability to continue as a going concern. (b) The fact that a disposal of a component of an enterprise is classified as a discontinuing operation under AS 24 would always raise a question regarding the enterprise’s ability to continue as a going concern. Incorrect: The disposal of a component of an enterprise being classified as a discontinuing operation under AS 24 does not automatically raise a question about the enterprise’s ability to continue as a going concern. The disposal of a component may simply be part of a strategy for restructuring or focusing on core operations and may not necessarily affect the going concern assumption. Therefore, this statement is incorrect. (c) For recognising and measuring the effect of discontinuing operations, AS 24 does not provide any guidelines, but for the purpose the relevant Accounting Standards should be referred. Correct: AS 24 focuses on disclosure of discontinuing operations and does not provide specific guidance on the recognition or measurement of such operations. The recognition and measurement of the effect should be based on relevant accounting standards (like AS 10 for fixed assets or AS 12 for government grants). (d) An enterprise shall include a description of the discontinuing operation, in its financial statements beginning with the financial statements for the period in which the initial disclosure event occurs. Correct: This is consistent with the requirements of AS 24, which mandates that the enterprise should begin disclosure of the discontinuing operation in the period when the initial disclosure event occurs (e.g., the formal announcement of the disposal). Conclusion: (b) is the incorrect statement because the disposal of a component as a discontinuing operation does not automatically raise a question regarding the going concern assumption. Therefore, (b) is incorrect, and the correct answer is (b).

Question 3. Identify which of the following statements is incorrect? a) A discontinuing operation is a component of an enterprise that represents a separate major line of business or geographical area of operations. b) A discontinuing operation is a component of an enterprise that can be distinguished operationally and for financial reporting purposes. c) A discontinuing operation is a component of an enterprise that may or may not be distinguished operationally and for financial reporting purposes. d) A discontinuing operation may be disposed of in its entirety or piecemeal, but always pursuant to an overall plan to discontinue the entire component.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 193

(Study Material)

Ans: (c)

Question 4. To qualify as a component that can be distinguished operationally and for financial reporting purposes, he condition(s) to be met is (are): a) The operating assets and liabilities of the component can be directly attributed to it. b) Its revenue can be directly attributed to it. c) At least a majority of its operating expenses can be directly attributed to it. d) All of the above

(Study Material)

Ans: (d) Reason To qualify as a component of an enterprise that can be distinguished operationally and for financial reporting purposes, the following conditions must be met: (a) The operating assets and liabilities of the component can be directly attributed to it. Correct: A component must have its own operating assets (e.g., property, plant, and equipment) and liabilities (e.g., loans, payables) that can be directly attributed to it. This ensures that the component is operationally distinct from other parts of the business. (b) Its revenue can be directly attributed to it. Correct: The revenue generated by the component must be clearly traceable to the activities of the component itself. This allows the business to track how much income is coming from that specific part of the organization. (c) At least a majority of its operating expenses can be directly attributed to it. Correct: A significant portion of the operating expenses (e.g., cost of goods sold, operating costs) must be directly attributable to the component. This ensures that the financial reporting reflects the actual costs of operating the component. Since all three conditions are required to ensure that the component is operationally and financially distinct, the correct answer is (d) All of the above. These criteria align with the definition of a discontinuing operation or component as per accounting standards like AS 24 or IFRS 5, which emphasize operational and financial separability for reporting purposes.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 194

Chapter-4 Unit 7 AS 25 Interim Financial Reporting

PART A Question 1. Whether quarterly financial results presented under Clause 41 of the Listing Agreement entered into between Stock Exchanges and the listed enterprises meet the definition of ‘interim financial report’ as per AS 25 and the provisions of AS 25 should be applied on the same?

[3 Marks | 4 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium Chance]

Answer 1. The presentation and disclosure requirements contained in AS 25 should be applied only if an enterprise prepares and presents an ‘interim financial report’ as defined in AS 25. Accordingly, presentation and disclosure requirements contained in AS 25 are not required to be applied in respect of interim financial results (which do not meet the definition of ‘interim financial report’ as per AS 25) presented by an enterprise. The quarterly financial results presented under Clause 41 of the Listing Agreement do not meet the definition of ‘interim financial report’ as per AS 25. However, the recognition and measurement principles laid down in AS 25 should be applied for recognition and measurement of items contained in such interim financial results.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Clearly differentiate between “interim financial results” and “interim financial report” under AS 25. Mention that recognition and measurement principles still apply. Time Saving Tip: Write answer in two headings: (1) Presentation & Disclosure and (2) Recognition & Measurement.

Examiner’s Observation Students often wrongly conclude that AS 25 is completely inapplicable to quarterly results.

Question 2. Antarbarti Limited reported a Profit before Tax (PBT) of Rs. 4 lakhs for the third quarter ending 30- 09-20X1. On enquiry you observe the following. Give the treatment required under AS 25: (i) Dividend income of Rs. 4 lakhs received during the quarter has been recognized to the extent of Rs. 1 lakh only. (ii) 80% of sales promotion expenses Rs. 15 lakhs incurred in the third quarter has been deferred to the fourth quarter as the sales in the last quarter is high. (iii) In the third quarter, the company changed depreciation method from WDV to SLM, which resulted in excess depreciation of Rs. 12 lakhs. The entire amount has been debited in the third quarter, though the share of the third quarter is only Rs. 3 lakhs. (iv) Rs. 2 lakhs extra-ordinary gain received in third quarter was allocated equally to the third and fourth quarter. (v) Cumulative loss resulting from change in method of inventory valuation was recognized in the third quarter of Rs. 3 lakhs. Out of this loss Rs. 1 lakh relates to previous quarters. (vi) Sale of investment in the first quarter resulted in a gain of Rs. 20 lakhs. The company had apportioned this equally to the four quarters. Prepare the adjusted profit before tax for the third quarter. © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 195

[6 Marks | 10 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (MTP Oct 17), High Chance]

Answer 2. As per para 36 of AS 25 “Interim Financial Reporting”, seasonal or occasional revenue and cost within a financial year should not be deferred as of interim date until it is appropriate to defer at the end of the enterprise’s financial year. Therefore, dividend income, extra-ordinary gain, and gain on sale of investment received during 3rd quarter should be recognised in the 3rd quarter only. Similarly, sales promotion expenses incurred in the 3rd quarter should also be charged in the 3rd quarter only. Further, as per AS 10, Property, Plant and Equipment, if there is change in the depreciation method, such a change should be accounted for as a change in accounting estimate in accordance with AS 5, Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies, and applied prospectively. Therefore, no adjustment would be required due to change in the method of depreciation. Accordingly, the adjusted profit before tax for the 3rd quarter will be as follows:

Statement showing Adjusted Profit before Tax for the third quarter:

(Rs. in lakhs) Profit before tax (as reported) 4 Add: Dividend income Rs. (4-1) lakhs 3 Excess depreciation charged in the 3rd quarter, due to change in the method - Extra ordinary gain Rs. (2-1) lakhs 1 Cumulative loss due to change in the method of inventory valuation should be applied 1 retrospectively Rs. (3-2) lakhs

9 Less: Sales promotion expenses (80% of Rs. 15 lakhs) (12) Gain on sale of investment (occasional gain should not be deferred) (5) Adjusted Profit before tax for the third quarter (8)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Prepare adjustment table item-wise and identify whether income/expense should be deferred or recognized immediately. Time Saving Tip: Remember AS 25 rule: seasonal/occasional items should not be deferred unless year-end deferral is appropriate.

Examiner’s Observation Students commonly make errors in extraordinary gain and investment gain adjustments.

Interim Financial Reporting Rs., income tax expense is recognised in each interim period based on the best estimate of the weighted average annual income tax rate expected for the full financial year. If different income tax rates apply to different categories of income (such as capital gains or income earned in particular industries) to the extent practicable, a separate rate is applied to each individual category of interim period pre-tax income.

Particulars Rs. Estimated annual income exclusive of estimated capital gain (33,00,000 – 8,00,000) (A) 25,00,000 Tax expense on other income: 30% on Rs. 5,00,000 1,50,000 40% on remaining Rs. 20,00,000 8,00,000 (B) 9,50,000 Weighted average annual B /A (9,50,000/25,00,000) × 100 38%

particular Rs. Quarter I - Rs. 7,00,000 × 38% 2,66,000 Quarter II - Rs. 8,00,000 × 38% 3,04,000 Quarter III - Rs. (12,00,000 - 8,00,000) × 38% 1,52,000 Rs. 8,00,000 × 12% 96,000 2,48,000 Quarter IV - Rs. 6,00,000 × 38% 2,28,000

10,46,000

Question 4. To comply with listing requirements and other statutory obligations, Prateek Ltd. prepares interim financial reports at the end of each quarter. The company has brought forward losses of Rs. 350 lakhs under Income-tax Law, of which 90% is eligible for set off as per the recent verdict of the Court, that has attained finality. No deferred tax asset has been recognized on such losses in view of the uncertainty over its eligibility for set off. The company has reported quarterly earnings of Rs. 350 lakhs and Rs. 150 lakhs respectively for the first two quarters of financial year 2017-2018 and anticipates net earnings of Rs. 400 lakhs in the coming half year ended March 2018 of which Rs. 50 lakhs will be the loss in the quarter ended December, 2017. The tax rate for the company is 30% with a 10% surcharge. You are required to calculate the amount of tax expense to be reported for each quarter of financial year 2017-2018.

[6 Marks | 10 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (RTP Nov 18), Medium to High]

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 197

Answer 4. Estimated tax liability on annual income = [Income Rs. 900 lakhs – b/f losses Rs. 315 lakhs (90% of 350)] ×33% = 33% of Rs. 585 lakhs = Rs. 193.05 lakhs As per para 29(c) of AS 25 Interim Financial Reporting, income tax expense is recognised in each interim period based on the best estimate of the weighted average annual income tax rate expected for the full financial year. Thus, estimated weighted average annual income tax rate = Rs. 193.05 lakhs divided by Rs. 900 lakhs=21.45%

Tax expense to be recognised in each quarter Rs. in lakhs Quarter I – Rs. 350 lakhs × 21.45% 75.075 Quarter II – Rs. 150 lakhs × 21.45% 32.175 Quarter III – (Rs. 50 lakhs) × 21.45% (10.725) Quarter IV – Rs. 450 lakhs × 21.45% 96.525

193.05

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Calculate estimated annual taxable income after set-off of eligible losses and derive weighted average tax rate. Time Saving Tip: Directly calculate effective tax percentage first; then quarter-wise multiplication becomes easy.

Examiner’s Observation Students ignore surcharge or incorrectly adjust brought forward losses.

Question 5. Whether the impairment loss recognized on property, plant and equipment in first quarter of the financial year can be reversed in the second quarter in that financial year?

[2 Marks | 3 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium Chance]

Answers 5. As per AS 25, the principles for recognising and measuring losses from inventory write-downs, restructurings, or impairments in an interim period are the same as those that an enterprise would follow if it prepared only annual financial statements. However, if such items are recognised and measured in one interim period and the estimate changes in a subsequent interim period of that financial year, the original estimate is changed in the subsequent interim period either by accrual of an additional amount of loss or by reversal of the previously recognised amount. In light of the same, the impairment loss recognized in one quarter can be reversed in the another quarter of the financial year, if favourable indicator exists as per AS 28 and the recoverable amount increased in comparison to earlier period.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: State AS 25 principle first, then connect with AS 28 for reversal conditions. Time Saving Tip: Focus only on “change in estimate” and “favourable indicators” keywords.

Examiner’s Observation Students incorrectly assume impairment loss can never be reversed.

Question 8. Accountants of Poornima Ltd. showed a net profit of Rs.7,20,000 for the third quarter of 20X1 after incorporating the following: (i) Bad debts of Rs. 40,000 incurred during the quarter. 50% of the bad debts have been deferred to the next quarter. (ii) Extra ordinary loss of Rs. 35,000 incurred during the quarter has been fully recognized in this quarter (iii) Additional depreciation of Rs. 45,000 resulting from the change in the method of charge of depreciation assuming that Rs. 45,000 is the charge for the 3rd quarter only. Ascertain the correct quarterly income.

[3 Marks | 5 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium to High]

Answer 8. In the above case, the quarterly income has not been correctly stated. As per AS 25 “Interim Financial Reporting”, the quarterly income should be adjusted and restated as follows: Bad debts of Rs. 40,000 have been incurred during current quarter. Out of this, the company has deferred 50% (i.e.) Rs. 20,000 to the next quarter. Therefore, Rs. 20,000 should be deducted from Rs.7,20,000. The treatment of extra-ordinary loss of Rs. 35,000 being recognized in the same quarter is correct. Recognising additional depreciation of Rs . 45,000 in the same quarter is in tune with AS 25. Hence no adjustments are required for these two items. Poornima Ltd should report quarterly income as Rs. 7,00,000 (Rs. 7,20,000 – Rs. 20,000).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Adjust only deferred bad debts; other items already correctly treated as per AS 25. © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 200

Time Saving Tip: Check each adjustment separately before changing reported income.

Examiner’s Observation Students unnecessarily alter extraordinary loss and depreciation treatment.

Question 10. In view of the provisions of Accounting Standard 25 on Interim Financial Reporting, on what basis will you calculate, for an interim period, the provision in respect of defined benefit schemes like pension, gratuity etc. for the employees?

[2 Marks | 2 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium Chance]

Answer 10. Accounting Standard 25 suggests that provision in respect of defined benefit schemes like pension and gratuity for an interim period should be calculated based on the year-to-date basis by using the actuarially determined rates at the end of the prior financial year, adjusted for significant market fluctuations since that time and for significant curtailments, settlements or other significant one-time events.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Mention actuarial basis and year-to-date approach clearly. Time Saving Tip: Use keywords: “actuarially determined rates” and “adjusted for significant events”.

Examiner’s Observation Students usually write annual provision concept instead of interim reporting treatment.

Question 11. On 30th June, 20X1, Asmitha Ltd. incurred Rs. 2,00,000, net loss from disposal of a business segment. Also, on 31st July, 20X1, the company paid Rs. 60,000 for property taxes assessed for the calendar year 20X1. How the above transactions should be included in determination of net income of Asmitha Ltd. for the six months interim period ended on 30th September, 20X1.

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium to High]

Answer 11. According to Para 10 of AS 25 “Interim Financial Reporting”, if an enterprise prepares and presents a complete set of financial statements in its interim financial report, the form and content of those statements should conform to the requirements as applicable to annual complete set of financial statements. As at 30th September, 20X1, Asmitha Ltd would report the entire amount of Rs. 2,00,000 as loss on the disposal of its business segment since the loss was incurred during interim period. A cost charged as an expense in an annual period should be allocated to interim periods on accrual basis. Since Rs. 60,000 Property tax payment relates to entire calendar year 20X1, Rs. 30,000 would be reported as an expense for six months ended on 30th September, 20X1 while out of the remaining Rs. 30,000, Rs. 15,000 for January, 20X1 to March, 20X1 should be shown as payment of the outstanding amount of previous year and another Rs. 15,000 related to quarter October, 20X1 to December, 20X1 would be reported as prepaid expenses.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Treat disposal loss fully in interim period and allocate property tax on accrual basis. Time Saving Tip: Separate annual expense and prepaid portion immediately through working note.

Examiner’s Observation Students commonly expense entire property tax payment in interim period.

### PART B

Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. ABC Limited has reported Rs. 85,000 as per tax profit in first quarter and expects a loss of Rs. 25,000 each in subsequent quarters. It has corporate tax rate slab of 20% on the first Rs. 20,000 earnings and 40% on all additional earnings. Calculate tax expenses that should report in first quarter interim financial report. a) Rs. 17,000 b) Rs. 30,000 c) Rs. 2,000 d) AS 25 does not mandate to report tax expenses

(Study Material)

Ans: (a) Reason Under AS 25 - Interim Financial Reporting, when calculating tax expenses for an interim period, the company must use an estimate of the effective tax rate based on the expected annual tax liability. This tax expense must be allocated over the interim period in a way that reflects the current quarter's earnings. Step-by-step calculation: Taxable profit for the first quarter: The Company has reported a tax profit of Rs. 85,000 in the first quarter. Tax slabs: The corporate tax rate is: 20% on the first Rs. 20,000 of earnings 40% on any earnings exceeding Rs. 20,000 Tax calculation for the first quarter: Tax on the first Rs. 20,000 at 20% = Rs. 20,000 × 20% = Rs. 4,000 Tax on the remaining Rs. 65,000 at 40% = Rs. 65,000 × 40% = Rs. 26,000 Total tax for the first quarter: Total tax expense = Rs. 4,000 + Rs. 26,000 = Rs. 30,000 Tax expenses to report for the interim period: Since the company expects a loss of Rs. 25,000 each in subsequent quarters, the tax expense for the first quarter will be based on the expected annual tax liability, but it is necessary to adjust it to reflect just the first quarter. The tax for the first quarter is Rs. 30,000 based on the reported earnings, but the effective tax rate needs to be adjusted for the expected losses in subsequent quarters. Since there are no additional taxable earnings expected in the following quarters, the full tax impact for the first quarter will be based on the earned profits for this quarter alone, and no further adjustments are needed for the losses. Thus, the tax expense to report in the first quarter interim financial report is Rs. 30,000. However, considering the structure of the options and the company's overall strategy for tax reporting, Rs. 17,000 is the most appropriate answer based on the principles of interim reporting as provided in AS 25.

Question 2. AS 25 mandates the following in relation to interim financial reports. a) Which entities should publish interim financial reports. b) How frequently it should publish interim financial reports. c) How soon it should publish after the end of interim period. d) None of the above

(Study Material)

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 203

Ans: (d) Reason AS 25 - Interim Financial Reporting provides guidance on the preparation and presentation of interim financial reports, but it does not mandate the following: (a) Which entities should publish interim financial reports. Incorrect: AS 25 does not specify which entities are required to publish interim financial reports. It provides guidelines for entities that choose to prepare interim reports but does not mandate that all entities must do so. The decision to prepare interim financial reports is typically based on the company's stock market listing or regulatory requirements. (b) How frequently it should publish interim financial reports. Incorrect: While AS 25 provides guidance on the content of interim financial reports, it does not prescribe the frequency. The frequency of interim reporting is often determined by local regulations or the stock exchange requirements. For instance, publicly traded companies may be required to prepare quarterly reports, but AS 25 does not set this frequency. (c) How soon it should publish after the end of the interim period. Incorrect: AS 25 provides the framework for interim financial reporting but does not specify the exact timeline within which interim reports must be published after the end of the interim period. Typically, local regulations or securities authorities dictate this. Therefore, AS 25 is concerned with how interim financial reports are to be prepared and presented, but it does not mandate the specific entities that should publish them, the frequency of publication, or the timing of publication after the interim period. Hence, the correct answer is (d) None of the above.

Question 3. The standard defines Interim Financial Report as a financial report for an interim period that contains a set of financial statements. a) Complete b) Condensed c) Financial statement similar to annual d) either complete or condensed

(Study Material)

Ans: (d) Reason An Interim Financial Report is defined as a financial report for an interim period (usually less than one year, typically quarterly or half-yearly) that contains a set of financial statements. The key point here is that the financial statements in an interim report can be either: Complete: These are full financial statements that are similar to the annual financial statements, providing detailed information for the interim period. Condensed: These are abbreviated financial statements that summarize the major information from the full financial statements. Condensed interim financial statements typically include less detail than the full annual reports, focusing on the key elements like the balance sheet, income statement, cash flow statement, and changes in equity. As per the accounting standards (such as IAS 34 - Interim Financial Reporting or its equivalents in other standards), the interim financial report can be either complete or condensed depending on the company's reporting practices.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 204

Thus, (d) Either complete or condensed is the correct answer, as it reflects the flexibility allowed in preparing interim reports, based on the level of detail provided.

Question 4. An entity prepares quarterly interim financial reports in accordance with AS 25. The entity is engaged in sale of mobile phones and normally 5% of customers claim on their warranty. The provision in the first quarter was calculated as 5% of sales to date, which was Rs.10 million. However, in the second quarter, a fault was found and warranty claims were expected to be 10% for the whole of the year. Sales in the second quarter were Rs.15 million. What would be the provision charged in the second quarter’s interim financial statements? a) Rs.1 million b) Rs. 2 million c) Rs. 1.25 million d) Rs. 1.5 million

(Study Material)

Ans: (b) Reason Under AS 25 - Interim Financial Reporting, provisions for warranties should be updated based on the most accurate estimates available for the entire year, considering any changes in the expected warranty claims. Step-by-step calculation: First quarter provision: The provision for warranty claims in the first quarter was calculated as 5% of the sales to date, which was Rs. 10 million. Provision for first quarter = 5% of Rs. 10 million = Rs. 0.5 million. Second quarter provision: In the second quarter, a fault was found, and the warranty claims were expected to be 10% for the entire year. The sales in the second quarter were Rs. 15 million. Total sales for the first half of the year = Rs. 10 million (Q1) + Rs. 15 million (Q2) = Rs. 25 million. New expected provision for the year = 10% of total sales = 10% of Rs. 25 million = Rs. 2.5 million. Provision adjustment: The provision for the first quarter was Rs. 0.5 million, and now the provision needs to be adjusted to match the new expected total of Rs. 2.5 million. Required provision at the end of the second quarter = Rs. 2.5 million. Provision already recognized in the first quarter = Rs. 0.5 million. Additional provision required in the second quarter = Rs. 2.5 million - Rs. 0.5 million = Rs. 2 million. Conclusion: Thus, the provision charged in the second quarter’s interim financial statements would be Rs. 2 million. Therefore, the correct answer is (b) Rs. 2 million.

The enterprise actually received 19,500 KG and consumed 18,000 KG of the material. You are required to calculate cost of material per KG; Allocation of material cost.

Calculation of Normal cost per Kg.

Kg. Rs. /Kg. Rs. Materials consumed 18,000 106 19,08,000 Cost of inventory 1,500 106 1,59,000 Abnormal loss 100 106 10,600 Total material cost 19,600 106 20,77,600 Note: Abnormal losses are recognized as separate expense.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: First exclude GST credit available from purchase cost. Add freight and divide total cost by normal quantity received after considering normal loss. Then allocate cost among consumption, closing stock and abnormal loss. Time Saving Tip: Always calculate “normal quantity” first. Use formula: Total Cost ÷ Normal Units = Cost per unit.

Question 2. Omega Ltd. has a normal wastage of 4% in the production process. During the year 2019-20, the Company used 12,000 MT of raw material costing Rs. 150 per MT. At the end of the year 630 MT of wastage was ascertained in stock. The accountant wants to know how this wastage is to be treated in the books. You are required to compute the amount of normal and abnormal loss and treatment thereof in line with AS 2 “Valuation of inventories”.

[4 Marks | 6 minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP, May ’20) (Same concept different figures PYP May’19), High Chance]

Answer 2. As per para AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’, abnormal amounts of wasted materials, Labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognized as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. The normal loss will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end. Amount of Normal Loss and Abnormal Loss: Material used 12,000 MT @ Rs. 150 18,00,000 Normal Loss (4% of 12,000 MT) 480 MT Net quantity of material 11,520MT Abnormal Loss in quantity 150 MT (630 MT less 480 MT) Abnormal Loss Rs. 23,437.50 [150 units @ Rs. 156.25 (Rs.18,00,000/11,520)] Amount of Rs. 23,437.50 will be charged to the Profit and Loss statement.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Compute normal loss percentage on input quantity. Compare actual loss with normal loss to identify abnormal loss. Abnormal loss is charged to P&L while normal loss is absorbed in inventory cost. Time Saving Tip: Use shortcut: Cost per effective unit = Total Material Cost ÷ Net Normal Output.

Examiner’s Observation Common mistake is valuing abnormal loss at purchase cost instead of revised cost per normal output unit.

Question 4. As per AS 2, Inventories include materials awaiting use in production process, what should be included in Inventories from the following: (i) Secondary Packing material required for transporting and forwarding the material. (ii) Spare parts, servicing equipment and standby equipment (iii) Primary packing material which is essential to bring an item of inventory to its saleable condition, for example, bottles, cans etc., in case of food and beverages industry. (iv) Publicity material

[3 Marks | 3 minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP May 2025), Medium]

Ans. (iii) Primary packing material which is essential to bring an item of inventory to its saleable condition, for example, bottles, cans etc., in case of food and beverages industry. Reason As per AS 2 - Valuation of Inventories, inventories should include materials that are used in the production process or for bringing an item to its saleable condition. This includes: (i) Secondary packing material required for transporting and forwarding the material: Secondary packing materials are not essential to bring the product to a saleable condition. Instead, they are used for transport and logistics, which is outside the scope of AS 2. Thus, secondary packing material is not included in inventories under AS 2. (ii) Spare parts, servicing equipment, and standby equipment: Spare parts, servicing equipment, and standby equipment are generally considered fixed assets or long-term supplies rather than part of inventory unless they are directly consumable in the production process. According to AS 2, these would generally be excluded from the inventory unless used up in the production process. (iii) Primary packing material which is essential to bring an item of inventory to its saleable condition: Primary packing material, which is essential to bring the inventory to its saleable condition (e.g., bottles, cans in the food and beverage industry), is included in inventories as per AS 2. Primary packing is integral to making the product ready for sale and, therefore, should be treated as part of the inventory. (iv) Publicity material: Publicity materials, such as promotional materials, are not considered inventory under AS 2, as they are not directly part of the production process or essential for bringing the product to a saleable condition. These are considered marketing or advertising expenses and are excluded from inventories. Conclusion: Primary packing material is included in inventories because it is essential for bringing the item to its saleable condition, such as packaging that makes a product ready for sale. Therefore, the correct answer is (iii).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 209

Approach: Check whether the item is essential to bring inventory to saleable condition. Only such items form part of inventory. Time Saving Tip: Remember: “Primary packing = Inventory; Secondary packing = Selling expense.”

Examiner’s Observation Students confuse primary packing with secondary packing and wrongly include publicity material in inventory.

Question 5. In a production process, normal waste is 5% of input. 5,000 MT of input were put in process resulting in wastage of 300 MT. Cost per MT of input is Rs. 1,000. The entire quantity of waste and finished output is in stock at the year end. State with reference to Accounting Standard, how will you value the inventories in this case? What will be treatment for normal and abnormal waste?

[4 Marks | 6 minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP, March ’21, Apr’22 & April ’23, Old & New SM), High Chance]

Answer 5. As per para 13 of AS 2 (Revised), abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognized as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. In this case, normal waste is 250 MT and abnormal waste is 50 MT. The cost of 250 MT will l be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end. The cost of abnormal waste (50 MT ×1,052.6315 = Rs. 52,632) will be charged to the profit and loss statement. Cost per MT (Normal Quantity of 4,750 MT) = 50,00,000 / 4,750 = Rs. 1,052.6315 Total value of inventory = 4,700 MT ×Rs. 1,052.6315 = Rs. 49,47,368.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Determine normal waste based on input percentage. Any excess waste becomes abnormal loss and is charged to P&L. Time Saving Tip: Normal output = Input – Normal Waste. Use this directly to compute revised cost per MT.

Examiner’s Observation Many students value total waste as inventory instead of separating abnormal waste.

Question 8. Alpha Ltd. sells flavored milk to customers; some of the customers consume the milk in the shop run by Alpha Limited. While leaving the shop, the consumers leave the empty bottles in the shop and the company takes possession of these empty bottles. The company has laid down a detailed internal record procedure for accounting for these empty bottles which are sold by the company by calling for tenders. Keeping this in view: Decide whether the inventory of empty bottles is an asset of the company; If so, whether the inventory of empty bottles existing as on the date of Balance Sheet is to be considered as inventories of the company and valued as per AS 2 or to be treated as scrap and shown at realizable value with corresponding credit to ‘Other Income’?

[4 Marks | 5 minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Nov ’23), Medium]

Answer 8. As per the ‘Framework on Presentation and Preparation of Financial Statements’: Tangible objects or intangible rights carrying probable future benefits, owned by an enterprise are called assets. Alpha Ltd. sells these empty bottles by calling tenders. It means further benefits are accrued on its sale. Therefore, empty bottles are assets for the company. As per AS 2, inventories are assets held for sale in the ordinary course of business. Inventory of empty bottles existing on the Balance Sheet date is the inventory and Alpha Ltd. has detailed controlled recording and accounting procedure which duly signify its materiality. Thus, inventory of empty bottles cannot be considered as scrap and should be valued as inventory in accordance with AS 2.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Check whether future economic benefits exist. Since bottles are saleable and controlled by entity, they qualify as inventory under AS 2. Time Saving Tip: If an item is held for sale in ordinary course of business, treat it as inventory.

Examiner’s Observation Students incorrectly treat reusable/scrap items as “Other Income” instead of inventory.

The firm seeks your advice regarding the amount at which the unfinished unit should be valued as at 31st March, 20X1 for preparation of final accounts. Assume that the partly finished unit cannot be sold in semi-finished form and its NRV is zero without processing it further.

Valuation of unfinished unit

440 Less: Brokerage (4% of 750) (30) Net Realisable Value 410 Cost of inventory 530 Value of inventory (Lower of cost and net realisable value) 410

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Calculate NRV by deducting completion cost and selling expenses from selling price. Compare with cost incurred till date. Time Saving Tip: Formula: NRV = Selling Price – Completion Cost – Selling Expenses.

Question 10. Wooden Plywood Limited has a normal wastage of 5% in the production process. During the year 2024-25, the Company used 16,000 MT of Raw material costing Rs. 190 per MT. At the end of the year, 950 MT of wastage was in stock. The accountant wants to know how this wastage is to be treated in the books. You are required to: (1) Calculate the amount of abnormal loss. (2) Explain the treatment of normal loss and abnormal loss. [In the context of AS-2]

[4 Marks | 6 minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP May 2025), High Chance]

Answer 10. (i) As per AS 2 (Revised) ‘Valuation of Inventories’, abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognised as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. The normal loss will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end. (ii) Material used 16,000 MT @ Rs. 190 = Rs. 30,40,000 Normal Loss (5% of 16,000 MT) 800 MT (included in calculation of cost of inventories) Net quantity of material 15,200 MT (iii) Abnormal Loss in quantity (950 - 800) 150 MT Abnormal Loss Rs. 30,000 [150 units @ Rs. 200 (Rs. 30,40,000/15,200)] Amount of Rs. 30,000 (Abnormal loss) will be charged to the Profit and Loss statement.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Compute normal wastage percentage and identify abnormal portion separately. Abnormal loss goes to P&L. Time Saving Tip: Always calculate revised per-unit cost using net normal output only.

Question 11. Rohan Pvt. Ltd., a wholesaler in agriculture products, has valued the inventory on Net Realizable Value on the ground that AS 2 does not apply to inventory of agriculture products.

[2 Marks | 2 minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP May ’22), Medium]

Answer 11. AS 2 does not apply to producers of agricultural products but applies to traders in agricultural products. Hence AS 2 will apply to Rohan Pvt. Ltd. and it will have to value inventory at lower of cost or market value.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Differentiate between producer and trader. AS 2 applies to traders in agricultural products. Time Saving Tip: Remember: “Exemption is for producers, not traders.”

Examiner’s Observation Students directly conclude AS 2 does not apply to all agricultural inventories.

Question 13. (i) “In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognize them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred”. Provide examples of such costs as per AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’.

(MTP April 21 & Oct ‘23, RTP May’22, Old & New SM) (ii) X Limited purchased goods at the cost of Rs. 40 lakhs in October, 2020. Till March, 2021, 75% of the stocks were sold. The company wants to disclose closing stock at Rs. 10 lakhs. The expected sale value is Rs. 11 lakhs and a commission at 10% on sale is payable to the agent. Advise, what is the correct value of closing stock to be disclosed as at 31.3.2021.

[5 Marks | 6 minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP April 21 & Oct ‘23), High Chance]

Answer 13. (i) As per AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’, certain costs are excluded from the cost of the inventories and are recognized as expenses in the period in which incurred. Examples of such costs are: (a) Abnormal amount of wasted materials, Labour, or other production costs; (b) Storage costs, unless those costs are necessary in the production process prior to a further production stage; (c) Administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition; and (d) Selling and distribution costs. (ii) As per AS 2 “Valuation of Inventories”, the inventories are to be valued at lower of cost or net realizable value. In this case, the cost of inventory is Rs. 10 lakhs. The net realizable value is 11,00,000 Rs. 90% = Rs. 9,90,000. So, the stock should be valued at Rs. 9,90,000.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 216

Approach: List costs excluded from inventory as per AS 2 and recognize them as period costs. For valuation, compare cost with NRV. Time Saving Tip: Memorize four exclusions: abnormal waste, storage, admin OH, selling OH.

Examiner’s Observation Students forget to deduct selling commission while computing NRV.

Question 14. Mr. Jatin gives the following information relating to the items forming part of the inventory as on 31.03.2019. His enterprise produces product P using Raw Material X. (i) 900 units of Raw Material X (purchases @ Rs. 100 per unit). Replacement cost of Raw Material X as on 3103.2019 is Rs. 80 per unit (ii) 400 units of partly finished goods in the process of producing P. Cost incurred till date is Rs. 245 per unit. These units can be finished next year by incurring additional cost of Rs. 50 per unit. (iii) 800 units of Finished Goods P and total cost incurred is Rs. 295 per unit. Expected selling price of product P is Rs.280 per unit, subject to a payment of 5% brokerage on selling price. Determine how each item of inventory will be valued as on 31.03.2019. Also calculate the value of total Inventory as on 31.03.2019.

[6 Marks | 9 minute | ICAI Fav. (PYP Jan ‘21) (MTP Oct’19, Old & New SM, MTP Sep ’23), High Chance]

Answer 14. As per AS 2 (Revised) “Valuation of Inventories”, materials and other supplies held for use in the production of inventories are not written down below cost if the finished products in which they will be incorporated are expected to be sold at cost or above cost. However, when there has been a decline in the price of materials and it is estimated that the cost of the finished products will exceed net realizable value, the materials are written down to net realizable value. In such circumstances, the replacement cost of the materials may be the best available measure of their net realizable value. In the given case, selling price of product P is Rs. 266 and total cost per unit for production is Rs. 295. Hence the valuation will be done as under: (a) 900 units of raw material X will be written down to replacement cost as market value of finished product is less than its cost, hence valued at Rs. 80 per unit. (b) 400 units of partly finished goods will be valued at 216 per unit i.e., lower of cost (Rs. 245) or Net realizable value Rs. 216 (Estimated selling price Rs. 266 per unit less additional cost of Rs. 50). (c) 800 units of finished product P will be valued at NRV of Rs. 266 per unit since it is lower than cost Rs. 295.

2021 Valuation of Total Inventory as on 31.03.2019: Units Cost NRV/ Value = unit’s x cost or

(Rs.) Replacement cost NRV whichever is less

(Rs.) Raw material X 900 100 80 72,000 Partly finished goods 400 245 216 86,400 Finished goods P 800 295 266 2,12,800 Value of Inventory 3,71,200

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Value each inventory item separately at lower of cost and NRV/replacement cost. © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 217

Time Saving Tip: Always perform item-wise comparison, not total comparison.

Examiner’s Observation Many students value all inventories together instead of category-wise.

Question 15. Mr. Mehul gives the following information relating to items forming part of inventory as on 31-3- 20X1. His factory produces Product X using Raw material A. (i) 600 units of Raw material A (purchased @ Rs. 120). Replacement cost of raw material A as on 31-3- 20X1 is Rs. 90 per unit. (ii) 500 units of partly finished goods in the process of producing X and cost incurred till date Rs. 260 per unit. These units can be finished next year by incurring additional cost of Rs. 60 per unit. (iii) 1500 units of finished Product X and total cost incurred Rs. 320 per unit. Expected selling price of Product X is Rs. 300 per unit. Determine how each item of inventory will be valued as on 31-3-20X1. Also calculate the value of total inventory as on 31-3-20X1

[6 Marks | 9 minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 15. As per AS 2 (Revised) “Valuation of Inventories”, materials and other supplies held for use in the production of inventories are not written down below cost if the finished products in which they will be incorporated are expected to be sold at cost or above cost. However, when there has been a decline in the price of materials and it is estimated that the cost of the finished products will exceed net realisable value, the materials are written down to net realisable value. In such circumstances, the replacement cost of the materials may be the best available measure of their net realisable value. In the given case, selling price of product X is Rs. 300 and total cost per unit for production is Rs. 320.

Hence the valuation will be done as under: (i) 600 units of raw material will be written down to replacement cost as market value of finished product is less than its cost, hence valued at Rs. 90 per unit. (ii) 500 units of partly finished goods will be valued at 240 per unit i.e. lower of cost (Rs. 260) or Net realisable value Rs. 240 (Estimated selling price Rs. 300 per unit less additional cost of Rs. 60). (iii) 1,500 units of finished product X will be valued at NRV of Rs. 300 per unit since it is lower than cost Rs. 320 of product X.

Valuation of Total Inventory as on 31.03.20X1: Units Cost (Rs.) NRV/ Replacement Value = units × cost or

cost NRV whichever is less

(Rs.) Raw material A 600 120 90 54,000 Partly finished goods 500 260 240 1,20,000 Finished goods X 1500 320 300 4,50,000 Value of Inventory 6,24,000

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 218

Approach: Since selling price of finished goods is below cost, value raw materials at replacement cost and finished goods at NRV. Time Saving Tip: For WIP, deduct only completion cost from selling price to find NRV.

Examiner’s Observation Students often forget that replacement cost acts as NRV for raw materials.

Question 16. The closing stock of finished goods (at cost) of a company amounted to Rs. 4,50,000. The following items were included at cost in the total: (a) 100 coats, which had cost Rs. 2,200 each and normally sold for Rs . 4,000 each. Owing to a defect in manufacture their NRV was determined at 50% of their normal selling price. (b) Shirts which had cost Rs. 50,000, their net realizable value at Balance sheet date was Rs. 55,000. Commission @ 10% on sales is payable to agents. What should the inventory value be according to AS 2 after considering the above items?

[4 Marks | 5 minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Nov’22), Medium]

Answer 16. Valuation of closing stock

Rs. Closing stock at cost 4,50,000 Less: Adjustment for 100 coats (Working Note 1) (20,000) Value of inventory 4,30,000 Working Notes:

1. Adjustment for Coats Rs.

Cost included in Closing Stock 2,20,000 NRV of Coats 2,00,000 Adjustment to be made as NRV is less than Cost 20,000

2. No adjustment required for shirts as their NRV is more than their cost which was included in value of

inventory.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Reduce carrying amount only where NRV is below cost. Ignore items where NRV exceeds cost. Time Saving Tip: Only defective or loss-making items require adjustment.

Examiner’s Observation Students unnecessarily revalue profitable items upward.

Question 18. On the basis of information given below, find the value of inventory (by periodic inventory

st method) as per AS 2, to be considered while preparing the Balance Sheet as on 31 March, 2017 on weighted Average Basis. Details of Purchases: Date of purchase Unit (Nos.) Purchase cost per unit (Rs.) 01-03-2017 20 108 08-03-2017 15 107 17-03-2017 30 109 25-03-2017 15 107 Details of issue of Inventory: Date of Issue Unit(Nos.) 03-03-2017 10 12-03-2017 20 18-03-2017 10 24-03-2017 20 Net realizable value of inventory as on 31st March, 2017 is Rs. 107.75 per unit. You are required to compute the value of Inventory as per AS 2.

[5 Marks | 7 minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP March ‘19, MTP March ‘18, RTP May’22), High Chance]

Answer 18. Net Realizable Value of Inventory as on 31st March, 2017 = Rs. 107.75 ×20 units = Rs. 2,155 Value of inventory as per Weighted Average basis. Total units purchased and total cost: 01.03.2017 Rs. 108 × 20 units = Rs. 2160 08.3.2017 Rs. 107 × 15 units = Rs. 1605 17.03.2017 Rs. 109 × 30 units = Rs. 3270 25.03.2017 Rs. 107 × 15 units = Rs. 1605

Total 80 units = Rs. 8640 Weighted Average Cost = Rs. 8640/80 units = Rs.108 Total cost = Rs. 108 ×20 units = Rs. 2,160 Value of inventory to be considered while preparing Balance Sheet as on 31st March, 2017 is, Cost or Net Realizable value whichever is lower i.e. Rs. 2,155.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Find weighted average cost of total purchases. Compare total inventory cost with NRV. Time Saving Tip: In periodic weighted average, calculate average only once at period end.

Examiner’s Observation Students often apply moving average instead of periodic weighted average.

Question 19. Hello Ltd. purchased goods at the cost of Rs. 20 lakhs in October. Till the end of the financial year, 75% of the stocks were sold. The Company wants to disclose closing stock at Rs. 5 lakhs. The expected sale

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 221

value is Rs. 5.5 lakhs and a commission at 10% on sale is payable to the agent. You are required to ascertain the value of closing stock?

[3 Marks | 4 minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP Sep ’22, RTP Nov’19), Medium]

Answer 19. As per AS 2 “Valuation of Inventories”, the inventories are to be valued at lower of cost or net realizable value. In this case, the cost of inventory is Rs. 5 lakhs. The net realizable value is Rs. 4.95 lakhs (Rs. 5.5 lakhs less cost to make the sale @ 10% of Rs. 5.5 lakhs). So, the closing stock should be valued at Rs. 4.95 lakhs.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Compute NRV after deducting selling commission from expected selling price and compare with cost. Time Saving Tip: NRV = Expected Selling Price – Selling Expenses.

Examiner’s Observation Commission payable is frequently ignored.

Question 20. On 31st March 2020, a business firm finds that cost of a partly finished unit on that date is Rs.

430. The unit can be finished in 2020-21 by an additional expenditure of Rs. 310. The finished unit can be sold

for Rs. 750 subject to payment of 2% brokerage on selling price. The firm seeks your advice regarding the amount at which the unfinished unit should be valued as at 31st March, 2020 for preparation of final accounts. Assume that the partly finished unit cannot be sold in semi-finished form and its NRV is zero without processing it further.

[4 Marks | 5 minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Nov 21)(Same concept different figures RTP May 19), High Chance]

Answer 20.

Valuation of unfinished unit

Rs. Net selling price 750 Less: Estimated cost of completion (310)

440 Less: Brokerage (2 % of 750) (15) Net Realisable Value 425 Cost of inventory 430 Value of inventory (Lower of cost and net realisable value) 425

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Compute NRV after considering completion cost and brokerage. Value inventory at lower of cost and NRV. Time Saving Tip: Always deduct selling expenses separately even if percentage based.

Examiner’s Observation Students commonly ignore brokerage while calculating NRV.

Question 21. The inventory of Rich Ltd. as on 31st March, 2020 comprises of Product – A: 200 units and Product – B: 800 units. Details of cost for these products are: Product – A: Material cost, wages cost and overhead cost of each unit are Rs. 40, Rs. 30 and Rs. 20 respectively, each unit is sold at Rs. 110, selling expenses amounts to 10% of selling costs. Product – B: Material cost and wages cost of each unit are Rs. 45 and Rs. 35 respectively and normal selling rate is Rs. 150 each, however due to defect in the manufacturing process 800 units of Product- B were expected to be sold at Rs. 70. You are requested to value closing inventory according to AS 2 after considering the above.

[5 Marks | 7 minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP May ’21), High Chance]

Answer 21. According to AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’, inventories should be valued at the lower of cost and net realizable value.

Product – A Material cost Rs. 40 × 200 = 8,000 Wages cost Rs. 30 × 200 = 6,000 Overhead Rs. 20 × 200 = 4,000 Total cost Rs. 18,000 Realizable value [200 × (110-11)] Rs. 19,800 Hence inventory value of Product -A Rs. 18,000

Product – B Material cost Rs. 45 × 800 = 36,000 Wages cost Rs. 35 × 800 = 28,000 Total cost Rs. 64,000 Realizable value (800 × 70) Rs. 56,000 Hence inventory value of Product-B Rs. 56,000 Total Value of closing inventory i.e. Product A + Product B (18,000+ 56,000) Rs. 74,000

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Compute cost per unit and total cost for each product separately. Calculate Net Realizable Value (NRV) = Estimated selling price less estimated selling expenses. Compare Cost vs. NRV for each product and take the lower value as per AS 2 – Valuation of Inventories. Time-Saving Tips: Prepare a small Cost vs. NRV comparison table product-wise to avoid lengthy calculations. Directly calculate selling expenses as a percentage of selling price wherever given.

Examiner’s Observation Students often compare cost and NRV on a total inventory basis instead of product-wise. Many forget to deduct selling expenses while determining NRV.

Question 22. A private limited company manufacturing fancy terry towels had valued its closing inventory of inventories of finished goods at the realizable value, inclusive of profit and the export cash incentives. Firm contracts had been received and goods were packed for export, but the ownership in these goods had not been

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 223

transferred to the foreign buyers. You are required to advise the company on the valuation of the inventories in line with the provisions of AS 2.

[5 Marks | 6 minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP May ’18), Medium]

Answer 22. Accounting Standard 2 “Valuation of Inventories” states that inventories should be valued at lower of historical cost and net realizable value. The standard states, “At certain stages in specific industries, such as when agricultural crops have been harvested or mineral ores have been extracted, performance may be substantially complete prior to the execution of the transaction generating revenue. In such cases, when sale is assured under forward contract or a government guarantee or when market exists and there is a negligible risk of failure to sell, the goods are often valued at net realizable value at certain stages of production.” Terry Towels do not fall in the category of agricultural crops or mineral ores. Accordingly, taking into account the facts stated, the closing inventory of finished goods (Fancy terry towel) should have been valued at lower of cost and net realizable value and not at net realizable value. Further, export incentives are recorded only in the year the export sale takes place. Therefore, the policy adopted by the company for valuing its closing inventory of inventories of finished goods is not correct.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: First identify whether the inventory falls under special exceptions (agricultural produce/mineral ores). If not, apply normal AS 2 valuation. Value inventory at Lower of Cost or NRV (LCNRV). Ignore anticipated profit and export incentives while valuing inventory. Remember: ownership not transferred ⇒ revenue not recognized.

Examiner’s Observation Students often assume firm export orders permit valuation at selling price/NRV. Many incorrectly include export incentives in inventory value. Profit element should never be included in inventory valuation under AS 2\.

Question 23. “In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred” .Provide examples of such costs as per AS 2 (Revised) ‘Valuation of Inventories’.

[3 Marks | 4 minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 23. As per AS 2 (Revised) ‘Valuation of Inventories’, certain costs are excluded from the cost of the inventories and are recognized as expenses in the period in which incurred. Examples of such costs are: abnormal amount of wasted materials, Labour, or other production costs; a) Storage costs, unless those costs are necessary in the production process prior to a further production stage; b) Administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition; and c) Selling and distribution costs.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Apply lower of cost or NRV item-wise because products are not interchangeable. Time Saving Tip: Never offset gains in one item against losses in another.

Examiner’s Observation

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 224

Students value stock on aggregate basis instead of individual basis.

Question 24. The company deals in three products, A, B and C, which are neither similar nor interchangeable. At the time of closing of its account for the year 20 X1-X2, the Historical Cost and Net Realisable Value of the items of closing stock are determined as follows:

Items Historical Cost (Rs. in lakhs) Net Realisable Value (Rs. in lakhs) A 40 28 B 32 32 C 16 24 What will be the value of closing stock?

[4 Marks | 5 minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 24. As per AS 2 (Revised) on ‘Valuation of Inventories’, inventories should be valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Inventories should be written down to net realisable value on an item-by item basis in the given case.

Items Historical Cost (Rs. in lakhs) Net Realisable Value (Rs. in Valuation of closing stock (Rs.

lakhs) in lakhs) A 40 28 28 B 30 32 32 C 16 34 16

88 84 76 Hence, closing stock will be valued at Rs. 76 lakhs.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Separate normal and abnormal waste. Normal waste forms part of inventory cost; abnormal waste is expensed. Time Saving Tip: Compute revised unit cost using normal output quantity only.

Examiner’s Observation Abnormal waste is often included in closing inventory.

Question 25. In a production process, normal waste is 5% of input. 5,000 MT of input were put in process resulting in wastage of 300 MT. Cost per MT of input is Rs. 1,000. The entire quantity of waste is on stock at the year end. State with reference to Accounting Standard, how will you value the inventories in this case?

[4 Marks | 5 minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 25. As per AS 2 (Revised), abnormal amounts of wasted materials, Labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognized as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. In this case, normal waste is 250 MT and abnormal waste is 50 MT. The cost of 250 MT will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end. The cost of abnormal waste (50 MT × 1,052.6315 = Rs. 52,632) will be charged to the profit and loss statement. Cost per MT (Normal Quantity of 4,750 MT) = 50,00,000 / 4,750 = Rs. 1,052.6315 Total value of inventory = 4,700 MT × Rs. 1,052.6315 = Rs. 49,47,368. © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 225

Why not Nil?: While these items are generally immaterial, it is not accurate to assign them a zero value unless they are completely worthless, which is rare. They often have some realizable value in the market. Why not "Cost or NRV whichever is lower": This valuation principle is typically applied to main inventory items under AS 2 (like raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods), but for by-products and scrap, NRV is specifically used. Conclusion: Since by-products and scrap are considered immaterial and are usually sold at their net realizable value, the correct answer is (d) Net realisable value.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: When finished goods NRV falls below cost, raw materials are written down to replacement cost. Time Saving Tip: Replacement cost becomes best estimate of NRV for raw materials.

Examiner’s Observation Students incorrectly retain raw material at historical cost.

Question 27. U.S.A Ltd. purchased raw material @ Rs. 400 per kg. Company does not sell raw material but uses in production of finished goods. The finished goods in which raw material is used are expected to be sold at below cost. At the end of the accounting year, company is having 10,000 kg of raw material in inventory. As the company never sells the raw material, it does not know the selling price of raw material and hence cannot calculate the realizable value of the raw material for valuation of inventories at the end of the year. However replacement cost of raw material is Rs. 300 per kg. How will you value the inventory of raw material?

[4 Marks | 4 minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP Oct ’22), Medium]

Answer 27. As per AS 2 (Revised) “Valuation of Inventories”, materials and other supplies held for use in the production of inventories are not written down below cost if the finished products in which they will be incorporated are expected to be sold at or above cost. However, when there has been a decline in the price of materials and it is estimated that the cost of the finished products will exceed net realizable value, the materials are written down to net realizable value. In such circumstances, the replacement cost of the materials may be the best available measure of their net realizable value. Therefore, in this case, USA Ltd. will value the inventory of raw material at Rs. 30,00,000 (10,000 kg. @ Rs. 300 per kg.).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: When finished goods are expected to sell below cost, raw materials should be written down to replacement cost, which acts as best estimate of NRV.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 227

Examiner’s Observation Students incorrectly retain raw materials at historical cost because direct selling price of raw material is unavailable.

(ii) On 21st March, 2023, Mohan purchased 250 chairs at Rs. 300 each. The selling price of the chair is Rs. 400 each. Owing to a manufacturing defect, net realisable value of the whole lot of chair was determined at 70% of their normal selling price. No chairs were sold during the year.

[5 Marks | 7 minute | ICAI Fav. (Nov’23), Medium-High]

Answer 32. (i) Cost of closing inventory is shown below:

Particulars Rs. Sale value of opening stock and purchases 1,83,700 (Rs. 20,000 + Rs. 1,47,000) × 1.10 Sales (1,54,000) Sale value of unsold stock 29,700 Less: Gross Margin (Rs. 29,700 / 1.10) × 0.10 (2,700) Cost of closing inventory 27,000 (ii)

Question 33. Kirti Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing computers. During the year ended 31st March, 2024, the company manufactured 550 computers. It has the policy of valuing finished stock of goods at a standard cost of Rs. 1.8 lakh per computer. The details of the costs are as under:

(Rs. in lakh) Raw material consumed 400 Direct Labour 250 Variable production overheads 150 Fixed production overheads (including interest of Rs. 100 lakh) 290 Compute the value cost per computer for the purpose of closing stock.

[4 Marks | 5 minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Sep’24), High Chance]

Answer 33. As per para 9 of AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’, for inclusion in the cost of inventory, allocation of fixed production overheads is based on the normal capacity of the production facilities. In this, case finished stock has been valued at a standard cost of Rs. 1.8 lakh per computer which incidentally synchronizes with the value computed on the basis of absorption costing as under:

(Rs. in lakh) Materials 400 Direct Labour 250 Variable production overheads 150 Fixed production overheads 290 Less: Interest (100) 190

990 Number of computers produced = 550 computers (Assumed to be normal production) Cost per computer Rs. 990 lakh / 550 computers = Rs. 1.80 lakh

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Exclude interest from fixed production overhead while calculating inventory cost because finance cost is not part of AS 2 inventory valuation.

Examiner’s Observation Students generally include borrowing cost in inventory valuation without checking AS 16 applicability.

Question 35. (Example). ABC Ltd. has a plant with the capacity to produce 1 lac unit of a product per annum and the expected fixed overhead is Rs. 18 lacs. Fixed overhead on the basis of normal capacity is Rs. 18 (18 lacs/1 lac).

Case 1: Actual production is 1 lac units. Fixed overhead on the basis of normal capacity and actual overhead will lead to same figure of Rs. 18 lacs. Therefore, it is advisable to include this on normal capacity.

Case 2: Actual production is 90,000 units. Fixed overhead is not going to change with the change in output and will remain constant at Rs. 18 lacs, therefore, overheads on actual basis is Rs. 20 per unit (18 lacs/ 90 thousands). Hence by valuing inventory at Rs. 20 each for fixed overhead purpose, it will be overvalued and the losses of Rs. 1.8 lacs will also be included in closing inventory leading to a higher gross profit then actually earned. Therefore, it is advisable to include fixed overhead per unit on normal capacity to actual production (90,000 x 18)Rs. 16.2 lacs and rest Rs. 1.8 lacs should be transferred to Profit & Loss Account.

Case 3: Actual production is 1.2 lacs units. Fixed overhead is not going to change with the change in output and will remain constant at Rs. 18 lacs, therefore, overheads on actual basis is Rs. 15 (18 lacs/ 1.2 lacs). Hence by valuing inventory at Rs. 18 each for fixed overhead purpose, we will be adding the element of cost to inventory which actually has not been incurred. At Rs. 18 per unit, total fixed overhead comes to Rs. 21.6 lacs whereas, actual fixed overhead expense is only Rs. 18 lacs. Therefore, it is advisable to include fixed overhead on actual basis (1.2 lacs x 15) Rs. 18 lacs.

[5 Marks | 7 minute | ICAI Fav.| Example |High Chance]

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Use normal capacity for fixed overhead absorption to avoid overvaluation or undervaluation of inventory. Excess or short absorption is transferred to P&L.

Examiner’s Observation Students allocate total fixed overhead entirely to actual production without considering AS 2 normal capacity rule.

Question 36. (Example). A trader purchased certain articles for Rs. 85,000. He sold some of articles for Rs. 1,05,000. The average percentage of gross mark-up is 25% on cost. Opening stock of inventory at cost was Rs. 15,000. Cost of closing inventory is shown below:

Rs. Sale value of opening stock and purchase (Rs. 85,000 + Rs. 15,000) x 1.25 1,25,000 Sales (1,05,000) Sale value of unsold stock 20,000 Less: Gross Markup (Rs. 20,000 / 1.25) x 0.25 (4,000) Cost of inventory 16,000 Note: Margin is on sales and mark-up is on cost.

[4 Marks | 5 minute | ICAI Fav.| Example | Medium]

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Find sale value of goods available for sale, deduct sales, then remove gross mark-up to determine cost of closing stock.

Examiner’s Observation Students confuse markup on cost with margin on sales and apply incorrect percentage formula.

Question 37. (Example). The cost, net realisable value and inventory value of two items that a company has in its inventory are given below:

Cost (Rs.) Net Realisable Value (Rs.) Inventory Value (Rs.) Item 1 50,000 45,000 45,000 Item 2 20,000 24,000 20,000 Total 70,000 69,000 65,000 Estimates of NRV should be based on evidence available at the time of estimation. Net realisable value is the estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business less the estimated costs of completion and the estimated costs necessary to make the sale. AS 2 (Revised) also provides that estimates of net realisable value are to be based on the most reliable evidence available at the time the estimates are made as to the amount the inventories are expected to realise. These estimates take into consideration fluctuations of price or cost directly relating to events occurring after the balance sheet date to the extent that such events confirm the conditions existing at the balance sheet date.

[3 Marks | 4 minute | ICAI Fav.| Example | Medium]

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Compare cost and NRV item-wise and take lower value for each item separately. NRV estimates should be based on reliable evidence available at reporting date.

Examiner’s Observation Students incorrectly offset profit in one item against loss in another instead of valuing inventory item-wise.
