Question 36. (Revaluation on a class by class basis) Entity A is a large manufacturing group. It owns a number of industrial buildings, such as factories and warehouses and office buildings in several capital cities. The industrial buildings are located in industrial zones, whereas the office buildings are in central business districts of the cities. Entity A’s management want to apply the revaluation model as per AS 10 (Revised) to the subsequent measurement of the office buildings but continue to apply the historical cost model to the industrial buildings. State whether this is acceptable under AS 10 (Revised) or not with reasons?

[4 Marks | 3 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material) ICAI Illustration, Medium- High Chance]

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 269

Answer 36. Entity A’s management can apply the revaluation model only to the office buildings. The office buildings can be clearly distinguished from the industrial buildings in terms of their function, their nature and their general location.AS 10 (Revised) permits assets to be revalued on a class by class basis. The different characteristics of the buildings enable them to be classified as different PPE classes. The different measurement models can, therefore, be applied to these classes for subsequent measurement. However, all properties within the class of office buildings must be carried at revalued amount.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Identify whether assets belong to different classes of PPE. AS 10 permits different models for different classes but not within the same class.

Examiner’s Observation Candidates incorrectly assume all PPE must follow a single measurement model. The concept of “class of assets” is often ignored.

Question 37. ABC Ltd. has entered into a binding agreement with XYZ Ltd. to buy a custom-made machine amounting to Rs. 4,00,000. As on 31st March, 2020 before delivery of the machine, ABC Ltd. had to change its method of production. The new method will not require the machine ordered and so it shall be scrapped after delivery. The expected scrap value is ‘NIL’. Show the treatment of machine in the books of ABC Ltd.

[4 Marks | 3 Minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP Oct 20, Oct 18, Mar 22, Aug 18, Oct’19), High Chance]

Answer 37. A liability is recognized when outflow of economic resources in settlement of a present obligation can be anticipated and the value of outflow can be reliably measured. In the given case, ABC Ltd. should recognize a liability of Rs. 4,00,000 payable to XYZ Ltd. When flow of economic benefit to the enterprise beyond the current accounting period is considered improbable, the expenditure incurred is recognized as an expense rather than as an asset. In the present case, flow of future economic benefit from the machine to the enterprise is improbable. The entire amount of purchase price of the machine should be recognized as an expense. Hence ABC Ltd. should charge the amount of Rs. 4,00,000 (being loss due to change in production method) to Profit and loss statement and record the corresponding liability (amount payable to XYZ Ltd.) for the same amount in the books for the year ended 31st March, 2020.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Check whether future economic benefits will flow from the asset. If benefits are not expected, recognize the amount as an expense and create the liability.

Examiner’s Observation Students tend to capitalize the machine merely because a purchase contract exists. Recognition criteria under AS 10 are frequently overlooked.

Question 38. (Consideration received comprising a combination of non-monetary and monetary assets) Entity A exchanges land with a book value of Rs. 10,00,000 for cash of Rs. 20,00,000 and plant and machinery valued at Rs. 25,00,000. What will be the measurement cost of the assets received. (Consider that the transaction has commercial substance)?

[5 Marks | 4 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 270

Answer 38. In the given case, Plant & Machinery is valued at Rs. 25,00,000, which is assumed to be fair value in absence of information. Further, since fair value of land (asset given up) is not given, the transaction will be recorded at fair value of assets acquired of Rs. 45,00,000 (Rs. Cash 20,00,000 + Rs. Plant & Machinery 25,00,000). Since land of book value Rs. 10,00,000 is transferred in exchange of assets worth Rs. 45,00,000, a gain of Rs. 35,00,000 will be recognised in the books of Entity A. The following journal entry will be passed in the books of Entity A: Cash/ Bank A/c Dr. 20,00,000 Plant & Machinery A/c Dr. 25,00,000 To Land 10,00,000 To Profit on Sale of Land (balancing figure) 35,00,000

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Measure the transaction at fair value of assets received (or asset surrendered if more reliable). Compare consideration received with carrying amount to compute gain/loss.

Examiner’s Observation Candidates often record the new asset at book value of the old asset. Commercial substance concept is commonly missed.

Question 39. Entity A carried plant and machinery in its books at Rs. 2,00,000 which were destroyed in a fire. These machines were insured ‘New for old’ and were replaced by the insurance company with new machines of fair value Rs. 20,00,000. The old destroyed machines were acquired by the insurance company and the company did not receive any cash compensation. State, how Entity A should account for the same?

[4 Marks | 3 Minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP Oct 20, Mar 22), Medium-High]

Answer 39. Entity A should account for a loss in the Statement of Profit and Loss on de-recognition of the carrying value of plant and machinery in accordance with AS 10 on Property, Plant and Equipment. Entity A should separately recognize a receivable and a gain in the income statement resulting from the insurance proceeds once receipt is virtually certain. The receivable should be measured at the fair value of assets provided by the insurer.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Derecognize the destroyed asset first. Recognize insurance receivable and gain separately when realization becomes virtually certain.

Examiner’s Observation Students often net off insurance compensation against asset cost. Separate recognition of loss and insurance claim is required.

Question 40. (Gain on replacement of Insured Assets) Entity A carried plant and machinery in its books at Rs. 2,00,000. These were destroyed in a fire. The assets were insured ‘New for old’ and were replaced by the insurance company with new machines that cost Rs. 20,00,000. The machines were acquired by the insurance company and the company did not receive Rs. 20,00,000 as cash compensation. State, how Entity A should account for the same?

[4 Marks | 3 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium-High]

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 271

Answer 40. Entity A should account for a loss in the Statement of Profit and Loss on de- recognition of the carrying value of plant and machinery in accordance with AS 10 (Revised). Entity A should separately recognize a receivable and a gain in the income statement resulting from the insurance proceeds under AS 29 (Revised)\* once receipt is virtually certain. The receivable should be measured at the fair value of assets that will be provided by the insurer.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Apply the same principle as insurance compensation cases. Treat replacement asset received as insurance proceeds measured at fair value.

Examiner’s Observation Candidates ignore the receivable recognition aspect. Loss on destruction and insurance compensation should not be combined.

Question 41. An amusement park has a ‘soft’ opening to the public, to trial run its attractions. Tickets are sold at a 50% discount during this period and the operating capacity is 80%. The official opening day of the amusement park is three months later. Management claim that the soft opening is a trial run necessary for the amusement park to be in the condition capable of operating in the intended manner. Accordingly, the net operating costs incurred should be capitalized. Comment.

[4 Marks | 3 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 41. The net operating costs should not be capitalized but should be recognized in the Statement of Profit and Loss. Even though it is running at less than full operating capacity (in this case 80% of operating capacity), there is sufficient evidence that the amusement park is capable of operating in the manner intended by management. Therefore, these costs are specific to the start-up and, therefore, should be expensed as incurred.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Determine whether the asset is already capable of operating as intended. Once operational capability exists, operating losses and start-up costs must be expensed.

Examiner’s Observation Students wrongly capitalize trial-run operating losses after the asset is capable of normal operations. Distinguish testing costs from operating costs.

Question 42. Omega Ltd, a supermarket chain, is renovating one of its major stores. The store will have more available space for store promotion outlets after the renovation and will include a restaurant. Management is preparing the budgets for the year after the store reopens, which include the cost of remodelling and the expectation of a 15% increase in sales resulting from the store renovations, which will attract new customers. Decide whether Omega Ltd. can capitalize the remodelling cost or not as per provisions of AS 10 “Property plant & Equipment”.

[4 Marks | 2 Minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP Oct 20, Oct’19, Mar 22), High Chance]

Answer 42. The expenditure in remodelling the store will create future economic benefits (in the form of 15% of increase in sales). Moreover, the cost of remodelling can be measured reliably, therefore, it should be capitalized in line with AS 10. © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 272

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Verify recognition criteria: Future economic benefits + Reliable measurement of cost. If both are satisfied, remodeling expenditure is capitalized.

Examiner’s Observation Candidates often expense remodeling costs despite clear future economic benefits. Recognition criteria should be explicitly mentioned.

Question 43. (Capitalizing the cost of “Remodelling” a Supermarket) Entity A, a supermarket chain, is renovating one of its major stores. The store will have more available space for in store promotion outlets after the renovation and will include a restaurant. Management is preparing the budgets for the year after the store reopens, which include the cost of remodelling and the expectation of a 15% increase in sales resulting from the store renovations, which will attract new customers. State whether the remodeling cost will be capitalized or not.

[4 Marks | 3 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium-High]

Answer 43. The expenditure in remodeling the store will create future economic benefits (in the form of 15% of increase in sales) and the cost of remodeling can be measured reliably, therefore, it should be capitalized.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips Focus on enhancement of future economic benefits and reliable cost measurement. Such renovation expenditure generally qualifies for capitalization.

Examiner’s Observation Students sometimes treat all renovation costs as repairs and charge them to revenue. Distinguish improvements from routine maintenance.

Question 44. Entity A has an existing freehold factory property, which it intends to knock down and redevelop. During the redevelopment period the company will move its production facilities to another (temporary) site. The following incremental costs will be incurred:

1. Setup costs of Rs. 5,00,000 to install machinery in the new location.
2. Rent of Rs. 15,00,000
3. Removal costs of Rs. 3,00,000 to transport the machinery from the old location to the temporary location.

Can these costs be capitalized into the cost of the new building?

[5 Marks | 3 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 44. Constructing or acquiring a new asset may result in incremental costs that would have been avoided if the asset had not been constructed or acquired. These costs are not to be included in the cost of the asset if they are not directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management. The costs to be incurred by the company are in the nature of costs of relocating or reorganizing operations of the company and do not meet the requirement of AS 10 (Revised) and therefore, cannot be capitalized.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 273

Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Ask whether the expenditure directly brings the new building to working condition. Relocation, rent, and temporary setup costs are reorganization costs and must be expensed.

Examiner’s Observation Candidates capitalize relocation costs merely because they arise during construction. Direct attribution principle is often ignored.

Question 45. (Capitalization of directly attributable costs) Entity A, which operates a major chain of supermarkets, has acquired a new store location. The new location requires significant renovation expenditure. Management expects that the renovations will last for 3 months during which the supermarket will be closed. Management has prepared the budget for this period including expenditure related to construction and remodelling costs, salaries of staff who will be preparing the store before its opening and related utilities costs. What will be the treatment of such expenditures?

[5 Marks | 4 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 45. Management should capitalize the costs of construction and remodelling the supermarket, because they are necessary to bring the store to the condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management. The supermarket cannot be opened without incurring the remodelling expenditure, and thus the expenditure should be considered part of the asset. However, if the cost of salaries, utilities and storage of goods are in the nature of operating expenditure that would be incurred if the supermarket was open, then these costs are not necessary to bring the store to the condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management and should be expensed.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Capitalize construction and remodeling costs necessary to make the store operational. Expense salaries, utilities, and storage costs if they represent normal operating expenses.

Examiner’s Observation Students frequently capitalize all pre-opening expenses without analyzing their nature. Distinguishing capital expenditure from operating expenditure is crucial.

Question 46. A company changed its method of depreciation from SLM to WDV. How should the change be recognised?

[4 Marks | 2 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance] Answer 46. As per AS 10, Property, Plant and Equipment, the depreciation method applied to an asset should be reviewed at least at each financial year-end and, if there has been a significant change in the expected pattern of consumption of the future economic benefits embodied in the asset, the method should be changed to reflect the changed pattern. Such a change should be accounted for as a change in an accounting estimate in accordance with AS 5. Accordingly, the change in method of depreciation should be accounting for as a change in accounting estimate, prospectively.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 274

Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Treat change in depreciation method as a change in accounting estimate. Apply the revised method prospectively from the date of change.

Examiner’s Observation Candidates often treat it as a change in accounting policy and recomputed past depreciation. Retrospective adjustment is incorrect.

Question 47. An entity is setting up a manufacturing plant. Construction of the plant is completed in August and the plant is ready for commercial production in November. However, the entity commences production in March. When should be company start charging depreciation.

[3 Marks | 2 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Very High Chance] Answer 47. As per AS 10, Property, Plant and Equipment, depreciation of an asset begins when it is available for use, i.e., when it is in the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management. In the given case, since the plant is ready for commercial production in November, depreciation shall commence from November. The date of commencement of commercial production is irrelevant for charging depreciation.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Identify the date when the asset is ready for commercial use. Depreciation begins from readiness date, not actual production date.

Examiner’s Observation Students commonly start depreciation from commencement of production. AS 10 focuses on “available for use,” not actual use.

Question 48. RS Ltd. has acquired a heavy plant at a cost of Rs. 2,00,00,000. The estimated useful life is 10 years. At the end of the 2nd year, one of the major components i.e., the Boiler has become obsolete (which was acquired at price of Rs. 50,00,000) and requires replacement, as further maintenance is uneconomical. The remainder of the plant is perfect and is expected to last for next 8 years. The cost of a new boiler is Rs. 60,00,000. Can the cost of the new boiler be recognised as an asset, and, if so, what should be the carrying value of the plant at the end of second year?

[5 Marks |6 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Nov’22), Very High Chance] Answer 48. Recognition of Asset: The new boiler will produce economic benefits to RS Ltd., and the cost is measurable. Hence, the item should be recognized as an asset. The cost old boiler should be derecognized and the new boiler will be added. Statement showing cost of new boiler and machine after year 2 Original cost of plant Rs. 2,00,00,000 Less: Accumulated depreciation [(2,00,00,000 /10) x 2] Rs. 40,00,000 Carrying value of the plant after two years Rs. 1,60,00,000 Less: Current Cost of Old Boiler to be derecognized Less: WDV of Boiler (replaced) after 2 years (50,00,000/10 x 8) Rs. 40,00,000

Rs. 1,20,00,000

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 275

Add: Cost of new Boiler to be recognized Rs. 60,00,000 Revised carrying amount of Plant Rs. 1,80,00,000

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach & Time-Saving Tips: Derecognize the carrying amount of the old boiler and capitalize the new boiler separately. Component accounting should be applied whenever a significant part is replaced.

Examiner’s Observation Candidates often add the cost of the new boiler without removing the old boiler’s carrying amount. Component replacement accounting is a frequently tested AS 10 concept.

Question 49. Precision Tools Ltd. provides the following details related to its fi xed assets for the year ended 31st March 2025: The company purchased a machine for Rs. 12,00,000 on 1st October 2024. The following expenses were also incurred: Freight and insurance: Rs. 60,000 Erection charges: Rs. 40,000 Testing Cost: Raw materials used Rs. 25,000, Wages Rs.10,000, Sale of fi nished goods from testing production Rs. 8,000. On 1st December 2024, it replaced the motor of an old machine with a new one costing Rs.1,20,000, improving the output capacity by 15%. The old motor had a Cost of Rs.50,000 and Accumulated Depreciation of Rs. 35,000. On 15th March 2025, the company shifted a machine from one factory to another. It incurred the following: Dismantling cost: Rs.12,000 Transport and installation: Rs.18,000 Loss due to damage in transit: Rs.6,000 You are required to calculate the amount to be capitalized for each of the above cases as per AS 10.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes | ICAI Fav. | High Chance]

Answer 49. As per AS 10, Property, Plant and Equipment, the cost of an item of PPE includes: (a) Purchase price including import duties and non-refundable taxes, (b) Directly attributable costs to bring the asset to working condition (e.g., transport, installation, trial run), (c) Any trial run net costs (i.e., cost – recoverable proceeds).

Particulars Amount (Rs.) Purchase Price 12,00,000 Freight & Insurance 60,000 Erection Charges 40,000 Net Cost of Testing (25,000 + 10,000 – 8,000) 27,000 Cost of Machinery 13,27,000 Recognition of Motors Replacement

Particulars Amount (Rs.) Cost of Motors 50,000 Less: Depreciation 35,000 Carrying Amount of Motors 15,000

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 276

Accounting: The company should derecognize the existing Carrying Amount of Motors replaced of Rs. 15,000. Further, the acquisition cost of new motors of Rs. 1,20,000 would be capitalized as a separate component. Costs of relocating or reorganising part or all of the operations of an enterprise are not included in the carrying amount of an item of PPE. Hence Costs of relocation of Rs. 36,000 (12,000 +18,000 +6,000) of PPE are not capitalized. Thus, entire expense to be charged off to Profit and Loss A/c. Thus, total capitalization (net off Derecognition) = 14,32,000 (13,27,2000 +1,20,000- 15,000).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Read the question once and classify each expense as either directly attributable, replacement, or relocation cost. Prepare a small working table showing Item → Treatment under AS 10 → Amount to avoid confusion. First compute the cost of PPE by adding all eligible costs and deducting testing receipts, then separately deal with component replacement by capitalizing the new part and derecognizing the old one. Remember the golden rule: relocation/shifting expenses are always charged to P&L, which saves valuable exam time.

Examiner’s Observation Students frequently commit errors by capitalizing relocation expenses, which is not permitted under AS 10. Many also fail to deduct sale proceeds from trial production while calculating testing costs. Another common mistake is ignoring the Derecognition of the carrying amount of the old component replaced. Proper working notes and clear presentation generally help in securing full marks.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 277

### Part B

### Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. Accounting Standard 10, Property, Plant and Equipment is applicable to: (i) Biological Assets (other than Bearer Plants) related to agricultural activity (ii) Wasting Assets including Mineral rights, Expenditure on the exploration for and extraction of minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non regenerative resources (iii) Inventories (iv) Bearer Plant (except produce on Bearer Plants)

(MTP Jan 2025)

Ans. (iv) Reason: Accounting Standard (AS) 10 - Property, Plant and Equipment applies to tangible assets that are used in the production or supply of goods and services, for rental to others, or for administrative purposes. However, it does not apply to certain categories of assets, such as biological assets (other than bearer plants), inventories, and wasting assets. Let’s analyse each option: (i) Biological Assets (other than Bearer Plants) related to agricultural activity: Excluded: AS 10 does not apply to biological assets related to agricultural activity, except for bearer plants. Biological assets (like crops, livestock, etc.) that are held for sale or consumption are typically covered under Ind AS 41 - Agriculture or the relevant accounting standard for agricultural activity. Hence, this is incorrect. (ii) Wasting Assets including Mineral rights, Expenditure on the exploration for and extraction of minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources: Excluded: Wasting assets such as mineral rights, and exploration and extraction expenditures, are covered by other specific accounting standards (like Ind AS 6 - Exploration for and Evaluation of Mineral Resources or Ind AS 38 - Intangible Assets). They are excluded from AS 10. Hence, this is incorrect. (iii) Inventories: Excluded: Inventories are not covered under AS 10. Instead, inventories are valued and accounted for under AS 2

- Valuation of Inventories. Hence, this is incorrect.

(iv) Bearer Plant (except produce on Bearer Plants): Included: Bearer plants (such as fruit trees or grapevines that are used in agricultural production) are considered property, plant, and equipment under AS 10, except for the produce on those bearer plants (e.g., fruits, which are inventories and not covered by AS 10). Therefore, this is correct. Conclusion: AS 10 - Property, Plant and Equipment is applicable to bearer plants (except for produce on those plants). Hence, the correct answer is (iv) Bearer Plant (except produce on Bearer Plants).

Case Study Question 2. Excellence Ltd. is a Real Estate Company which constructs residential and commercial projects for selling. The Company has commenced a new project and the expenses incurred are as follows:

- The cost of land acquired for Project is Rs. 10 crore
- Cost of construction incurred is Rs. 25 crores.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 278

- The Company also incurred cost of Rs. 10 lacs for various administrative meetings in relation to planning of

the building.

- The construction of building completed and at the end of the year 1, the net realisable value of the building

was Rs. 40 crore.

- At the beginning of the next year (year 2), the Company decided to use the building as its corporate office.
- The Company further incurred Rs. 50 lacs for making necessary changes in the structure for using it as

corporate office in accordance with government norms for commercial spaces. Without these changes the office cannot be set up.

- Ignore the effect of depreciation, if any. (MTP Jan 2025) (i) At the end of Year 1, how the building should be classified:

(a) Inventory (b) Investments (c) Property, Plant and Equipment (d) Intangible Asset

Ans (a) Reason At the end of Year 1, the building is a part of the real estate project under construction by Excellence Ltd., which is a real estate company that constructs residential and commercial projects for sale. Let’s break down the classification: Inventory: Correct Classification: Since the company is constructing the building for the purpose of selling it as part of its real estate business, the building, at the end of Year 1, should be classified as inventory. According to AS 2 - Valuation of Inventories, inventories include goods that are held for sale in the ordinary course of business, which is exactly the situation here. The cost incurred on the land and construction is capitalized and classified as inventory because the company intends to sell the building to customers in the normal course of business. The net realizable value at the end of Year 1 (Rs. 40 crore) further confirms that the building is held for sale. Investments: Incorrect: An investment typically refers to assets held for earning income (interest, dividends, etc.) or capital appreciation, not for resale in the normal course of business. Since the building is under construction for sale and not for long-term holding, it is not an investment. Property, Plant and Equipment: Incorrect at this stage: While the company may later use the building as its corporate office (which would make it eligible for classification as Property, Plant, and Equipment under AS 10 - Property, Plant and Equipment), at the end of Year 1, the building is still being constructed for sale. It is not yet used for operational purposes, and thus it does not qualify as Property, Plant, and Equipment at this stage. Intangible Asset: Incorrect: The building is a tangible asset and cannot be classified as an intangible asset. Intangible assets are non-physical assets like patents, trademarks, or goodwill, which does not apply here. Conclusion: At the end of Year 1, since the building is intended for sale as part of the company’s normal business of real estate development, it should be classified as inventory. Therefore, the correct answer is (a) Inventory.

(ii) At the end of Year 1, at value Project should be recognised:

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 279

(a) Rs. 40 Crore (b) Rs. 35 Crore (c) Rs. 35.10 Crore (d) Rs. 25 Crore

Ans (b) Reason: At the end of Year 1, the building was completed, and the company is engaged in real estate business where the building was constructed for sale. The correct way to recognize the value of the project at this point is based on the lower of cost or net realizable value as per the Accounting Standard AS 2 - Valuation of Inventories, since the company intended to sell the building. Here is the breakdown of the costs and recognition: Cost of Land: Rs. 10 Crore The land is part of the project and is included in the cost of the building. Cost of Construction: Rs. 25 Crore This cost is directly related to the building's construction and forms part of the total project cost. Administrative Meetings Cost: Rs. 10 Lacs Administrative expenses for planning the building are not capitalized as part of the project cost under AS 2. These are treated as period costs and should not be included in the valuation of the project at the end of Year 1. Calculation of the Cost of the Project at the End of Year 1: Total Cost = Cost of Land + Cost of Construction Total Cost = Rs. 10 Crore + Rs. 25 Crore = Rs. 35 Crore Net Realizable Value (NRV): NRV of the building is given as Rs. 40 Crore at the end of Year 1. Since the company is still in the process of deciding whether to sell the building or use it as an office (decided in Year 2), the value should be recognized based on the lower of cost or net realizable value. In this case, the cost is Rs. 35 Crore, and the net realizable value is Rs. 40 Crore. Since the building is held for sale and the cost of the project is lower than the NRV, the building should be recognized at Rs. 35 Crore. Conclusion: The value of the project at the end of Year 1 should be recognized at Rs. 35 Crore (the lower of cost or net realizable value). Therefore, the correct answer is (b) Rs. 35 Crore.

(iii) At the end of Year 2, when the intention is to use the building as corporate office, it should be classified as: (a) Inventory (b) Investments (c) Property, Plant and Equipment (d) Intangible Assets

Ans (c) Reason: At the end of Year 2, the company has decided to use the building as its corporate office. Based on this decision, the classification of the building will change, as the building is no longer being held for sale as part of the real estate development business but is now intended for use in operations. The correct accounting treatment for such a scenario is governed by AS 10 - Property, Plant and Equipment. Let's analyse the situation step by step: Initial Classification (End of Year 1): At the end of Year 1, the building was classified as inventory because it was under construction with the intention to sell it as part of the company’s real estate business. Change in Use (End of Year 2): © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 280

The company has decided to use the building as a corporate office, which indicates a shift in the purpose of the building. The building is no longer held for sale but will be used to support the company's operations. According to AS 10 - Property, Plant and Equipment, assets that are used in the production or supply of goods and services, or for administrative purposes, are classified as Property, Plant, and Equipment (PPE). Necessary Modifications: The company incurred Rs. 50 lacs for making necessary changes to the building in accordance with government norms for commercial spaces. These modifications are directly related to preparing the building for its intended use as a corporate office. Such expenditures are considered capital expenditures and should be added to the cost of the building as part of PPE. Final Classification: Since the building is now intended for use in operations (as a corporate office) and not for sale, it should be classified as Property, Plant, and Equipment (PPE) under AS 10. Conclusion: At the end of Year 2, when the building is intended for use as the company's corporate office, it should be classified as Property, Plant, and Equipment (PPE). Therefore, the correct answer is (c) Property, Plant, and Equipment.

(iv) At the end of Year 2, the Project should be valued at: (a) Rs. 40 Crore (b) Rs. 35.50 Crore (c) Rs. 35.10 Crore (d) Rs. 25 Crore

Ans (b) Reason: At the end of Year 2, the building is no longer held for sale but is intended to be used as the company’s corporate office. According to the accounting treatment, the building should be reclassified from inventory to Property, Plant, and Equipment (PPE), based on its new intended use. However, it will be valued at its cost at this point, since it is now part of the company's assets. Let's break down the valuation: Cost at the end of Year 1 (Inventory valuation): The total cost of the project at the end of Year 1 (when the building was still intended for sale) was Rs. 35 Crore (which included the cost of land, construction, and administrative expenses related to the project). At the end of Year 1, the net realizable value (NRV) of the building was Rs. 40 Crore, but it was carried at cost (Rs. 35 Crore), since the building was classified as inventory and valued at the lower of cost or NRV. Reclassification at the beginning of Year 2: Now, at the beginning of Year 2, the building is reclassified as Property, Plant, and Equipment (PPE) because it will be used as the company's corporate office. According to AS 10 - Property, Plant and Equipment, when a property is reclassified from inventory to PPE, it is valued at the lower of cost or net realizable value (NRV), which, in this case, is Rs. 35 Crore (as the cost is lower than the NRV at Year 1). Further Costs (Modification for Corporate Office): The company further incurred Rs. 50 Lacs for modifications required to make the building suitable for use as a corporate office, in accordance with government norms for commercial spaces. This Rs. 50 Lacs should be added to the carrying amount of the building as capital expenditure because it is part of the costs necessary to prepare the building for its intended use. © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 281

Therefore, the new total cost at the end of Year 2 will be: Rs. 35 Crore (carrying amount at the end of Year 1) + Rs. 50 Lacs (modification costs) = Rs. 35.50 Crore. Conclusion: At the end of Year 2, when the building is reclassified as PPE and after the necessary modifications are added, the project should be valued at Rs. 35.50 Crore. Therefore, the correct answer is (b) Rs. 35.50 Crore.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Focus on the purpose of the asset at each point (for sale → inventory, for own use → PPE). Identify costs that are capitalizable vs. period expenses. Apply the “lower of cost or NRV” rule for inventory and add necessary modifications for PPE. Reading the question carefully for timing and classification changes saves time.

Examiner’s Observation Examiners look for correct classification at each stage, proper application of AS 2 and AS 10, and clear distinction between capital and period costs. Partial marks are given if reasoning is shown even if the final number is slightly off.

Question 3. As per AS 10 (Revised) ‘Property, plant and equipment’, which of the following costs is not included in the carrying amount of an item of PPE a) Costs of site preparation b) Costs of relocating c) Installation and assembly costs d) Initial delivery and handling costs

(Study Material)

Ans: (b) Reason: According to AS 10 (Revised) - Property, Plant, and Equipment, the costs that can be included in the carrying amount of an item of Property, Plant, and Equipment (PPE) are those that are directly attributable to bringing the asset to its intended location and condition for use. Here’s a breakdown of each option: (a) Costs of site preparation: Included: The costs of preparing the site (such as clearing, leveling, or removing obstacles) are directly attributable to getting the asset ready for use. These costs are capitalized as part of the cost of the asset. (b) Costs of relocating: Not Included: The cost of relocating an item of PPE (such as moving it from one place to another, or moving equipment to a new location) is not typically included in the cost of the asset. Relocation costs are generally considered as operating expenses rather than capital expenditures. These costs are usually expensed as incurred unless they are necessary to prepare the asset for its intended use at its new location (which would be an exception). (c) Installation and assembly costs: Included: Costs incurred for the installation and assembly of an item of PPE are considered directly attributable to getting the asset ready for use. These costs are capitalized as part of the cost of the asset. (d) Initial delivery and handling costs: Included: The cost of delivering and handling the asset to the location where it will be used is capitalized as part of the asset's cost, as these costs are necessary to bring the asset to its intended location and condition.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 282

Conclusion: Costs of relocating are not typically capitalized under AS 10 (Revised), and instead, are generally treated as operating expenses. Therefore, the correct answer is (b) Costs of relocating.

Question 4. A machinery was purchased having an invoice price Rs. 1,18,000 (including GST Rs. 18,000) on 1 April 20X1. The GST amount is available as input tax credit. The rate of depreciation is 10% on SLM basis. The depreciation for 20X2 -X3 would be a. Rs. 10,000 b. Rs. 11,800 c. Rs. 9,000 d. Rs. 10,500

(Study Material)

Ans: (a) Reason: To calculate the depreciation for the year 20X2-X3 (i.e., the second year of depreciation), let's break down the information step by step: Cost of the machinery: The machinery was purchased for Rs. 1,18,000, which includes GST of Rs. 18,000. However, the GST is available as an input tax credit, so it does not form part of the actual cost of the machinery for depreciation purposes. The actual cost of the machinery is: Cost excluding GST = Rs. 1,18,000 - Rs. 18,000 = Rs. 1,00,000. Depreciation method: The depreciation is calculated using the Straight Line Method (SLM). Under SLM, the annual depreciation is calculated by dividing the cost of the asset (excluding GST) by the useful life of the asset. Depreciation rate: The rate of depreciation is 10% on the original cost (Rs. 1,00,000). Depreciation for the year: Using the SLM method, the depreciation for one year is calculated as: Depreciation for one year = 10% of Rs. 1,00,000 = Rs. 10,000. Conclusion: The depreciation for the year 20X2-X3 would be Rs. 10,000, since the depreciation is calculated on the original cost of Rs. 1,00,000, excluding GST. Therefore, the correct answer is (a) Rs. 10,000.

Question 5: A plot of land with carrying amount of Rs. 1,00,000 was revalue to Rs. 1,50,000 at the end of Year

2. Subsequently, due to drop in market values, the land was determined to have a fair value of Rs. 1,30,000at

the end of Year 4. Assuming that the entity adopts Revaluation Model, what would be the accounting treatment of Revaluation? a) Initial upward valuation of Rs . 50,000 credited to Revaluation Reserve. Subsequent downward revaluation of Rs. 20,000 debited to P/L. b) Initial upward valuation of Rs. 50,000 credited to P/L. Subsequent downward revaluation of Rs. 20,000 debited to P/L. c) Initial upward valuation of Rs . 50,000 credited to Revaluation Reserve. Subsequent downward revaluation of Rs. 20,000 debited to Revaluation Reserve. d) Initial upward valuation of Rs. 50,000 debited to P/L. Subsequent downward revaluation of Rs. 20,000 credited to P/L.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 283

Ans: (c) Reason: When an entity adopts the Revaluation Model under Ind AS 16 - Property, Plant and Equipment or AS 10

- Property, Plant and Equipment, the accounting treatment for the upward and downward revaluations follows

specific guidelines. Let’s break down the scenario and determine the appropriate accounting treatment: Step-by-Step Breakdown: Initial Upward Revaluation (Year 2): The plot of land was initially carried at Rs. 1,00,000. The revaluation increased its fair value to Rs. 1,50,000 at the end of Year 2, resulting in an increase of Rs. 50,000. Accounting treatment for the upward revaluation: The increase in value of Rs. 50,000 should be credited to the Revaluation Reserve. According to the revaluation model, any increase in value should go to Revaluation Reserve unless it reverses a previous downward revaluation that was recognized in the Profit and Loss (P&L) account. Hence, the initial upward revaluation of Rs. 50,000 is credited to Revaluation Reserve. Subsequent Downward Revaluation (Year 4): Due to a drop in market values, the fair value of the land decreased to Rs. 1,30,000 at the end of Year 4. The decrease in value is Rs. 20,000 (from Rs. 1,50,000 to Rs. 1,30,000). Accounting treatment for the downward revaluation: The downward revaluation of Rs. 20,000 should be debited to the Revaluation Reserve, but only to the extent of any credit balance existing in the Revaluation Reserve for that asset. If there is any remaining balance in the Revaluation Reserve from the earlier upward revaluation (Rs. 50,000), the downward revaluation is first debited to the Revaluation Reserve. If the decrease exceeds the balance in the Revaluation Reserve, the excess is debited to the Profit and Loss account. In this case, the decrease of Rs. 20,000 is less than the Revaluation Reserve balance (Rs. 50,000), so the entire Rs. 20,000 downward revaluation is debited to the Revaluation Reserve. Conclusion: Initial upward valuation of Rs. 50,000 is credited to Revaluation Reserve. Subsequent downward revaluation of Rs. 20,000 is debited to Revaluation Reserve (not P&L, because the downward revaluation does not exceed the revaluation reserve balance). Thus, the correct accounting treatment is (c) Initial upward valuation of Rs. 50,000 credited to Revaluation Reserve. Subsequent downward revaluation of Rs. 20,000 debited to Revaluation Reserve.

Question 6: A plot of land with carrying amount of Rs. 1,00,000 was revalue to Rs. 90,000 at the end of Year 2. Subsequently, due to increase in market values, the land was determined to have a fair value of Rs. 1,05,000 at the end of Year 4. Assuming that the entity adopts Revaluation Model, what would be the accounting treatment of Revaluation? a) Initial downward valuation of Rs. 10,000 debited to Revaluation Reserve. Subsequent upward revaluation of Rs. 15,000 credited to P/L. b) Initial downward valuation of Rs. 10,000 debited to P/L. Subsequent upward revaluation of Rs. 15,000 credited to P/L. (c) Initial downward valuation of Rs. 10,000 credited to P/L. Subsequent upward revaluation of Rs. 10,000 debited to P/L and Rs. 5,000 debited to Revaluation Reserve. d) Initial downward valuation of Rs. 10,000 debited to P/L. Subsequent upward revaluation of Rs. 10,000 credited to P/L and Rs. 5,000 credited to Revaluation Reserve. © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 284

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason: Let’s break down the accounting treatment for revaluation under the Revaluation Model: Step 1: Initial Downward Revaluation (End of Year 2) The carrying amount of the land was Rs. 1,00,000. The land was revalued to Rs. 90,000 at the end of Year 2, which means a decrease of Rs. 10,000. According to the revaluation model, if an asset’s fair value decreases, and if there was a previous upward revaluation of that asset in the revaluation reserve, the downward revaluation should first be debited to the Revaluation Reserve (if there is a balance). If the revaluation reserve is not enough to absorb the loss, the loss is debited to the Profit and Loss (P&L) account. In this case, the carrying value of the land decreased from Rs. 1,00,000 to Rs. 90,000. Since this is a downward revaluation, the loss of Rs. 10,000 should be debited to P&L because there was no indication of any prior revaluation surplus for this land. Step 2: Subsequent Upward Revaluation (End of Year 4) After two years, the land’s fair value increased to Rs. 1,05,000. The increase in value is Rs. 15,000 (from Rs. 90,000 to Rs. 1,05,000). When a revaluation increases an asset’s fair value, the increase is first recognized in the Revaluation Reserve. However, if there was a previous downward revaluation that was debited to the Profit and Loss account, the reversal of that decrease should be recognized in the Profit and Loss account to the extent of the previous loss recognized in the P&L. Any remaining increase after reversing the previous loss is credited to the Revaluation Reserve. Since the initial downward revaluation of Rs. 10,000 was debited to P&L, the first Rs. 10,000 of the upward revaluation will be credited to P&L (to reverse the previous loss). The remaining Rs. 5,000 will be credited to the Revaluation Reserve. Conclusion: Thus, the correct accounting treatment is: Initial downward valuation of Rs. 10,000 debited to P&L. Subsequent upward revaluation of Rs. 10,000 (to reverse the loss) credited to P&L, and the remaining Rs. 5,000 is credited to the Revaluation Reserve. Hence, the correct answer is (c) Initial downward valuation of Rs. 10,000 credited to P/L. Subsequent upward revaluation of Rs. 10,000 debited to P/L and Rs. 5,000 debited to Revaluation Reserve

Question 7. On sale of an asset which was revalued upwards, what would be the treatment of Revaluation Reserve? a) The Revaluation Reserve is credited to P/L since the profit on sale of such asset is now realized. b) The Revaluation Reserve is credited to Retained Earnings as a movement in reserves without impacting the P/L. c) No change in Revaluation Reserve since profit on sale of such asset is already impacting the P/L. The Revaluation Reserve is reduced from the asset value to compute profit or loss.

(Study Material)

Ans: (b)

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 285

Reason: When an asset that was revalued upwards is sold, the Revaluation Reserve associated with that asset must be treated according to Accounting Standards (such as AS 10 - Property, Plant, and Equipment, or Ind AS 16). The treatment is based on the idea that the Revaluation Reserve represents unrealized gains that were recognized in the past. Here’s the detailed explanation of the treatment: On Sale of the Asset: The Revaluation Reserve associated with the asset does not directly impact the Profit and Loss (P&L) statement because the unrealized gain was already recognized through the revaluation process and had been credited to the Revaluation Reserve in equity. Revaluation Reserve Adjustment: The amount of the Revaluation Reserve related to the sold asset is transferred to Retained Earnings. This movement is treated as a movement within equity (from Revaluation Reserve to Retained Earnings), and it does not affect the Profit and Loss statement. This reflects that the unrealized gain has now become realized due to the sale. Profit or Loss on Sale: The profit or loss on the sale of the asset is determined based on the difference between the sale proceeds and the carrying amount of the asset at the time of sale. The sale proceeds and carrying amount will have already accounted for the revaluation, so the realized revaluation gain is now reflected in the retained earnings. Why Option (b) is Correct: The Revaluation Reserve associated with the asset is not credited to P&L because it represents a previous unrealized gain, which was already recognized as part of equity. The reserve is credited to Retained Earnings as a movement in reserves, reflecting the realization of the revaluation gain. This does not impact the Profit and Loss account because the revaluation gain was already recorded in equity. Why Other Options are Incorrect: Option (a) ("The Revaluation Reserve is credited to P/L since the profit on sale of such asset is now realized"): This is incorrect because the revaluation reserve is not transferred to P&L on sale. Instead, it is transferred to Retained Earnings. Option (c) ("No change in Revaluation Reserve since profit on sale of such asset is already impacting the P/L. The Revaluation Reserve is reduced from the asset value to compute profit or loss"): This is incorrect because the revaluation reserve related to the asset should still be transferred to Retained Earnings, and the treatment mentioned here is not consistent with the standard accounting treatment for revaluation reserve on sale. Conclusion: The correct accounting treatment is to transfer the Revaluation Reserve related to the asset to Retained Earnings without impacting the Profit and Loss statement. Therefore, the correct answer is (b).

Question 8. As per AS 10 (Revised) ‘Property, Plant and Equipment’, an enterprise holding investment properties should value Investment property. a. As per fair value b. Under discounted cash flow model c. Under cost model d. Under cash flow model

(Study Material)

Ans: (c)

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 286

Reason: According to AS 10 (Revised) - Property, Plant, and Equipment, an investment property is typically treated under the Cost Model (unless it is classified under the Revaluation Model). Here's a breakdown of the accounting treatment: Investment Property Definition: An investment property is property held to earn rental income or for capital appreciation, or both, and not for use in production or supply of goods and services, or for administrative purposes. Accounting Treatment: Under AS 10, the treatment of investment property is generally governed by the Cost Model, which means that investment properties are carried at their cost (which includes acquisition cost and any directly attributable expenditure) less accumulated depreciation (if applicable) and impairment losses (if applicable). Fair Value Model (not part of AS 10): While fair value is an acceptable method under Ind AS 40 - Investment Property, AS 10 does not allow the fair value model for investment properties. Therefore, AS 10 mandates the use of the cost model for valuing investment properties. Revaluation Model: The Revaluation Model (under Ind AS) is an alternative to the Cost Model for valuing Property, Plant, and Equipment but does not apply to Investment Property under AS 10. Conclusion As per AS 10 (Revised) - Property, Plant, and Equipment, investment properties should be valued using the Cost Model unless a different standard applies (e.g., Ind AS 40 for Investment Property). Therefore, the correct answer is (c) Under cost model.

Chapter-5 Unit 3 AS 13-Accounting for Investments

PART A Question 1. How will you classify the investments as per AS 13? Explain in Brief

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 1. The investments are classified into two categories as per AS 13, viz., Current Investments and Long- term Investments. A current Investment is an investment that is by its nature readily realisable and is intended to be held for not more than one year from the date on which such investment is made. The carrying amount for current investments is the lower of cost and fair value. Any reduction to fair value and any reversals of such reductions are included in the statement of profit and loss. A long-term investment is an investment other than a current investment. Long term investments are usually carried at cost. However, when there is a decline, other than temporary, in the value of a long term investment, the carrying amount is reduced to recognise the decline. The reduction in carrying amount is charged to the statement of profit and loss.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Remember the classification and valuation rule together: Current Investment = Lower of Cost & Fair Value; Long-term Investment = Cost unless permanent decline. Use a comparison table for quick presentation.

Examiner’s Observation Students often interchange valuation rules and forget to mention “other than temporary decline” for long- term investments.

Question 2. Whether the accounting treatment ‘at cost’ under the head ‘Long Term Investments’ without providing for any diminution in value is correct and in accordance with the provisions of AS 13. If not, what should have been the accounting treatment in such a situation? Explain in brief.

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 2. The accounting treatment ‘at cost’ under the head ‘Long Term Investment’ in the financial statements of the company without providing for any diminution in value is correct and is in accordance with the provisions of AS 13 provided that there is no decline, other than temporary, in the value of investment. If the decline in the value of investment is, other than temporary, compared to the time when the shares were purchased, provision is required to be made.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips First determine whether the decline is temporary or permanent. Provision is required only when the decline is other than temporary.

Examiner’s Observation Many students conclude directly without discussing the nature of diminution in value.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 288

Question 3. Omega Equity Investments Ltd., wants to re-classify its investments in accordance with AS 13. State the values, at which the investments have to be reclassified in the following cases: (a) Long term investments in Company A, costing Rs.8.5 lakhs are to be re-classified as current. The company had reduced the value of these investments to Rs.6.5 lakhs to recognize a permanent decline in value. The fair value on date of transfer is Rs.6.8 lakhs. (b) Current investment in Company C, costing Rs.10 lakhs are to be re-classified as long term as the company wants to retain them. The market value on date of transfer is Rs.12 lakhs. (c) Certain long term investments no longer considered for holding purposes, to be reclassified as current investments. The original cost of these investments was Rs.18 lakhs but had been written down to Rs.12 lakhs to recognize permanent decline as per AS 13.

[5 Marks | 7 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP May 20), High Chance]

Answer 3. As per AS 13 ‘Accounting for Investments’, where long-term investments are reclassified as current investments, transfers are made at the lower of cost and carrying amount at the date of transfer. And where investments are reclassified from current to long term, transfers are made at lower of cost and fair value on the date of transfer. Accordingly, the re-classification will be done on the following basis: (i) In this case, carrying amount of investment on the date of transfer is less than the cost; hence this re- classified current investment should be carried at Rs.6.5 lakhs in the books. (ii) In this case, reclassification of current investment into long-term investments will be made at Rs.10 lakhs as cost is less than its market value of Rs.12 lakhs. (iii) In this case, the book value of the investment is Rs.12 lakhs, which is lower than its cost i.e.Rs.18 lakhs. Here, the transfer should be at carrying amount and hence this re-classified current investment should be carried at Rs.12 lakhs

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Identify the transfer direction first. Apply: LT→ Current = Lower of Cost & Carrying Amount; Current→LT = Lower of Cost & Fair Value.

Examiner’s Observation Students frequently confuse carrying amount with fair value while reclassifying investments.

Question 4. Mother Mart Ltd., wants to re-classify its investment in accordance with AS 13. Decide the treatment to be given in each of the following cases assuming that the market value has been determined in an arm’s length transaction between knowledgeable and willing buyer and seller: (a) A portion of current investments purchased for Rs. 25 lakhs to be reclassified as long-term investments, as the company has decided to retain them. The market value as on the date of balance sheet was Rs. 30 lakhs. The fair value of the investments on the date of transfer is same as the market value on the balance sheet date (b) Another portion of current investments purchased for Rs. 20 lakhs has to be re- classified as long-term investments. The Fair value of these investments as on the date of the balance sheet was Rs. 12.5 lakhs. (c) One portion of long-term investments, no longer considered for holding purposes, to be reclassified as current investments. The original cost of these was Rs. 15 lakhs, but had been written down to Rs. 11 lakhs to recognize permanent decline as per AS 13.

[5 Marks | 8 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Nov’22, Old & New SM), Very High Chance]

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 289

Answer 4. As per AS 13 ‘Accounting for Investments’, where investments are reclassified from current to long- term, transfers are made at the lower of cost and fair value at the date of transfer. When long-term investments are re-classified as current investments, transfers are made at the lower of cost and carrying amount at the date of transfer. (i) In the first case, the market value of the investments is Rs. 30 lakhs, which is higher than its cost i.e. Rs. 25 lakhs. Therefore, the transfer to long term investments should be made at cost i.e. Rs. 25 lakhs (ii) In the second case, the market value of the investment is Rs. 12.5 lakhs, which is lower than its cost i.e. Rs. 20 lakhs. Therefore, the transfer to long term investments should be made in the books at the market value i.e. Rs. 12.5 lakhs. The loss of Rs. 7.50 lakhs (20-12.5) should be charged to Profit and Loss statement. (iii) In the third case, the book value of the investments is Rs. 11 lakhs, which is lower than its cost, i.e. Rs. 15 lakhs. As the transfer should be at carrying amount, hence this re-classified current investment should be carried at Rs. 11 lakhs.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Apply AS 13 reclassification rules separately for each case. Compare cost and fair value carefully and calculate any resulting loss immediately. Present each answer with brief reasoning.

Examiner’s Observation Loss arising on transfer is often ignored or wrongly adjusted.

Question 5. Blue-chip Equity Investments Ltd., wants to re-classify its investments in accordance with AS 13 (Revised). State the values, at which the investments have to be reclassified in the following cases: (i) Long term investments in Company A, costing Rs. 8.5 lakhs are to be re- classified as current. The company had reduced the value of these investments to Rs. 6.5 lakhs to recognise ‘other than temporary’ decline in value. The fair value on date of transfer is Rs. 6.8 lakhs. (ii) Long term investments in Company B, costing Rs. 7 lakhs are to be re- classified as current. The fair value on date of transfer is Rs. 8 lakhs and book value is Rs. 7 lakhs. (iii) Current investment in Company C, costing Rs. 10 lakhs are to be re- classified as long term as the company wants to retain them. The market value on date of transfer is Rs. 12 lakhs.

[5 Marks | 7 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), very High Chance]

Answer 5. As per AS 13 (Revised) ‘Accounting for Investments’, where long-term investments are reclassified as current investments, transfers are made at the lower of cost and carrying amount at the date of transfer. And where investments are reclassified from current to long term, transfers are made at lower of cost and fair value on the date of transfer. Accordingly, the re-classification will be done on the following basis: (i) In this case, carrying amount of investment on the date of transfer is less than the cost; hence this reclassified current investment should be carried at Rs. 6.5 lakhs in the books. (ii) The carrying / book value of the long term investment is same as cost i.e. Rs. 7 lakhs. Hence this long term investment will be reclassified as current investment at book value of Rs. 7 lakhs only. (iii) In this case, reclassification of current investment into long-term investments will be made at Rs. 10 lakhs as cost is less than its market value of Rs. 12 lakhs.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

Examiner’s Observation Candidates wrongly use fair value instead of carrying amount in LT→ Current reclassification cases.

Question 6. ABC Ltd. wants to re-classify its investments in accordance with AS 13 (Revised). Decide and state on the amount of transfer, based on the following information: (1) A portion of current investments purchased for Rs. 20 lakhs, to be reclassified as long term investment, as the company has decided to retain them. The market value as on the date of Balance Sheet was Rs. 25 lakhs. (2) Another portion of current investments purchased for Rs. 15 lakhs, to be reclassified as long term investments. The market value of these investments as on the date of balance sheet was Rs. 6.5 lakhs. (3) Certain long term investments no longer considered for holding purposes, to be reclassified as current investments. The original cost of these was Rs. 18 lakhs but had been written down to Rs. 12 lakhs to recognise other than temporary decline as per AS 13 (Revised).

[5 Marks | 8 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 6. As per AS 13 (Revised), where investments are reclassified from current to long- term, transfers are made at the lower of cost and fair value at the date of transfer. (1) In the first case, the market value of the investment is Rs. 25 lakhs, which is higher than its cost i.e. Rs. 20 lakhs. Therefore, the transfer to long term investments should be carried at cost i.e. Rs. 20 lakhs. (2) In the second case, the market value of the investment is Rs. 6.5 lakhs, which is lower than its cost i.e. Rs. 15 lakhs. Therefore, the transfer to long term investments should be carried in the books at the market value i.e. Rs. 6.5 lakhs. The loss of Rs. 8.5 lakhs should be charged to profit and loss account. As per AS 13 (Revised), where long-term investments are re-classified as current investments, transfers are made at the lower of cost and carrying amount at the date of transfer. (3) In the third case, the book value of the investment is Rs. 12 lakhs, which is lower than its cost i.e. Rs. 18 lakhs. Here, the transfer should be at carrying amount and hence this re-classified current investment should be carried at Rs. 12 lakhs.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Classify each transfer separately before calculating the amount. Prepare short workings showing cost, fair value and carrying amount. This minimizes calculation mistakes.

Examiner’s Observation Students often forget to recognize the loss when fair value is lower than cost.

Question 7. Z Bank has classified its total investment on 31-3-2021 into three categories (a) held to maturity (b) available for sale (c) held for trading as per the RBI Guidelines. ‘Held to maturity’ investments are carried at acquisition cost less amortized amount. ‘Available for sale’ investments are carried at marked to market. ‘Held for trading’ investments are valued at weekly intervals at market rates. Net depreciation, if any, is charged to revenue and net appreciation, if any, is ignored. You are required to comment whether the policy of the bank is in accordance with AS 13?

[5 Marks | 8 Minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP Nov ’21, RTP Nov 21, Nov 19), High Chance]

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 291

Answer 7. As per AS 13 ‘Accounting for Investments’, the accounting standard is not applicable to Bank, Insurance Company, Mutual Funds. In this case Z Bank is a bank, therefore, AS 13 does not apply to it. For banks, the RBI has issued separate guidelines for classification and valuation of its investment and Z Bank should comply with those RBI Guidelines/Norms. Therefore, though Z Bank has not followed the provisions of AS 13, yet it would not be said as non-compliance since, it is complying with the norms stipulated by the RBI.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Before applying AS 13, verify whether the entity falls within its scope. Remember that Banks, Insurance Companies and Mutual Funds are excluded. Mention RBI guidelines for banks.

Examiner’s Observation Many students unnecessarily apply AS 13 provisions to banks despite its non-applicability.

Question 8. A Limited invested in the shares of XYZ Ltd. on 1st December, 2019 at a cost of Rs 50,000. Out of these shares, Rs 25,000 shares were purchased with an intention to hold for 6 months and Rs 25,000 shares were purchased with an intention to hold as long-term Investment.

st A Limited also earlier purchased Gold of Rs 1,00,000 and Silver of Rs 30,00,000 on 1 April, 2019. Market value as on 31st March, 2020 of above investments are as follows: Shares Rs 47,500 (Decline in the value of shares is temporary.) Gold Rs 1,80,000 Silver Rs 30,55,000 How above investments will be shown in the books of accounts of M/s A Limited for the year ended 31st March, 2020 as per the provisions of AS 13 (Revised)?

[5 Marks | 8 Minute | ICAI Fav. (PYP Nov ’20), High Chance]

Answer 8. As per AS 13 (Revised) ‘Accounting for Investments, for investment in shares - if the investment is purchased with an intention to hold for short-term period (less than one year), then it will be classified as current investment and to be carried at lower of cost and fair value. In the given case Rs 25,000 shares held as current investment will be carried in the books at Rs 23,750 (Rs 47,500/2). If equity shares are acquired with an intention to hold for long term period (more than one year), then should be considered as long-term investment to be shown at cost in the Balance Sheet of the company. However, provision for diminution should be made to recognize a decline, if other than temporary, in the value of the investments. Hence, Rs 25,000 shares held as long-term investment will be carried in the books at Rs 25,000. Gold and silver are generally purchased with an intention to hold them for long term period (more than one year) until and unless given otherwise. Hence, the investment in Gold and Silver (purchased on 1st March, 2019) should continue to be shown at cost (since there is no ‘other than temporary’ diminution) as on 31st March, 2020. Thus Gold at Rs 1,00,000 and Silver at Rs 30,00,000 respectively will be shown in the books.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Classify investments based on the intention of holding. Value current investments at lower of cost and fair value, while long-term investments remain at cost unless decline is permanent. Solve each investment separately.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 292

Examiner’s Observation Temporary decline in long-term investments is often wrongly treated as permanent diminution.

Question 9. State whether the following statements are ‘True’ or ‘False’. Also give reason for your answer. As per the provisions of AS-13, a current investment is an investment that by its nature, is readily realizable and is intended to be held for not more than six months from the date on which such investment is made

[2 Marks | 2 Minute | ICAI Fav. (PYP May’19), Medium]

Answer 9. False: A current investment is an investment that is by its nature readily realizable and is intended to be held for not more than one year from the date on which such investment is made.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Memorize the exact definition of current investment under AS 13. State True/False first and then provide the reason. Keep the answer concise and standard-oriented.

Examiner’s Observation Students commonly write six months instead of one year, leading to loss of marks.

Question 12. On 15th June, 2018, Y limited wants to re-classify its investments in accordance with AS 13 (revised). Decide and state the amount of transfer, based on the following information: (1) A portion of long term investments purchased on 1st March, 2017 are to be re-classified as current investments. The original cost of these investments was Rs. 14 lakhs but had been written down by Rs. 2 lakhs (to recognize ‘other than temporary’ decline in value). The market value of these investments on 15th June, 2018 was Rs. 11 lakhs. (2) Another portion of long term investments purchased on 15th January, 2017 are to be re-classified as current investments. The original cost of these investments was Rs. 7 lakhs but had been written down to Rs. 5 lakhs (to recognize ‘other than temporary’ decline in value). The fair value of these investments on 15th June, 2018 was Rs. 4.5 lakhs. (3) A portion of current investments purchased on 15th March, 2018 for Rs. 7 lakhs are to bere-classified as long term investments, as the company has decided to retain them. The market value of these investments on 31st March, 2018 was Rs. 6 lakhs and fair value on 15th June 2018 was Rs. 8.5 lakhs.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 295

(4) Another portion of current investments purchased on 7th December, 2017 for Rs. 4 lakhs are to be re- classified as long term investments. The market value of these investments was: on 31st March, 2018 Rs. 3.5 lakhs on 15th June, 201 Rs. 3.8 lakhs.

[6 Marks | 10 Minute | ICAI Fav. (PYP May ‘19,), High Chance]

Answer 12. As per AS 13 (Revised) ‘Accounting for Investments’, where long-term investments are reclassified as current investments, transfers are made at the lower of cost and carrying amount at the date of transfer; and where investments are reclassified from current to long term, transfers are made at lower of cost and fair value on the date of transfer.

Accordingly, the re-classification will be done on the following basis: (i) In this case, carrying amount of investment on the date of transfer is less than the cost; hence this re- classified current investment should be carried at Rs. 12 lakhs in the books. (ii) In this case also, carrying amount of investment on the date of transfer is less than the cost; hence this re- classified current investment should be carried at Rs. 5 lakhs in the books. (iii) In this case, reclassification of current investment into long-term investments will be made at Rs. 7 lakhs as cost is less than its fair value of Rs.8.5 lakhs on the date of transfer. (Rs. 8,56,667 - Rs. 2,00,000) Considering that Rs. 13,00,000 was debited to Building WIP A/c earlier. (iv) In this case, market value (considered as fair value) is Rs. 3.8 lakhs on the date of transfer which is lower than the cost of Rs. 4 lakhs. The reclassification of current investment into long-term investments will be made at Rs. 3.8 lakhs.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Identify whether the transfer is from Current to Long-term or vice versa before applying the rule. Compare cost, carrying value and fair value systematically. Use a small comparison table.

Examiner’s Observation Students often use fair value where carrying amount should be considered, resulting in incorrect transfer values.

Examiner’s Observation Common mistakes included wrong treatment of pre-acquisition dividend, incorrect average cost calculation for shares sold, and omission of accrued interest on bonds at year-end.

Question 18. Mr. X acquires 200 shares of a company on cum-right basis for Rs. 70,000. He subsequently receives an offer of right to acquire fresh shares in the company in the proportion of 1:1 at Rs. 107 each. He does not subscribe but sells all the rights for Rs. 12,000. The market value of the shares after their becoming- rights has also gone down to Rs. 60,000. What should be the accounting treatment in this case?

[5 Marks | 4 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium]

Answer 18. As per AS 13, where the investments are acquired on cum-right basis and the market value of investments immediately after their becoming ex-right is lower than the cost for which they were acquired, it may be appropriate to apply the sale proceeds of rights to reduce the carrying amount of such investments to the market value. In this case, the amount of the ex-right market value of 200 shares bought by X immediately after the declaration of rights falls to Rs. 60,000. In this case, out of sale proceeds of Rs.12,000, Rs. 10,000 may be applied to reduce the carrying amount to bring it to the market value and Rs.2,000 would be credited to the profit and loss account

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Compare cost of investment with ex-right market value immediately after rights issue. Adjust sale proceeds of rights first against reduction in carrying amount and transfer only the excess to Profit & Loss Account.

Examiner’s Observation Many students credited the entire proceeds from sale of rights to Profit & Loss Account without reducing the carrying amount of investments where required by AS 13.
