Question 19. Legal Ltd. is engaged in the manufacturing of rubber. For its plant, it required machineries of latest technology. It usually resorts to Long Term Foreign Currency Borrowings for its fund requirements. On 1st April, 2023, it borrowed US \$1 million from International Funding Agency, USA when exchange rate was 1 \$ = Rs. 63. The funds were used for acquiring machineries, on the same date, to be used in three different plants. The useful life of the machineries is 10 years and their residual value is Rs. 30,00,000. Earlier also the company used to purchase machineries out of foreign borrowings. The exchange differences arising on such borrowings were charged to profit and loss account and were not capitalized even though the company had an option to capitalize it as per notified AS 11. Now for this new purchase of machinery, Legal Ltd, is interested to avail the option of capitalizing the same to the cost of asset. Exchange rate on 31st March, 2024 is 1 US \$ = Rs. 62. Assume that on 31st March, 2024, Legal Ltd. is not having any old long term foreign currency borrowings except for the amount borrowed for machinery purchased on 1st April, 2023. Comment whether Legal Ltd. can capitalize the exchange difference to the cost of asset on 31st March, 2024. If yes, then calculate the depreciation amount on machineries as on 31st March, 2024.

[5 Marks | 6 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP May 2025), High Chance]

Answer 19. As per paragraph 46A of AS 11, ‘The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates’, in respect of accounting periods commencing on or after 1st April, 2011, for an enterprise which had earlier exercised the option under paragraph 46 or not (such option to be irrevocable and to be applied to all such foreign currency monetary items), the exchange differences arising on reporting of long term foreign currency monetary items at rates different from those at which they were initially recorded during the period, or reported in previous financial statements, in so far as they relate to the acquisition of a depreciable capital asset, can be added to or deducted from the cost of the asset and shall be depreciated over the balance life of the asset. Accordingly, though Legal Ltd. had not earlier exercised the option, yet it can avail the option to capitalize the exchange difference to the cost of machinery by virtue of para 46A of AS 11. Further, since Legal Ltd. has no earlier long term foreign currency borrowings, it is not required to apply capitalization option to earlier borrowing also. Exchange difference to be capitalized and depreciation amount Rs. Cost of the asset in \$ 1 million Exchange rate on 1st April, 2023 Rs. 63 = 1\$ Cost of the asset in Rs.(1 million ×Rs. 63) 63 million Less: Exchange differences as on 31st March, 2024 (63-62) × \$ 1 million (1 million) (Gain)

62 million Less: Depreciation for 2023-2024 (62 million - 3 million)/ 10 years (5.90 million)

56.10 million

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 528

Check whether Para 46A option is available. Exchange gain/loss adjusts PPE cost and depreciation is computed on revised amount.

Examiner’s Observation Many students forget that Para 46A can be exercised even if not used earlier.

Question 20. Bansal Company Ltd. imported raw material worth US Dollars 12,000 on 15th January, 2024 when the exchange rate was Rs. 68 per US Dollar. The payment for the transaction was made on 5th May, 2024 when exchange rate was Rs. 64 per US Dollar. At the year end, 31st March, 2024, the rate of exchange was Rs. 65 per US Dollar. The accountant of the company passed entry on 31st March, 2024 adjusting the cost of raw material consumed for the difference between Rs. 64 and Rs. 68 per US Dollar. Discuss whether this treatment is justified as per the provisions of AS-11 (Revised).

[4 Marks | 4 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Sept. 2025), High Chance]

Answer 20. As per AS 11, ‘The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates’, initial recognition of a foreign currency transaction is done in the reporting currency by applying the exchange rate at the date of the transaction. Accordingly, on 15th January, 2024, the raw material purchased and its creditors will be recorded at US dollar 12,000× Rs. 68 = Rs. 8,16,000. Also, on balance sheet date such transaction is reported at closing rate of exchange, hence it will be valued at the closing rate i.e. Rs. 65 per US dollar (USD 12,000 ×Rs. 65 = Rs. 7,80,000) at 31st March, 2024, irrespective of the payment made for the same subsequently at lower rate in the next financial year. The difference of Rs. 3 (65 – 68) per US dollar i.e. Rs. 36,000 (USD 12,000 ×Rs. 3) will be shown as an exchange gain in the profit and loss account for the year ended 31st March, 2024 and will not be adjusted against the cost of raw materials. In the subsequent year on settlement date, the company would recognize or provide in the Profit and Loss account an exchange gain of Rs. 1 per US dollar, i.e. the difference from balance sheet date to the date of settlement between Rs. 65 and Rs. 64 per US dollar i.e. Rs. 12,000. Hence, the accounting treatment adopted by the Accountant of the company is incorrect i.e. it is not in accordance with the provisions of AS 11.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Always value outstanding trade payable at closing rate. Subsequent settlement difference belongs to next year.

Examiner’s Observation Students wrongly adjust exchange gain against raw material cost.

Question 22.

Particulars Exchange Rate per \$ Goods purchased on 1.1.20X1 for US \$ 15,000 RS 75 Exchange rate on 31.3.20X1 RS 74 Date of actual payment 7.7.20X1 RS 73 You are required to ascertain the loss/gain to be recognized for financial years ended 31st March, 20X1 and 31st March, 20X2 as per AS 11.

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 22. As per AS 11 on ‘The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates’, all foreign currency transactions should be recorded by applying the exchange rate on the date of transactions. Thus, goods purchased on 1.1.20X1 and corresponding creditors would be recorded at Rs. 11,25,000 (i.e. \$15,000 × Rs. 75) According to the standard, at the balance sheet date all monetary transactions should be reported using the closing rate. Thus, creditors of US \$15,000 on 31.3.20X1 will be reported at Rs. 11,10,000 (i.e. \$15,000 × Rs. 74) and exchange profit of Rs. 15,000 (i.e. 11,25,000 – 11,10,000) should be credited to Profit and Loss account in the year ended 31st March, 20X1. On 7.7.20X1, creditors of \$15,000 is paid at the rate of Rs. 73. As per AS 11, exchange difference on settlement of the account should also be transferred to Profit and Loss account. Therefore, Rs. 15,000 (i.e. 11,10,000 – 10,95,000) will be credited to Profit and Loss account in the year ended 31st March, 20X2.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Year-end gain/loss and settlement gain/loss should be calculated separately.

Examiner’s Observation Students tend to ignore the gain arising on final settlement.

Question 24. Assets and liabilities and income and expenditure items in respect of foreign branches (integral foreign operations) are translated into Indian rupees at the prevailing rate of exchange at the end of the year. The resultant exchange differences in the case of profit, is carried to other Liabilities Account and the Loss, if any, is charged to the statement of profit and loss. Comment.

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium]

Answer 24. The financial statements of an integral foreign operation (for example, dependent foreign branches) should be translated using the principles and procedures described in AS 11. The individual items in the financial statements of a foreign operation are translated as if all its transactions had been entered into by the reporting enterprise itself. Individual items in the financial statements of the foreign operation are translated at the actual rate on the date of transaction. For practical reasons, a rate that approximates the actual rate at the date of transaction is often used, for example, an average rate for a week or a month may be used for all transactions in each foreign currency during the period. The foreign currency monetary items (for example cash, receivables, and payables) should be reported using the closing rate at each balance sheet date. Non-monetary items (for example, fixed assets, inventories, investments in equity shares) which are carried in terms of historical cost denominated in a foreign currency should be reported using the exchange date at the date of transaction. Thus the cost and depreciation of the tangible fixed assets is translated using the exchange rate at the date of purchase of the asset if asset is carried at cost. If the fixed asset is carried at fair value, translation should be done using the rate existed on the date of the valuation. The cost of inventories is translated at the exchange rates that existed when the cost of inventory was incurred and realizable value is translated applying exchange rate when realizable value is determined which is generally closing rate. Exchange difference arising on the translation of the financial statements of integral foreign operation should be charged to profit and loss account. Exchange difference arising on the translation of the financial statement of foreign operation may have tax effect which should be dealt as per AS 22 ‘Accounting for Taxes on Income’.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 531

Thus, the treatment by the management of translating all assets and liabilities; income and expenditure items in respect of foreign branches at the prevailing rate at the year end and also the treatment of resultant exchange difference is not in consonance with AS 11.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Memorize translation rules item-wise: Monetary–Closing, Non-monetary–Historical, Revenue/Expense– Actual/Average.

Examiner’s Observation Students frequently apply NFO treatment instead of IFO treatment.

Question 28. A Ltd. purchased fixed assets costing Rs. 3,000 lakhs on 1.1.20X1 and the same was fully financed by foreign currency loan (U.S. Dollars) payable in three annual equal instalments. Exchange rates were 1 Dollar = Rs. 40.00 and Rs. 42.50 as on 1.1.20X1 and 31.12.20X1 respectively. First instalment was paid on 31.12.20X1. The entire difference in foreign exchange has been capitalised. You are required to state, how these transactions would be accounted for.

[5 Marks | 6 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium]

Answer 28. As per AS 11 ‘The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates’, exchange differences arising on the settlement of monetary items or on reporting an enterprise’s monetary items at rates different from those at which they were initially recorded during the period, or reported in previous financial statements, should be recognised as income or expenses in the period in which they arise. Thus exchange differences arising on repayment of liabilities incurred for the purpose of acquiring fixed assets are recognised as income or expense. Calculation of Exchange Difference:

3,000 lakhs Foreign currency loan = = 75 lakhs US Dollars

40 Exchange difference = 75 lakhs US Dollars = (42.50 – 40.00) = 187.50 Lakhs (including exchange loss on payment of first instalment) Therefore, entire loss due to exchange difference amounting 187.50 lakhs should be charged to profit and loss account for the Year. Note: The above answer has been given on the basis that the company has not exercised the option of capitalisation available under paragraph 46 of AS 11. However, if the company opts to avail the benefit given in paragraph 46A, then nothing is required to be done since the company has done the correct treatment.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Check whether Para 46A option is exercised. Without option → P\&L; with option → capitalization.

Question 30. Karna Ltd., an Indian Company, has the following foreign currency transactions during the financial year 2022-23: (i) On 1st July, 2022, imported goods from Try Ltd., a German based company, amounting to Rs. 30,96,000. (ii) On 1st October, 2022, imported plant and machinery from Lucy Ltd., a German based company, for € 18,500. The amount was paid on the date of import itself. (Ignore depreciation). (iii) On 1st December, 2022, exported good on credit to Cream Ltd., a German based company, amounting to Rs. 50,40,000. All the above transactions were recorded in the books of account at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of the transactions. Ignore taxes and duty on the above transactions. Payment due from Cream Ltd. and payment due to Try Ltd. is outstanding as on 31st March, 2023. Rate of exchange between reporting currency (Rs.) and foreign currency (€) on different dates are as under: On 1st July, 2022 1 € = Rs. 86 On 1st October, 2022 1 € = Rs. 88 On 1st December, 2022 1 € = Rs. 84 On 31st March, 2023 1 € = Rs. 90 You are required, as per AS-11: (i) To show value at which above items will appear in Balance sheet as on 31st March, 2023; (ii) To calculate the amount of gain/loss on each of above transactions on account of exchange differences, if any.

[6 Marks | 8 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Past Exam Nov’23), High Chance]

Answer 30. As per AS 11 “The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates”, Foreign currency monetary items should be reported using the closing rate. Non-monetary items which are carried in terms of historical cost denominated in a foreign currency should be reported using the exchange rate at the date of the transaction. Exchange differences arising on the settlement of monetary items or on reporting an enterprise’s monetary items at rates different from those at which they were initially recorded during the period, or reported in previous financial statements, should be recognised as income or as expenses in the period in which they arise. (i) Items given in the question will appear in the Balance Sheet at the following values: Trade Payables (30,96,000/86= 36,000 German Currency) x Rs. 90 = Rs. 32,40,000 Plant and Machinery 18,500 German Currency X Rs. 88 = Rs.16,28,000 © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 537

Trade Receivables (50,40,000/84= 60,000 German Currency) x Rs. 90 = Rs. 54,00,000 (ii) Amount of gain / loss on each transaction on account of exchange difference: Exchange loss on Transaction of import of goods from Try Ltd. = Rs. (1,44,000) [36,000 German Currency X Rs. 4 (i.e. 90-86)] Exchange gain on Transaction of export of goods to Cream Ltd = Rs. 3,60,000 [60,000 German Currency X Rs. 6 (i.e. 90-84)]

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Monetary items (payables/receivables) → Closing rate. PPE → Historical rate. Compute gain/loss separately for each item.

Examiner’s Observation Students commonly restate PPE at closing rate, which is incorrect under AS 11.

### PART B

### Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. Which of the following can be classified as an integral foreign operation? a) Branch office serving as an extension of the head office in terms of operations b) Independent subsidiary of the parent company c) Branch office independent of the head office in terms of operational decisions d) None of the above

(Study Material)

Ans: (a) Reason An integral foreign operation refers to an operation whose financial activities are so closely connected with the parent company's activities that they form an extension of the parent company, rather than being considered as separate entities. In accounting, integral foreign operations are typically accounted for using the functional currency of the parent company, and their financial statements are consolidated with those of the parent. Let's analyse the options: (a) Branch office serving as an extension of the head office in terms of operations: This describes an integral foreign operation. A branch that operates as an extension of the head office means it is closely tied to the operations of the parent company. Its financial activities are aligned with those of the parent, and its results are typically consolidated directly with the parent company's financials. Therefore, this fits the definition of an integral foreign operation. (b) Independent subsidiary of the parent company: An independent subsidiary operates as a separate entity from the parent company. The parent company may have a controlling interest, but the subsidiary's financial activities are accounted for separately and are not an extension of the parent. This makes it a foreign operation, but not an integral foreign operation. (c) Branch office independent of the head office in terms of operational decisions: A branch that is independent of the head office in terms of operations is considered a foreign operation, but since it is not an extension of the parent company, it would typically be classified as a self-sustaining foreign operation, not an integral one. (d) None of the above: Since option (a) is correct, this option is not applicable. Thus, (a) Branch office serving as an extension of the head office in terms of operations is the correct answer because it best describes an integral foreign operation.

Question 2. The debit or credit balance of “Foreign Currency Monetary Item Translation Difference Account” a) Is shown as “Miscellaneous Expenditure” in the Balance Sheet b) Is shown under “Reserves and Surplus” as a separate line item c) Is shown as “Other Non-current” in the Balance Sheet d) Is shown as “Current Assets” in the Balance Sheet

(Study Material)

Ans: (b) Reason

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 539

The Foreign Currency Monetary Item Translation Difference Account (FCMITDA) arises due to the translation of foreign currency monetary items (such as foreign currency loans or borrowings) that are carried at amortized cost and are subject to fluctuations in exchange rates. According to Accounting Standard 11 (AS 11) – The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates, any exchange difference on these monetary items is recognized in the financial statements in the period in which it occurs, and it is accumulated in a separate line item under Reserves and Surplus in the Balance Sheet. Here’s a breakdown of the options: (a) Is shown as “Miscellaneous Expenditure” in the Balance Sheet: This is incorrect because the FCMITDA is not classified as miscellaneous expenditure, but as part of reserves and surplus. (b) Is shown under “Reserves and Surplus” as a separate line item: This is correct. The foreign currency translation differences are transferred to a separate line item in Reserves and Surplus, and they are amortized over the life of the monetary item (such as a loan) to which they relate. (c) Is shown as “Other Non-current” in the Balance Sheet: This is incorrect because FCMITDA is not classified as a non-current asset or liability; it is a part of reserves. (d) Is shown as “Current Assets” in the Balance Sheet: This is incorrect, as FCMITDA is not classified under current assets. It is shown in the equity section of the Balance Sheet. Therefore, the correct classification is (b) Is shown under “Reserves and Surplus” as a separate line item. This ensures the proper accounting treatment of the foreign currency translation differences in accordance with AS 11\.

Question 3. Which of the following items should be converted to closing rate for the purposes of financial reporting? a) Items of Property, Plant and Equipment b) Inventory c) Trade Payables, Trade Receivables and Foreign Currency Borrowings d) All of the above

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason When preparing financial statements in the context of foreign operations or transactions, different items are translated using different exchange rates depending on the nature of the item. Here’s how the exchange rates are applied to each of the listed items: (a) Items of Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE): These are typically translated at the historical exchange rate (the rate at the date of acquisition). This is because PPE represents long-term assets, and it’s important to use the rate that reflects the cost at the time the asset was acquired, rather than fluctuating rates. (b) Inventory: Inventory is generally translated at the exchange rate at the date of purchase or at the rate prevailing at the end of the reporting period for the closing stock, depending on the method used. However, it does not require conversion to the closing rate specifically unless it has been purchased recently or is subject to currency fluctuations. (c) Trade Payables, Trade Receivables and Foreign Currency Borrowings: These items must be converted to the closing rate as of the balance sheet date. This is because they represent monetary items, which are typically

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 540

adjusted to reflect the current exchange rate. The balances are affected by exchange rate fluctuations up until the reporting date. Trade Payables: These represent amounts owed to creditors and are adjusted based on the closing exchange rate. Trade Receivables: These are amounts owed by customers, and their value should reflect the closing exchange rate. Foreign Currency Borrowings: These represent loans or borrowings in foreign currency and are similarly adjusted to reflect the closing exchange rate. Thus, the correct answer is (c) Trade Payables, Trade Receivables and Foreign Currency Borrowings, as these monetary items are translated at the closing exchange rate on the balance sheet date.

Question 4. If asset of an integral foreign operation is carried at cost, cost and depreciation of tangible fixed asset is translated at a) Average exchange rate b) Closing exchange rate c) Exchange rate at the date of purchase of asset d) Opening exchange rate

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason For integral foreign operations, the treatment of tangible fixed assets (like property, plant, and equipment) is in accordance with Accounting Standard 11 (AS 11) - The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates. When an asset is carried at cost (including tangible fixed assets), the exchange rate applied is the rate at the date of purchase of the asset. Here’s why: Exchange rate at the date of purchase of the asset is used because the historical cost of an asset needs to reflect the rate at which it was acquired. The cost of an asset, including tangible fixed assets, is determined based on the exchange rate on the date of acquisition or purchase, as this reflects the true cost incurred to acquire the asset in its original currency. Average exchange rate (Option a) is not applicable for assets carried at cost, as this rate reflects an average over a period and doesn't represent the specific acquisition cost of the asset. Closing exchange rate (Option b) is used for monetary items (such as trade payables or receivables), not for the historical cost of assets like tangible fixed assets. Opening exchange rate (Option d) is not relevant for determining the historical cost of an asset. It would not reflect the correct acquisition cost of the asset. Thus, the correct approach is to use the exchange rate at the date of purchase (Option c) for assets carried at cost, as it ensures that the asset is correctly valued based on the rate at which it was acquired.

Question 5. As per AS 11 assets and liabilities of non-integral foreign operations should be converted at rate a) Opening b) Average c) Closing d) Transaction

(Study Material)

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 541

Ans: (c) Reason As per Accounting Standard 11 (AS 11) - The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates, when dealing with non-integral foreign operations, the exchange rates applied to the assets and liabilities are as follows: Assets and liabilities of non-integral foreign operations should be converted at the closing exchange rate (the exchange rate at the balance sheet date). This is because non-integral foreign operations are considered as separate entities, and the balance sheet items must reflect the value of assets and liabilities at the prevailing exchange rate as of the reporting date. Here’s a breakdown of the options: (a) Opening exchange rate: This is typically used for translating opening balances at the start of the period, but not for converting assets and liabilities of non-integral foreign operations. (b) Average exchange rate: The average exchange rate is often used for translating income statement items (revenues, expenses, etc.) over the period but is not applied to the conversion of assets and liabilities, which must be converted at the closing exchange rate. (c) Closing exchange rate: This is the correct rate for converting assets and liabilities of non-integral foreign operations. The closing exchange rate reflects the value of the assets and liabilities at the end of the reporting period. (d) Transaction exchange rate: The exchange rate at the time of each individual transaction is used for translating specific transactions but is not applicable for converting the assets and liabilities of non-integral foreign operations. Therefore, the correct treatment as per AS 11 is to convert assets and liabilities of non-integral foreign operations using the closing exchange rate (Option c).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips First convert the INR amount into foreign currency (USD) using the transaction date rate, then restate it using the closing rate. Remember AS 11 rule: Monetary items like Trade Receivables and Loan are always translated at closing rate. Use shortcut formula: Closing Value = Original INR × (Closing Rate ÷ Initial Rate) to save calculation time in MCQs. For gain/loss, simply compare revised closing value with original booked amount; increase in receivable = gain, increase in liability = loss.

Examiner’s Observation Students often directly multiply INR amount by closing rate without first deriving USD amount. Common mistake: treating increase in foreign loan liability as “gain”; actually it is exchange loss for borrower. Many candidates confuse treatment of receivables and payables under AS 11. ICAI frequently tests exchange difference concepts in MCQs and case-based questions, so conceptual clarity is essential.

Chapter-7 Unit 4 AS 22- Accounting for Taxes on Income

PART A Question 1. Beta Ltd. is a full tax free enterprise for the first ten years of its existence and is in the second year of its operation. Depreciation timing difference resulting in a tax liability in year 1 and 2 is Rs. 1,000 lakhs and Rs. 2,000 lakhs respectively. From the third year it is expected that the timing difference would reverse each year by Rs. 50 lakhs. Assuming tax rate of 40%, find out the deferred tax liability at the end of the second year and any charge to the Profit and Loss account.

(5 Marks | 8 minute | ICAI Fav. [MTP Oct 19, RTP Nov’18) (Same concept different figures Old & New SM), High Chance]

Answer 1. As per para 13 of Accounting Standard (AS) 22, Accounting for Taxes on Income”, deferred tax in respect of timing differences which originate during the tax holiday period and reverse during the tax holiday period, should not be recognized to the extent deduction from the total income of an enterprise is allowed during the tax holiday period as per the provisions of sections 10A and 10B of the Income-tax Act. Deferred tax in respect of timing differences which originate during the tax holiday period but reverse after the tax holiday period should be recognized in the year in which the timing differences originate. However, recognition of deferred tax assets should be subject to the consideration of prudence. For this purpose, the timing differences which originate first should be considered to reverse first. Out of Rs. 1,000 lakhs depreciation, timing difference amounting Rs. 400 lakhs (Rs. 50 lakhs x 8 years) will reverse in the tax holiday period and therefore, should not be recognized. However, for Rs. 600 lakhs (Rs. 1,000 lakhs. Rs. 400 lakhs), deferred tax liability will be recognized for Rs. 240 lakhs (40% of Rs. 600 lakhs) in first year. In the second year, the entire amount of timing difference of Rs. 2,000 lakhs will reverse only after tax holiday period and hence, will be recognized in full. Deferred tax liability amounting Rs. 800 lakhs (40% of Rs. 2,000 lakhs) will be created by charging it to profit and loss account and the total balance of deferred tax liability account at the end of second year will be Rs. 1,040 lakhs (240 lakhs + 800 lakhs).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Identify the portion of timing differences reversing during the tax holiday period and exclude it. Apply FIFO (earliest originating difference reverses first) and compute DTL only on post-tax-holiday reversals.

Examiner’s Observation Most students create DTL on the entire timing difference and ignore the tax holiday exception and FIFO rule under AS 22.

Answer 3. (a) Accounting income and taxable income for a period are seldom the same. Permanent differences are those which arise in one period and do not reverse subsequently. Question 5. Is it permissible not to recognize deferred tax liability on the ground that the Company expects that there will be losses both for accounting and tax purposes in near future? You are required to give advice to the company.

(3 Marks | 3 minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP May 19), Medium]

Answer 5. The Company should provide for deferred tax liability on the timing differences irrespective for the fact that these timing differences will reverse in the period in which the Company expects to be in loss both from the accounting as well as tax point of view. It may, however, be added that the deferred tax liability recognized at the balance sheet date will give rise to future taxable income at the time of reversal thereof.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Remember that DTL recognition is mandatory whenever timing differences exist, irrespective of future losses. Prudence applies mainly to DTA recognition.

Examiner’s Observation Many students incorrectly conclude that expected future losses eliminate the need to recognize DTL.

Question 6 (i) Define followings as per AS 22: (ii) Accounting income (loss) (iii) Taxable income (tax loss) Tax expense (tax saving)

(3 Marks | 2 minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Nov’22), Medium]

Answer 6. Accounting income (loss) is the net profit or loss for a period, as reported in the statement of profit and loss, before deducting income-tax expense or adding income tax saving. Taxable income (tax loss) is the amount of the income (loss) for a period, determined in accordance with the tax laws, based upon which income- tax payable (recoverable) is determined. Taxable expenses is the aggregate of current tax and deferred tax charged or credited to the statement of profit and loss for the period.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Memorize ICAI definitions using keywords: Accounting Income, Taxable Income, and Tax Expense. Write them exactly as prescribed.

Examiner’s Observation Students provide practical meanings instead of standard definitions and lose theory marks.

Question 10. Can an enterprise offset deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities? If yes, prescribe the conditions required for such offset as per provisions of AS 22. ?

(3 Marks | 2 minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Nov ‘21), Medium Chance]

Answer 10. Yes. It can offset deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities. As per AS 22, an enterprise should offset deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities if: (i) the enterprise has a legally enforceable right to set off assets against liabilities representing current tax; and (ii) the deferred tax assets and the deferred tax liabilities relate to taxes on income levied by the same governing taxation laws.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Remember the two conditions: legally enforceable right of set-off and taxes governed by the same tax laws.

Examiner’s Observation Students usually mention only one condition, making the answer incomplete.

Question 11. Y Ltd. is a full tax free enterprise for the first ten years of its existence and is in the second year of its operation. Depreciation timing difference resulting in a tax liability in year 1 and 2 is Rs. 200 lakhs and Rs. 400 lakhs respectively. From the third year it is expected that the timing difference would reverse each year by Rs. 10 lakhs. Assuming tax rate of 40%, find out the deferred tax liability at the end of the second year and any charge to the Profit and Loss account.

(4 Marks | 5 minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 11. As per AS 22, ‘Accounting for Taxes on Income’, deferred tax in respect of timing differences which originate during the tax holiday period and reverse during the tax holiday period, should not be recognised to the extent deduction from the total income of an enterprise is allowed during the tax holiday period as per the provisions of sections 10A and 10B of the Income-tax Act. Deferred tax in respect of timing differences which originate during the tax holiday period but reverse after the tax holiday period should be recognised in the year in which the timing differences originate. However, recognition of deferred tax assets should be subject to the consideration of prudence. For this purpose, the timing differences which originate first should be considered to reverse first. Out of Rs. 200 lakhs timing difference due to depreciation, difference amounting Rs. 80 lakhs (Rs. 10 lakhs x 8 years) will reverse in the tax holiday period and therefore, should not be recognised. However, for Rs. 120 lakhs (Rs. 200 lakhs – Rs. 80 lakhs), deferred tax liability will be recognised for Rs. 48 lakhs (40% of Rs. 120 lakhs) in first year. In the second year, the entire amount of timing difference of Rs. 400 lakhs will reverse only after tax holiday period and hence, will be recognised in full. Deferred tax liability amounting Rs. 160 lakhs (40%

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 553

of Rs. 400 lakhs) will be created by charging it to profit and loss account and the total balance of deferred tax liability account at the end of second year will be Rs. 208 lakhs (48 lakhs + 160 lakhs).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Same approach as Q1—separate timing differences reversing within and after the tax holiday period and recognize DTL only for post-holiday reversals.

Examiner’s Observation Full DTL is often recognized incorrectly without considering the tax holiday exemption.

Question 15. Write short note on Timing difference and Permanent Difference as per AS 22.

(4 Marks | 4 minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP May 2025), High Chance]

Answer 15. Matching of taxes against revenue for a period poses special problems arising from the fact that in number of cases, taxable income may be different from the accounting income. The divergence between taxable income may be different from the accounting income arises due to two main reasons: Firstly, there are differences between items of revenue and expenses as appearing in the statement of profit and loss and the items which are considered as revenue, expenses or deductions for tax purposes, known as Permanent Difference. Secondly, there are differences between the amount in respect of a particular item of revenue or expense as recognised in the statement of profit and loss and the corresponding amount which is recognised for the computation of taxable income, known as Timing Difference. Permanent differences are the differences between taxable income and accounting income which arise in one accounting period and do not reverse subsequently. For example, an income exempt from tax or an expense that is not allowable as a deduction for tax purposes. Timing differences are those differences between taxable income and accounting income which arise in one accounting period and are capable of reversal in one or more subsequent periods. For e.g., Depreciation, Bonus, etc.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Focus on the key distinction—timing differences reverse, permanent differences never reverse. Always support with examples.

Examiner’s Observation Answers are often theoretical but lack examples and discussion of reversibility.

ABC Ltd. has profits before depreciation and taxes of Rs. 2,00,000 each year and corporate tax rate is 40 percent each year. The purchase of machine at a cost of Rs. 1,50,000 in 2022 gives rise to a tax saving of Rs. 60,000. The corporate tax rate has been assumed to be same in each of the three years. Calculate deferred tax and pass necessary journal entries. What will be the amount of deferred tax, if the substantively enacted tax rates for 2022, 2023 and 2024 are 40%, 35% and 38% respectively.

This gives rise to a deferred tax liability of Rs. 40,000. In 2023 and 2024 accounting income is lower than taxable income because the amount of depreciation charged for accounting purposes exceeds the amount of depreciation allowed for tax purposes by Rs. 50,000 each year. Accordingly, deferred tax liability is reduced by Rs. 20,000 each in both the years. As may be seen, tax expense in based on the accounting income of each period. In year 2024, the balance of deferred tax liability account would be nil. If the rate of tax changes, it would be necessary for the enterprises to adjust the amount of deferred tax liability carried forward by applying the tax rate that has been enacted or substantively enacted by the balance sheet date on accumulated timing differences at the end of the accounting year The amount of deferred tax liability would be computed as follows: The deferred tax liability carried forward each year would appear in the balance sheet as under: 31st March, 2022 = 0.40 (1,00,000) = Rs. 40,000 31st March, 2023 = 0.35 (50,000) = Rs. 17,500 31st March, 20224 = 0.38 (Zero) = Rs. Zero Accordingly, the amount debited (credited) to the profit and loss account (with corresponding credit or debit to deferred tax liability) for each year would be as under: 31st March, 2022 Debit = Rs. 40,000 31st March, 2023 (Credit) = Rs. (22,500) 31st March, 2024 (Credit) = Rs. (17,500)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips First prepare a year-wise table showing accounting depreciation, tax depreciation and timing differences. Compute Current Tax on taxable income and Deferred Tax on timing differences separately. Remember that excess tax depreciation in initial years creates DTL, while reversal in later years reduces DTL. If tax rates change, always value closing deferred tax balance using the substantively enacted tax rate applicable on the balance sheet date.

Examiner’s Observation Students often compute deferred tax on annual differences instead of cumulative timing differences. Many ignore the requirement of re-measuring deferred tax when tax rates change. Journal entries and presentation aspects are also frequently omitted, leading to loss of marks.

### PART B

### Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. As per AS 22 on ‘Accounting for Taxes on Income’, tax expense is a) Current tax + deferred tax charged to profit and loss account b) Current tax-deferred tax credited to profit and loss account c) Either (a) or (b)

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason As per AS 22 - Accounting for Taxes on Income, tax expense is determined as the total of current tax and deferred tax. Current Tax: This is the amount of tax payable or recoverable for the current period, based on the taxable income for the period. Deferred Tax: This represents the effect of timing differences between accounting income and taxable income that will reverse in the future. Deferred tax is recognized for both deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities. Tax Expense Calculation: Tax expense is the sum of the current tax and deferred tax. The deferred tax can either be: Charged to the profit and loss account (i.e., when it increases the tax expense), or Credited to the profit and loss account (i.e., when it reduces the tax expense). Thus, both the following scenarios are valid: (a) Current tax + deferred tax charged to profit and loss account: This scenario represents the total tax expense when the deferred tax is charged to the profit and loss account (for example, when there is a deferred tax liability). (b) Current tax - Deferred tax credited to profit and loss account: This scenario represents the total tax expense when the deferred tax is credited to the profit and loss account (for example, when there is a deferred tax asset). Conclusion Since both approaches are valid depending on whether deferred tax is charged or credited to the profit and loss account, option (c) - Either (a) or (b) is the correct answer. Thus, the correct answer is (c) Either (a) or (b).

Question 2. G Ltd. has provided the following information: Depreciation as per accounting records =Rs. 2,00,000 Depreciation as per tax records = Rs. 5,00,000 There is adequate evidence of future profit sufficiency. How much deferred tax asset/liability should be recognized as transition adjustment when the tax rate is 50%? a) Deferred Tax asset = Rs. 2,70,000. b) Deferred Tax asset = Rs. 1,35,000. c) Deferred Tax Liability = Rs. 2,70,000 d) Deferred Tax Liability = Rs. 1,35,000.

(Study Material)

Ans: (d) © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 565

Reason In this scenario, there is a timing difference between depreciation as per accounting records and tax records. Here's how to approach the solution: Step 1: Determine the Timing Difference Depreciation as per accounting records = Rs. 2,00,000 Depreciation as per tax records = Rs. 5,00,000 Since the depreciation in tax records is higher than the depreciation in the accounting records, this results in a temporary difference. The tax depreciation is greater than the accounting depreciation, meaning that taxable income is lower in the current period due to the higher depreciation in the tax records. This results in the recognition of a deferred tax liability, because the tax benefit (lower tax in the current period) will reverse in future periods when the depreciation under accounting records exceeds the depreciation under tax records. Step 2: Calculate the Timing Difference Timing Difference = Depreciation as per tax records - Depreciation as per accounting records Timing Difference=5,00,000−2,00,000=3,00,000 Step 3: Calculate the Deferred Tax Liability The deferred tax liability is calculated by multiplying the timing difference by the tax rate. Tax rate = 50% Deferred Tax Liability=Timing Difference Tax Rate Deferred Tax Liability=3,00,000×50%=1,50,000 So, the deferred tax liability is Rs. 1,50,000. However, there is a slight confusion in the options provided. The correct calculation would lead to a deferred tax liability of Rs. 1,50,000, but option (d) states Rs. 1,35,000. This could be an error in the question or the provided options. Conclusion According to the correct calculation, the deferred tax liability should be Rs. 1,50,000 based on the timing difference of Rs. 3,00,000 and the tax rate of 50%.

Question 3. State which of the followings statements are correct: (1) There are no pre-conditions required to recognize deferred tax liability, (2) Deferred tax asset under all circumstances can only be created if and only if there is reasonable certainty that future taxable income will arise. a) Both are correct. b) Only (1) is correct. c) Only (2) is correct. d) None of the statements are correct.

(Study Material)

Ans: (a) Reason Let's analyse each statement: Statement (1): "There are no pre-conditions required to recognize deferred tax liability." Correct. According to AS 22 - Accounting for Taxes on Income, a deferred tax liability should be recognized for all taxable temporary differences, except in specific situations where the reversal of the liability is not expected in the foreseeable future (e.g., investments in subsidiaries or joint ventures).

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 566

There are no specific pre-conditions required to recognize a deferred tax liability, except for ensuring that the liability is arising due to temporary differences. Statement (2): "Deferred tax asset under all circumstances can only be created if and only if there is reasonable certainty that future taxable income will arise." Correct. Deferred tax assets can only be recognized when there is reasonable certainty that the company will have sufficient future taxable profits to utilize the benefit of the tax deduction. This is a key principle in AS 22 to ensure that the deferred tax asset is not overstated. If there is doubt about the future profitability, a valuation allowance or non-recognition of the asset may be necessary. The recognition of a deferred tax asset depends on the expectation of future taxable income, and reasonable certainty is required to recognize it.

Conclusion: Both statements are correct because: Deferred tax liability is recognized without any specific pre-conditions, but subject to the existence of taxable temporary differences. Deferred tax assets can only be recognized when there is reasonable certainty that sufficient taxable income will be available to use the tax benefit in the future. Thus, the correct answer is (a) Both are correct.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 567

Chapter-8 Unit 1 AS 7- Construction Contracts

PART A Question 1. X Ltd. negotiates with Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL), for construction of “Franchise Retail Petrol Outlet Stations”. Based on proposals submitted to different Zonal offices of BPCL, the final approval for one outlet each in Zone A, Zone B, Zone C, Zone D, is awarded to X Ltd. Agreement (in single document) is entered into with BPCL for Rs. 490 lakhs. The agreement lays down values for each of the four outlets (Rs. 88 + 132 + 160 + 110 lakhs) in addition to individual completion time. You are required to examine and comment whether X Ltd., will treat it as a single contract or four separate contracts.

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP Oct ‘19, MTP Mar’18, MTP) (Same concepts different figures RTP May’19), High Chance]

Answer 1. As per AS 7 on ‘Construction Contracts’, when a contract covers a number of assets, the construction of each asset should be treated as a separate construction contract when: (a) Separate proposals have been submitted for each asset; (b) Each asset has been subject to separate negotiation and the contractor and customer have been able to accept or reject that part of the contract relating to each asset; and (c) The costs and revenues of each asset can be identified. In the given case, each outlet is submitted as a separate proposal to different Zonal Office, which can be separately negotiated, and costs and revenues thereof can be separately identified. Hence, each asset will be treated as a “single contract” even if there is one document of contract. Therefore, four separate contract accounts have to be recorded and maintained in the books of X Ltd. For each contract, principles of revenue and cost recognition have to be applied separately and net income will be determined for each asset as per AS 7.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Check AS 7 criteria for segmentation of contracts. Verify separate proposals, negotiations, and identifiable costs/revenues. If all three conditions are satisfied, treat each asset as a separate contract.

Examiner’s Observation Students often conclude it is a single contract because only one agreement document exists. Focus on substance rather than form. AS 7 permits division into separate contracts despite a common agreement.

A single agreement is entered into between the two parties. The agreement lays down the value of each of the 3 units i .e. Rs. 50 lakh, Rs. 60 lakh and Rs. 75 lakh respectively. Agreement also lays down the completion time for each unit. Comment, with reference to AS 7, whether ABC Ltd., should treat it as a single contract or three separate contracts.

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP May ‘21 May ’23 & Nov ’23), High Chance]

Answer 2. (b) As per AS 7 ‘Construction Contracts’, when a contract covers a number of assets, the construction of each asset should be treated as a separate construction contract when:

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 568

(a) separate proposals have been submitted for each asset; (b) each asset has been subject to separate negotiation and the contractor and customer have been able to accept or reject that part of the contract relating to each asset; and the costs and revenues of each asset can be identified. (c) ABC Ltd. has submitted separate proposals for each of the 3 units of commercial complex. Also the revenue and completion time has been laid down for each unit separately which implies separate negotiation for them. Therefore, ABC Ltd. is required to treat construction of each unit as a separate construction contract as the above- mentioned conditions of AS 7 are fulfilled in the given case.

Examiner’s Observation Many candidates forget to mention separate negotiation. Merely stating separate values is insufficient. Full marks require quoting AS 7 conditions.

Question 12. On 1st December, 2021, GR Construction Co. Ltd. undertook a contract to construct a building for Rs. 45lakhs. On 31st March, 2022, the company found that it had already spent Rs. 32.50 lakhs on the construction. Additional cost of completion is estimated at Rs. 15.10 lakhs. What amount should be charged to revenue in the final accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2022 as per provisions of AS-7?

[5 Marks | 8 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP May ’23 & Nov ’23, PYP May ’19), Medium-High]

Answer 12.

Particulars Rs. in lakhs Cost of construction incurred till date 32.50 Add: Estimated future cost 15.10 Total estimated cost of construction 47.60 Percentage of completion till date to total estimated cost of construction = (32.50/47.60)X 100 = 68.28% Proportion of total contract value recognized as revenue for the year ended 31st March, 2022 per AS 7 (Revised) = Contract price x percentage of completion = Rs. 45 lakh × 68.28% = Rs. 30.73 lakhs.

Particulars (Rs. in lakhs) Total cost of construction 47.60 Less: Total contract price (45.00) Total foreseeable loss to be recognized as expense 2.60 According to of AS 7, when it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss should be recognized as an expense immediately.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Compute total estimated cost and completion percentage. Apply percentage completion method for revenue. Check for foreseeable loss separately.

Examiner’s Observation Candidates frequently stop after revenue calculation. Expected loss must also be evaluated.

Answer 13. Calculation of total estimated cost of construction

Question 16. Rose Constructions undertake to construct a bridge for the Government of Uttar Pradesh. The construction commenced during the financial year ending 31.03.2024 and is likely to be completed by the next financial year. The contract is for a fixed price of Rs. 12 crore with an escalation clause. You are given the following information for the year ended 31.03.2024: Cost incurred upto 31.03.2024 Rs. 4 crore Cost estimated to complete the contract Rs. 6 crore Escalation in cost was by 5%. Hence, the contract price is also increased by 5%. You are required to ascertain the stage of completion and compute the amount of revenue and profit to be recognized for the year as per AS 7.

[5 Marks | 8 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Sept. 2025), Very High Chance] © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 580

Answer 16.

Particulars Rs.in crore Cost of construction of bridge incurred upto 31.3.2024 4.00 Add: Estimated future cost 6.00 Total estimated cost of construction 10.00 Contract Price (12 crore × 1.05) 12.60 crore Stage of completion Percentage of completion till date to total estimated cost of construction = (4/10)×100 = 40% Revenue and Profit to be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2024 as per AS 7: Proportion of total contract value recognized as revenue = Contract price x percentage of completion = Rs. 12.60 crore x 40% = Rs. 5.04 crore Profit for the year ended 31st March, 2024 = Rs. 5.04 crore – Rs. 4 crore = 1.04 crore.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Revise contract price for escalation. Determine percentage completion using estimated total cost. Revenue and profit follow percentage completion method.

Question 20. (b) Mr. ‘X’ as a contractor has just entered into a contract with a local municipal body for building a flyover. As per the contract terms, ‘X’ will receive an additional Rs. 2 crore if the construction of the flyover were to be finished within a period of two years of the commencement of the contract. Mr. X wants to recognize this revenue since in the past he has been able to meet similar targets very easily. Is X correct in his proposal? Discuss.

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Nov ‘21), High Chance]

Answer 20. (b) According to AS 7 (Revised) ‘Construction Contracts’, incentive payments are additional amounts payable to the contractor if specified performance standards are met or exceeded. For example, a contract may allow for an incentive payment to the contractor for early completion of the contract. Incentive payments are included in contract revenue when:

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 584

(i) the contract is sufficiently advanced that it is probable that the specified performance standards will be met or exceeded; and (ii) the amount of the incentive payment can be measured reliably. In the given problem, the contract has not even begun and hence the contractor (Mr. X) should not recognize any revenue of this contract.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Focus on conditions for recognizing incentive payments. Contract must be sufficiently advanced. Probability and reliable measurement are both required.

Examiner’s Observation Past experience alone is not enough for recognition. Incentive revenue cannot be booked at contract inception.

Question 21. (a) Sky Limited belongs to Heavy Engineering Contractors specializing in construction of Flyovers. The company just entered into a contract with a local municipal corporation for building a flyover. No activity has started on this contract. As per the terms of the contract, Sky Limited will receive an additional Rs. 50 lakhs if the construction of the flyover were to be finished within a period of two years from the commencement of the contract. The Accountant of the entity wants to recognize this revenue since in the past the company has been able to meet similar targets very easily. Give your opinion on this treatment.

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP May ‘21 May ’23 & Nov ’23), High Chance]

Answer 21. (a) According to AS 7 ‘Construction Contracts’, incentive payments are additional amounts payable to the contractor if specified performance standards are met or exceeded. For example, a contract may allow for an incentive payment to the contractor for early completion of the contract. Incentive payments are included in contract revenue when both the conditions are met: (i) the contract is sufficiently advanced that it is probable that the specified performance standards will be met or exceeded; and the amount of the incentive payment can be measured reliably. (a) In the given problem, the contract has not even begun and hence the contractor (Sky Limited) should not recognize any revenue of this contract. Therefore, the accountant’s contention for recognizing Rs. 50 lakhs as revenue is not correct.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Apply same AS 7 rules relating to incentive payments. Verify completion probability and reliable measurement. No recognition before contract progress exists.

Examiner’s Observation Candidates often assume certainty from past performance. Contract advancement is a mandatory condition.

Question 22. A contractor has entered into a contract with a municipal body for construction of a flyover. As per the contract terms, the contractor will receive an additional Rs. 2 Crore as incentive if the construction of the flyover were to be finished within a period of two years from the start of the contract. The contractor wants to recognize this revenue since in the past he has been able to meet similar targets very easily. Explain whether the contractor’s view-point is correct?

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium]

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 585

Answer 22. The contractor’s view is not entirely correct in considering the variation as a part of contract revenue. There is an argument that he has been able to complete similar contracts within stipulated time. However, each contract needs to be assessed in isolation with respect to the specific challenges associated with the timing and uncertainty in completion. Accordingly, the contractor needs to validate the assumptions with respect to the specific contract. Only after that assessment is done, the incentive of Rs. 2 crore may be included within the contract revenue.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Evaluate incentive based on contract-specific circumstances. Do not rely solely on previous experience. Recognition depends on probability assessment.

Examiner’s Observation Students tend to conclude immediately without analysis. Each contract must be assessed independently.

Question 23. AB contactors enters into a contract on 1st January 20X1 with XY to construct a 5- storied building. Under the contract, AB is required to complete the construction in 3 years (i.e., by 31st December 20X3). The following information is relevant: Fixed price (agreed) Rs.5 crore Material cost escalation (to the extent of 20% of increase in material cost) Labour cost escalation (up to 30% of increase in minimum wages)

In case AB is able to complete the construction in less than 2 years and 10 months, it will be entitled for an additional incentive of Rs.50 lakh. However, in case the construction is delayed beyond 3 years and 2 months, XY will charge a penalty of Rs.20 lakh. At the start of the contract, AB has a reason to believe that construction will be completed in 2 years and 8 months. Assume that the construction was actually completed in 2 years 9 months.

Labour cost was originally estimated to be Rs.1.20 crore (based on initial minimum wages). However, the costs have increased by 25% during the construction period. Material costs have increased by 40% due to short-supply. The total increase in material cost due to the 40% escalation is Rs.80 lakh. You are required to suggest what should be the contract revenue in above case? Assume that in year 20X2, XY has requested AB to increase the scope of the contract. An additional floor is required to be constructed and there is an increase in contract fee by Rs.1 crore. AB has incurred a cost of Rs.20 lakh for getting the local authority approvals which it will be entitled to claim from XY in addition to the increase in the fixed fee. Also measure the total contract revenue in this case.

[8 Marks | 12 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 23. Total Revenue after considering the escalation costs, claims and incentives:

Particulars Rs. Fixed Price: 5.00 crore Incentive for early completion 0.50 crore Material costs recovery (to the extent of 20%) 0.40 crore © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 586

Labour costs recovery (Actual increase is less than 30%) [1.20 crore × 25%] 0.30 crore Total Contract Revenue 6.20 crore Add: Variation to the contract 1.00 crore Add: Claims recoverable from XY 0.20 crore Total Contract Revenue 7.40 crore (a) Contract costs should comprise: (i) costs that relate directly to the specific contract; (ii) costs that are attributable to contract activity in general and can be allocated to the contract; and (iii) such other costs as are specifically chargeable to the customer under the terms of the contract.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Include escalation, incentives, claims, and approved variations in contract revenue. Calculate each component separately. Present total contract revenue systematically.

Examiner’s Observation Claims and variations are often omitted. Revenue should include all reliably measurable components.

Question 24. PQ & Associates undertakes a construction contract the details of which are provided below: Total Contract Value Rs.40 lakh Costs incurred to date Rs.3 lakh Estimated future costs of completion Rs.30 lakh Work completed 10% The work has started some time ago and there is an uncertainty with respect to the outcome of the contract due to expected changes in regulations. PQ is certain that it would be able to recover the costs incurred to date.

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 24. In the given case, revenue and costs can only be recognised to the extent of the costs incurred and those which are expected to be recovered. Therefore, the profit & loss statement would appear as under: Contract Revenue Rs.3 lakh Contract Costs Rs.3 lakh Contract Profit Nil When the uncertainties that prevented the outcome of the contract being estimated reliably cease to exist, revenue and expenses associated with the construction contract should be recognised by the percentage completion method.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips When outcome cannot be estimated reliably, recognize revenue only to recoverable costs. No profit should be recognized. Mention AS 7 exception clearly.

Examiner’s Observation Students often apply percentage completion incorrectly. Reliable estimation is a prerequisite for profit recognition.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 587

Question 25. (a) In the case of a fixed price contract, the outcome of a construction contract can be estimated reliably only when certain conditions prescribed under AS 7 are satisfied. You are required to describe these conditions mentioned in the standard.

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Nov ‘21), High Chance]

Answer 25. (a) In the case of a fixed price contract, the outcome of a construction contract can be estimated reliably when all the following conditions are satisfied: (i) total contract revenue can be measured reliably; (ii) it is probable that the economic benefits associated with the contract will flow to the enterprise; (iii) both the contract costs to complete the contract and the stage of contract completion at the reporting date can be measured reliably; and (iv) the contract costs attributable to the contract can be clearly identified and measured reliably so that actual contract costs incurred can be compared with prior estimates.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Pure theory question. Memorize the four conditions for reliable estimation in fixed-price contracts. Present answer in point format.

Examiner’s Observation Incomplete listing of conditions leads to loss of marks. Exact AS 7 wording fetches better scores.

Question 27. It is argued that profit on construction contracts should not be recognized until the contract is completed. Please explain whether you believe that this suggestion would improve the quality of financial reporting for long-term construction contracts.

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav.] Answer 27. Usually, construction contracts are long term nature i.e., the contracts are entered in one accounting period, however, the work performed will flow into more than one accounting year. If the profit on construction contracts is not recognised over the construction period, then the costs incurred during the earlier years of the contract would be recognised without any corresponding revenue. This will result in losses for initial years followed high profits in future years.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Discuss matching concept and percentage completion method. Compare with completed contract approach. Explain impact on financial reporting quality.

Examiner’s Observation Answers should be conceptual, not numerical. Focus on matching revenue with related costs.

Question 28. B Ltd. undertook a construction contract for Rs. 50 crores in April, 2020. The cost of construction was initially estimated at Rs. 35 crores. The contract is to be completed in 3 years. While executing the contract, the company estimated that the cost of completion of the contract would be Rs. 53 crores. Can the company provide for the expected loss in the financial Statements for the year ended 31st March, 2021? Explain.

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP May 22), High Chance]

Answer 28. As per para 35 of AS 7 “Construction Contracts”, when it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss should be recognized as an expense immediately. Therefore, the foreseeable loss of Rs. 3 crores (Rs. 53 crores less Rs. 50 crores) should be recognized as an expense immediately in the year ended 31st March, 2021. The amount of loss is determined irrespective of (i) Whether or not work has commenced on the contract; (ii) Stage of completion of contract activity; or (iii) The amount of profits expected to arise on other contracts which are not treated as a single construction contract in accordance provisions of AS 7.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 589

The current treatment under AS 7 results in matching of revenue and associated costs as they are recognised during the same period. Also, the current accounting incorporates the prudence concept as any foreseeable losses are accounted for immediately. Therefore, AS 7 results in a fair representation of the underlying financial substance of the transaction.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Directly apply AS 7 Para 35. Expected loss is recognized immediately. Mention that stage of completion is irrelevant.

Examiner’s Observation Students sometimes defer recognition of loss. Prudence principle is the key point.

17,35,000

4,75,000+8,60,000 % of work completed = = 76.95% (Rounded off)

17,35,000 Revenue to be recognized (cumulative) = 20,00,000 ×76.95% = 15,39,000 Less: revenue recognized in Year 1 = (9,24,800) Revenue to be recognized in Year 1 = Rs. 6,14,200 © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 590

Year 3 Whole contract got completed therefore total contract value less revenue recognized up to year 2 will be amount of revenue to be recognized in year 3 i.e. 20,00,000 – 15,39,000 (9,24,800 + 6,14,200) = Rs. 4,61,000. Note: Calendar year has been considered as accounting year.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Compute completion percentage annually. Determine cumulative revenue first. Current year revenue equals cumulative revenue less prior years’ revenue.

Examiner’s Observation Retention money should not affect revenue recognition. Percentage completion method must be applied consistently.

### PART B

### Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Questions 1- – 3: XY Ltd. agrees to construct a building on behalf of its client GH Ltd. on 1st April 20X1. The expected completion time is 3 years. XY Ltd. incurred a cost of Rs. 30 lakh up to 31st March 20X2. It is expected that additional costs of Rs. 90 lakh. Total contract value is Rs. 112 lakh. As at 31st March 20X2, XY Ltd. has billed GH Ltd. For Rs. 42 lakh as per the agreement. Assume that the work is completed to the extent of 75% by the end of Year 2.

1. Revenue to be recognized by XY Ltd. for the year ended 31st March 20X2 is

(a) Rs. 28 lakh (b) Rs. 42 lakh (c) Rs. 30 lakh (d) Rs. 32 lakh

Answer: (a) Rs. 28 lakh Reason: 75% completion = Rs. 112 lakh × 75% = Rs. 84 lakh. Less Rs. 42 lakh billed = Rs. 28 lakh.

2. Total expense to be recognised in Year 1 is

(a) Rs. 30 lakh (b) Rs. 120 lakh (c) Rs. 38 lakh (d) Rs. 36 lakh

Answer: (d) Rs. 36 lakh Reason: Total incurred cost by Year 2 = Rs. 30 lakh in Year 1 + Rs. 6 lakh in Year 2.

3. Revenue to be recognised for year 2 is

(a) Rs. 84 lakh (b) Rs. 42 lakh (c) Rs. 56 lakh (d) Rs. 28 lakh

Answer: (c) Rs. 56 lakh Reason: Revenue for Year 2 = Rs. 84 lakh (75% of Rs. 112 lakh) - Rs. 28 lakh (Year 1) = Rs. 56 lakh.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips First compute the total estimated contract cost and determine the stage of completion using the cost-to-cost method. Calculate cumulative revenue as: Contract Revenue × Percentage of Completion. For subsequent years, derive current-year revenue by deducting revenue already recognized in earlier years.

Examiner’s Observation Students often treat amount billed as contract revenue, leading to incorrect answers. Many candidates fail to distinguish between cumulative revenue and current-year revenue. Errors are also observed in calculating the percentage of completion and allocating revenue between years.
