Question 12. A Ltd. acquired 60% shares of B Ltd. @ Rs. 20 per share. Following is the extract of Balance Sheet of B Ltd.:

Particulars Rs. 10,00,000 Equity Shares of Rs. 10 each 1,00,00,000 10% Debentures 10,00,000 Trade Payables 55,00,000 Property, Plant and Equipment 70,00,000 Investments 45,00,000 Current Assets 68,00,000 Loans and Advances 22,00,000 On the same day B Ltd. declared dividend at 20% and as agreed between both the companies Property, Plant and Equipment were to be depreciated @ 10% and investment to be taken at market value of Rs. 60,00,000. Calculate the Goodwill or Capital Reserve to be recorded in Consolidated Financial Statements.

[5 Marks | 6 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 12. Since dividend is declared by B Ltd. on the date of acquisition itself, it would be out of the divisible profits of B Ltd. existing on the date of acquisition i.e., pre- acquisition profits from the perspective of A Ltd. Accordingly, as per AS 13, such pre-acquisition dividend would be reduced from the cost of investment, as seen below in the determination of Goodwill on the date of acquisition.

Particulars Rs. Rs. Assets Property, Plant and Equipment 70,00,000 Less: Value written off (Rs. 70 lakhs × 10%) (7,00,000)

63,00,000 Investments at Market Value 60,00,000 Current Assets 68,00,000 Loans and Advances 22,00,000 2,13,00,000 Less: Liabilities Trade Payables 55,00,000 10% Debentures 10,00,000 (65,00,000) Net Assets of B Ltd. 1,48,00,000 Share of A Ltd. in Net Assets of B Ltd.: 60% 88,80,000 Less: Cost of Investment in B Ltd. (60% stake): 10,00,000 Equity Shares x 60% × Rs. 20 per share 1,20,00,000 Less: Pre-acquisition dividend: 6,00,000 shares × Rs. 2 (12,00,000) (1,08,00,000) Goodwill on Date of Acquisition 19,20,000

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Calculate net assets after considering agreed valuation changes. Since dividend is declared on the acquisition date, treat it as pre-acquisition dividend and deduct it from acquisition cost before computing goodwill or capital reserve.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 709

Examiner’s Observation Students frequently fail to identify the dividend as pre-acquisition. Many also ignore valuation adjustments in PPE and investments, resulting in incorrect net asset values.

Would restatement be necessary to make the accounting policies adopted by A Ltd. and B Ltd. uniform.

[5 Marks | 7 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium-High]

Answer 17. As per para 20 and 21 of AS 21, Consolidated financial statements: Consolidated financial statements should be prepared using uniform accounting policies for like transactions and other events in similar circumstances. If it is not practicable to use uniform accounting policies in preparing the consolidated financial statements, that fact should be disclosed together with the proportions of the items in the consolidated financial statements to which the different accounting policies have been applied. If a member of the group uses accounting policies other than those adopted in the consolidated financial statements for like transactions and events in similar circumstances, appropriate adjustments are made to its financial statements when they are used in preparing the consolidated financial statements. Accordingly, in the given case, restatement would be required to make the accounting policies of A Ltd and B Ltd uniform. Adjusted reserves of B Ltd.:

Question 20. A Ltd. holds 80% of the equity capital and voting power in B Ltd. A Ltd sells inventories costing Rs. 180 lacs to B Ltd at a price of Rs. 200 lacs. The entire inventories remain unsold with B Ltd at the financial year end i.e. 31 March 2020. What will be the accounting treatment for this transaction in the consolidated financial statements of A Ltd?

[4 Marks | 3 Minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP Oct 20, MTP Mar 22 & Oct ‘23), Very High Chance]

Answer 20. This would be the case of downstream transaction. In the consolidated profit and loss account for the year ended 31 March 2020, entire transaction of sale and purchase of Rs. 200 lacs each, would be eliminated by reducing both sales and purchases (cost of sales). Further, the unrealized profits of Rs. 20 lacs (i.e. Rs. 200 lacs – Rs. 180 lacs), would be eliminated from the consolidated financial statements for financial year ended 31 March 2020, by reducing the consolidated profits/ increasing the consolidated losses, and reducing the value of closing inventories as of 31 March 2020.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips First identify the transaction as a downstream sale (parent to subsidiary). Eliminate the entire intra-group sale and purchase and remove unrealized profit from both consolidated profit and closing inventory.

Examiner’s Observation Students often treat downstream transactions like upstream transactions and incorrectly adjust minority interest. The unrealized profit should be eliminated entirely against the parent’s profits only.

Question 21. Hemant Ltd. purchased 80% shares of Power Ltd. on 1st January, 2019 for Rs. 2,10,000. The issued capital of Power Ltd., on 1st January, 2019 was Rs. 1,50,000 and the balance in the Profit & Loss Account was Rs. 90,000. During the year ended 31st December, 2019, Power Ltd. earned a profit of Rs. 30,000 and at year end, declared and paid a dividend of Rs. 22,500. What is the amount of minority interest as on 1st January, 2019 and 31st December, 2019? Also compute goodwill/ capital reserve at the date of acquisition.

[5 Marks | 8 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (MTP Oct 20, Old & New SM), High Chance]

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 726

Answer 21. Total dividend paid is Rs. 22,500 (out of post-acquisition profits), hence dividend received by Hemant will be credited to P & L account. Hemant Ltd.’s share of dividend = Rs. 22,500 × 80% = Rs. 18,000 Goodwill on consolidation (at the date of acquisition): Rs. Rs. Cost of shares 2,10,000 Less: Face value of capital i.e. 80% of capital 1,20,000 Add: Share of capital profits [90,000 X 80 %] 72,000 (1,92,000) Goodwill 18,000 Minority interest on:

- 1st January, 2019:

20% of Rs. 2,40,000 [1,50,000 + 90,000] 48,000 31st December, 2019: 20% of Rs.2,47,500 [1,50,000 + 90,000 + 30,000 – 22,500] 49,500

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Identify net assets at acquisition (Share Capital + Pre-acquisition P&L) first. Compute Goodwill/Capital Reserve using Parent’s share in net assets. For Minority Interest, apply minority percentage to net assets at acquisition and consolidation dates. Adjust post-acquisition dividend before calculating closing MI.

Examiner’s Observation Students frequently ignore dividend adjustment while calculating closing Minority Interest. Errors are also seen in classifying pre- and post-acquisition profits correctly.

Examiner’s Observation Many students apply holding company percentage instead of minority percentage. Some calculate MI only on share capital and omit reserves/profits.

5. Capital Reserve 1,05,000

Price paid by White Ltd. for 2,250 shares (A) 2,70,000 © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 747

Intrinsic value of the shares- Paid-up value of 2,250 shares held by White Ltd. i.e. 2,250 ×Rs. 100 2,25,000 Add 75% share of pre-acquisition reserves & profit (70,000 × 75%) 52,500 (B)

2,77,500 Capital reserve (A – B) 7,500

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Determine pre- and post-acquisition profits based on the acquisition date. Compute capital reserve/goodwill and minority interest before preparing the final balance sheet. Adjust cash-in-transit and remove inter- company balances carefully.

Examiner’s Observation Students frequently overlook cash-in-transit adjustment. Incorrect apportionment of profits between pre- and post-acquisition periods leads to wrong consolidation figures.

Question 32. Hemant Ltd. purchased 80% shares of Power Ltd. on 1st January, 20X1 for Rs. 2,10,000. The Issued capital of Power Ltd., on 1st January, 20X1 was Rs. 1,50,000 and the balance in the Profit &Loss Account was Rs. 90,000. During the year ended 31st December, 20X1, Power Ltd. earned a profit of Rs. 30,000 and at year end, declared and paid a dividend of Rs. 22,500. What is the amount of minority interest as on 1st January, 20X1 and 31st December, 20X1? Also compute goodwill/ capital reserve at the date of acquisition.

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 32. Total dividend paid is Rs. 22,500 (out of post-acquisition profits), hence dividend received by Hemant will be credited to P & L account. Hemant Ltd.’s share of dividend = Rs. 22,500 × 80% = Rs.18,000 Goodwill on consolidation (at the date of acquisition): Rs. Rs. Cost of shares 2,10,000 Less: Face value of capital i.e. 80% of capital 1,20,000 Add: Share of capital profits [90,000 ×80 %] 72,000 (1,92,000) Goodwill 18,000 Minority interest on: Minority interest on: 20% of Rs. 2,40,000 [1,50,000 + 90,000] 48,000

- 31st December, 20X1:

20% of Rs. 2,47,500 [1,50,000 + 90,000 + 30,000 – 22,500] 49,500

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Calculate Goodwill first using cost of investment and parent’s share in net assets at acquisition. Compute Minority Interest separately at acquisition and consolidation dates using the minority percentage. Use a direct formula approach instead of preparing detailed statements.

Examiner’s Observation Candidates commonly forget that dividend is paid out of post-acquisition profits. This results in incorrect Minority Interest and Goodwill calculations.

Question 36. H Ltd. acquire 70% of equity share of S Ltd. as on 1st January, 2021 at a cost of Rs. 5,00,000 when S Ltd. had an equity share capital of Rs. 5,00,000 and reserves and surplus of Rs. 40,000. Both the companies follow calendar year as the accounting year. In the four consecutive years, S Ltd. performed badly and suffered losses of Rs. 1,25,000, Rs. 2,00,000, Rs. 2,50,000 and Rs. 60,000 respectively. Thereafter in 2025, S Ltd. experienced turnaround and registered an annual profit of Rs. 25,000. In the next two years i.e. 2026 and 2027, S Ltd. recorded annual profits of Rs. 50,000 and Rs. 75,000 respectively. Show the Minority Interests and Cost of Control at the end of each year for the purpose of consolidation.

[8 Marks | 10 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (MTP May 2025), Medium]

Answer 36. The losses applicable to the minority in a consolidated subsidiary may exceed the minority interest in the equity of the subsidiary. The excess, and any further losses applicable to the minority, are adjusted against the majority interest except to the extent that the minority has a binding obligation to, and is able to, make good the losses. If the subsidiary subsequently reports profits, all such profits are allocated to the majority interest until the minority's share of losses previously absorbed by the majority has been recovered.

Question 42. A Ltd. holds 80% of the equity capital and voting power in B Ltd. A Ltd. sells inventories costing Rs. 180lacs to B Ltd at a price of Rs. 200 lacs. The entire inventories remain unsold with B Ltd. at the A Ltd. holds 75% of the equity capital and voting power in B Ltd. A Ltd. purchases inventories costing Rs.150 lacs from B Ltd at a price of Rs. 200 lacs. The entire inventories remain unsold with A Ltd. at the financial year-end i.e. 31 March 20X1. Suggest the accounting treatment for the above mentioned transactions in the consolidated financial statements of A Ltd. giving reference of the relevant guidance/standard.

[4 Marks | 8 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 770

Answer 42. As per para 16 and 17 of AS 21, intragroup balances and intragroup transactions and resulting unrealized profits should be eliminated in full. Unrealized losses resulting from intragroup transactions should also be eliminated unless cost cannot be recovered. Intragroup balances and intragroup transactions, including sales, expenses and dividends, are eliminated in full. Unrealized profits resulting from intragroup transactions that are included in the carrying amount of assets, such as inventory and fixed assets, are eliminated in full. Unrealized losses resulting from intragroup transactions that are deducted in arriving at the carrying amount of assets are also eliminated unless cost cannot be recovered. One also needs to see whether the intragroup transaction is “upstream” or “down-stream”. Upstream transaction is a transaction in which the subsidiary company sells goods to holding company. While in the downstream transaction, holding company is the seller and subsidiary company is the buyer. In the case of upstream transaction, since the goods are sold by the subsidiary to holding company; profit is made by the subsidiary company, which is ultimately shared by the holding company and the minority shareholders. In such a transaction, if some goods remain unsold at the balance sheet date, the unrealized profit on such goods should be eliminated from minority interest as well as from consolidated profit on the basis of their share-holding besides deducting the same from unsold inventory. But in the case of downstream transaction, the whole profit is earned by the holding company, therefore, whole unrealized profit should be adjusted from unsold inventory and consolidated profit and loss account only irrespective of the percentage of the shares held by the parent.

Using above mentioned guidance, following adjustments would be required: a) This would be the case of downstream transaction. In the consolidated profit and loss account for the year ended 31 March 20X1, entire transaction of sale and purchase of Rs. 200 lacs each, would be eliminated by reducing both sales and purchases (cost of sales). Further, the unrealized profits of Rs. 20 lacs (i.e. Rs. 200 lacs – Rs. 180 lacs), would be eliminated from the consolidated financial statements for financial year ended 31 March 20X1, by reducing the consolidated profits/ increasing the consolidated losses, and reducing the value of closing inventories as of 31 March 20X1. b) This would be the case of upstream transaction. In the consolidated profit and loss account for the year ended 31 March 20X1, entire transaction of sale and purchase of Rs. 200 lacs each, would be eliminated by reducing both sales and purchases (cost of sales). Further, the unrealized profits of Rs. 50 lacs (i.e. Rs. 200 lacs – Rs. 150 lacs), would be eliminated in the consolidated financial statements for financial year ended 31 March 20X1, by reducing the value of closing inventories by Rs.50 lacs as of 31 March 20X1. In the consolidated balance sheet as of 31 March 20X1, A Ltd.’s share of profit from B Ltd will be reduced by Rs. 37.50lacs (being 75% of Rs. 50 lacs) and the minority’s share of the profits of B Ltd would be reduced by Rs.12.50 lacs (being 25% of Rs.50 lacs).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips First determine whether the transaction is upstream or downstream. Compute unrealized profit in closing inventory and eliminate it appropriately. Remember that minority interest is affected only in upstream transactions.

Examiner’s Observation Many students fail to distinguish between upstream and downstream transactions. Unrealized profit adjustments are frequently made incorrectly, especially regarding the treatment of minority interest.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 771

In the books of XYZ Ltd. Particulars Rs. Rs. Approach & Time-Saving Tips Classify profits into pre-acquisition and post-acquisition categories before calculating goodwill and minority interest. [4 Marks | 8 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium]

Answer 45. The profits of S Ltd., have to be divided between capital and revenue profits from the point of view of the holding company:

Capital Profit (Pre- Revenue Profit (Post- acquisition) Rs. acquisition) Rs. Balance on 1.1.20X1 1,25,000 — Profit for 20X1 (3,00,000 ×7/12) 1,75,000 (3,00,000×5/12) 1,25,000 Total 3,00,000 1,25,000 Proportionate share of H Ltd. (3/5) 1,80,000 75,000 Total dividend declared = Rs. 5,00,000 X 40 % = Rs. 2,00,000 H Ltd.’s share in the dividend = Rs. 2,00,000 X 3/5 = Rs. 1,20,000 There can be two situations as regards the treatment of dividend of Rs. 1,20,000: (1) The profit for 20X1 has been utilised to pay the dividend. The share of H Ltd in profit for the first seven months of S Ltd = Rs. 1,05,000 (i.e. Rs. 1,75,000 ×3/5) Profit for the remaining five months = Rs. 75,000 (i.e.Rs. 1,25,000 × 3/5). The dividend of Rs. 1,20,000 will be adjusted in this ratio of 1,05,000: 75,000 = Rs. 70,000 out of profits up to 31.7.20X1 and Rs. 50,000 out of profits after that date. The dividend out of profits subsequent to 31.7.20X1 will be revenue income and that out of earlier profits will be capital receipt. Hence the entry will be:

### PART B

### Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. Minority interest should be presented in the consolidated balance sheet as a part of liabilities. (a) As a part of equity of the parent’s shareholders. (b) Separately from liabilities and the equity of the parent’s shareholders. (c) As a part of assets.

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason In some accounting frameworks or in a particular presentation style, minority interest could be considered part of the overall assets of the group in terms of how it's related to the total equity and net assets of the subsidiary. This treatment might emphasize the fact that the minority shareholders have a claim on the assets of the subsidiary. For example: Under certain interpretations, the minority interest is seen as a claim on the net assets of the subsidiary, and so it could be argued that it should be considered as part of the assets of the consolidated entity. In this specific case, the study material could be referring to an older or jurisdiction-specific standard where minority interest is recognized as a type of equity related to the assets of the subsidiary. However, this treatment is not standard in most modern accounting frameworks, including IFRS or US GAAP, where minority interest is generally shown separately within equity, not as part of the assets. Standard Accounting Practice (IFRS/US GAAP): Under IFRS and US GAAP, minority interest (or non-controlling interest) is generally presented: Within the equity section of the consolidated balance sheet but separately from the equity of the parent. It does not appear as part of liabilities or assets, as it represents the portion of the equity in the subsidiary that is attributable to the non-controlling shareholders. Conclusion: While (c) might be suggested in your study material, minority interest is typically not presented as part of the assets in standard consolidated balance sheets. It is most commonly classified separately in the equity section, distinct from both the liabilities and the parent’s equity. The treatment in your study material could be unique or represent a different jurisdiction's accounting practices.

Question 2. Minority of the subsidiary is entitled to (a) Capital profits of the subsidiary company. (b) Revenue profits of the subsidiary company. (c) Both capital and revenue profits of the subsidiary company. (d) Neither capital nor revenue profits of the subsidiary

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 783

Minority interest (or non-controlling interest) represents the portion of the subsidiary that is owned by parties other than the parent company. Capital Profits: These are profits that arise from transactions or events affecting the long-term capital of the company, such as the sale of a subsidiary, revaluation of assets, or issue of new capital. The minority shareholders are entitled to a share in these profits because they have a claim on the entire subsidiary, including its capital. Revenue Profits: These are profits that arise from the regular business operations of the company, such as sales, income, and other operational activities. Again, minority shareholders are entitled to a share of these profits because they hold equity in the subsidiary. Therefore, minority shareholders are entitled to both capital profits and revenue profits as they represent a portion of the subsidiary’s ownership, and both types of profits affect the overall value of the subsidiary and the distribution to all shareholders. Why other options are incorrect: (a) Capital profits of the subsidiary company: Minority interest is entitled to capital profits, but not only capital profits. (b) Revenue profits of the subsidiary company: Minority interest is entitled to revenue profits, but not only revenue profits. (d) Neither capital nor revenue profits of the subsidiary: This is incorrect because minority interest does share in both types of profits. In conclusion, minority shareholders are entitled to both capital and revenue profits, which is why (c) is the correct answer.

Question 3. In consolidation of accounts of holding and subsidiary company is eliminated in full. (a) Current liabilities of subsidiary company. (b) Reserves and surplus of both holding and subsidiary company. (c) Mutual indebtedness. (d) Nothing.

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason In the consolidation of accounts for a holding company and its subsidiary company, the primary objective is to present the financial position and results of the entire group as if it were a single entity. This involves eliminating intra-group transactions to avoid double-counting of income, assets, liabilities, etc. Mutual indebtedness refers to amounts owed between the holding company and the subsidiary, such as inter- company loans or trade payables and receivables between the two entities. These inter-company transactions are eliminated in full during the consolidation process to ensure that the consolidated financial statements do not overstate assets or liabilities. For example: If the holding company owes money to the subsidiary (or vice versa), this liability and corresponding receivable would be eliminated because, from a group perspective, they represent internal transactions and not external obligations. Why other options are incorrect:

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 784

(a) Current liabilities of subsidiary company: While current liabilities of the subsidiary may be included in the consolidation, they are not eliminated in full unless there is mutual indebtedness. (b) Reserves and surplus of both holding and subsidiary company: The reserves and surplus of the subsidiary are consolidated, but they are not eliminated in full. The parent company’s equity is adjusted for the subsidiary’s retained earnings, but not fully eliminated. (d) Nothing: This is incorrect because certain elements, such as mutual indebtedness, are eliminated during consolidation. Conclusion: Mutual indebtedness between the parent and subsidiary is eliminated in full to avoid double-counting of inter- company liabilities and receivables in the consolidated financial statements. Therefore, (c) is the correct answer.

Question 4. In consolidated balance sheet, the share of the outsiders in the net assets of the subsidiary must be shown as (a) Minority interest. (b) Capital reserve. (c) Current liability. (d) Current assets.

(Study Material)

Ans: (a) Reason In a consolidated balance sheet, the portion of the subsidiary’s net assets that is attributable to the outsiders (i.e., shareholders who are not part of the parent company, also known as the minority interest or non-controlling interest) must be shown as minority interest. This is because: Minority interest represents the portion of the equity of the subsidiary that is not owned by the parent company. The consolidated balance sheet combines the assets, liabilities, and equity of the parent and subsidiary, but the minority interest is separately shown to reflect the claim of external shareholders on the subsidiary's net assets. The minority interest is classified under equity in the consolidated balance sheet, separately from the parent’s equity. Why other options are incorrect: (b) Capital reserve: A capital reserve represents surplus funds that cannot be distributed as dividends. It does not represent the interest of the minority shareholders in the subsidiary's net assets. (c) Current liability: Minority interest is not considered a liability. It is part of the equity of the consolidated group, representing the ownership claim of the minority shareholders. (d) Current assets: Minority interest is not classified as an asset. It represents a portion of the equity in the subsidiary, not a resource owned by the group. Conclusion: The share of outsiders (minority shareholders) in the net assets of the subsidiary must be shown as minority interest in the equity section of the consolidated balance sheet. Therefore, (a) is the correct answer.

Question 5. Provision for Tax made by the subsidiary company will appear in the consolidated balance sheet as an item of (a) Current liability. (b) Revenue profit. (c) Capital profit. (d) Current assets.

(Study Material)

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 785

Ans: (a) Reason In the consolidated balance sheet, provision for tax made by the subsidiary company represents an obligation for the payment of taxes that the subsidiary has incurred due to its operations. This provision will be classified as a current liability in the consolidated balance sheet for the following reasons: Current liability: The provision for tax is an amount that the company expects to pay in the near future, typically within one year, making it a current liability. This is true for both the parent and subsidiary when preparing consolidated financial statements. Consolidation process: During consolidation, the tax provision made by the subsidiary is carried over into the consolidated balance sheet. It is not eliminated because it is an external liability (not an intra-group transaction), and it needs to be settled by the subsidiary in the future. Why other options are incorrect: (b) Revenue profit: Provision for tax is not considered a revenue profit. It is an expense item, not income or profit. (c) Capital profit: The provision for tax does not represent a capital profit. Capital profits arise from transactions related to long-term capital, such as revaluation or sale of assets, which is not applicable to a tax provision. (d) Current assets: A provision for tax is not an asset. It is an obligation to pay taxes and thus classified as a liability. Conclusion: Provision for tax made by the subsidiary will appear as a current liability in the consolidated balance sheet because it represents an obligation that must be settled in the near future. Therefore, (a) is the correct answer.

PART A

Question 1. Long Limited acquired 60% stake in Short Limited for a consideration of Rs. 112 lakhs. On the date of acquisition Short Limited’s Equity Share Capital was Rs. 100 lakhs, Revenue Reserve was Rs. 40 lakhs and balance in Profit & Loss Account was Rs. 30 lakhs. From the above information you are required to calculate Goodwill / Capital Reserve in the following situations: (i) On consolidation of Balance Sheet. (ii) If Long Limited showed the investment in subsidiary at a carrying amount of Rs. 104 lakhs. (iii) If the consideration paid for acquiring the 60% stake was Rs. 92 lakhs.

[4 Marks | 6 Minute | ICAI Fav. (PYP, July 21), High Chance]

Answer 1.

Particulars Rs. 60% of the Equity Share Capital Rs. 100 Lakhs 60 60% of Accumulated Reserve Rs. 70 Lakhs (40+30) Lakhs 42 Book value of shares of Short Ltd. 102 Goodwill / Capital Reserve computation on consolidation of balance sheet Long Ltd. paid a positive differential of Rs. 10 Lakhs (112 - 102). This differential Rs. 10 Lakhs is called goodwill and is shown in the balance sheet under the head intangibles (i) If Long Ltd. showed the investment in Short Ltd. at carrying amount of Rs. 104 Lakhs, then the goodwill will be Rs. 2 Lakhs. (ii) If the consideration paid is Rs. 92 lakhs, then there would have been capital reserve amounting Rs. 10 Lakhs (102- 92).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips First calculate the parent's share in net assets (Share Capital + Pre-acquisition Reserves + P&L). Compare this amount with the cost/carrying value of investment. Excess of cost over net assets = Goodwill; excess of net assets over cost = Capital Reserve.

Examiner’s Observation Students often forget to include all pre-acquisition reserves while computing net assets. Some also confuse carrying amount with purchase consideration.

Associate as per AS 23 - If, under the equity method, an investor’s share of losses of an associate equals or exceeds the carrying amount of the investment, the investor ordinarily discontinues recognising its share of further losses and the investment is reported at nil value. Additional losses are provided for to the extent that the investor has incurred obligations or made payments on behalf of the associate to satisfy obligations of the associate that the investor has guaranteed or to which the investor is otherwise committed. If the associate subsequently reports profits, the investor resumes including its share of those profits only after its share of the profits equals the share of net losses that have not been recognised. a) As far as possible the reporting date of the financial statements should be same for consolidated financial statement. If practically it is not possible to draw up the financial statements of one or more enterprise to such date and, accordingly, those financial statements are drawn up to reporting dates different from the reporting date of the investor, adjustments should be made for the effects of significant transactions or other events that occur between those dates and the date of the consolidated financial statements. In any case, the difference between reporting dates of the concern and consolidated financial statement should not be more than six months. b) Accounting policies followed in the preparation of the financial statements of the investor, investee and consolidated financial statement should be uniform for like transactions and other events in similar circumstances. If accounting policies followed by different enterprises in the group are not uniform, then adjustments should be made in the items of the individual financial statements to bring it in line with the accounting policy of the consolidated statement. c) The carrying amount of investment in an associate should be reduced to recognise a decline, other than temporary, in the value of the investment, such reduction being determined and made for each investment individually.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Apply Equity Method year-wise. Reduce carrying amount by investor's share of losses. Once investment reaches zero, stop recognizing further losses unless the investor has additional obligations.

Examiner’s Observation

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 791

Students generally continue recognizing losses even after carrying amount becomes nil, which is contrary to AS 23 requirements.

Question 5. Describe the cases when AS 23 does not allow the use of equity method of accounting?

[4 Marks | 4 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium]

Answer 5. Equity method of accounting is to be followed by all the enterprises having significant influence on their associates except in the following cases: a) Control is intended to be temporary because the investment is acquired and held exclusively with a view to its subsequent disposal in the near future. The term ‘Near Future’ is explained with AS 21. Or; b) It operates under severe long-term restrictions, which significantly impair its ability to transfer funds to the investor. In both the above cases, investment of investor in the share of the investee is treated as investment according to AS 13.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Memorize the two exceptions: temporary control for disposal and severe long-term restrictions on fund transfer. Write AS 13 treatment along with the exceptions.

Examiner’s Observation Students often remember only one exception or fail to mention that AS 13 becomes applicable.

Question 6. When is an investor required to discontinue the use of the equity method of accounting?

[4 Marks | 4 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium Chance]

Answer 6. An investor should discontinue the use of the equity method from the date that: a) It ceases to have significant influence in an associate but retains, either in whole or in part, its investment. b) The use of the equity method is no longer appropriate because the associate operates under severe long-term restrictions that significantly impair its ability to transfer funds to the investor. From the date of discontinuing the use of the equity method, investments in such associates should be accounted for in accordance with AS 13, Accounting for Investments. For this purpose, the carrying amount of the investment at that date should be regarded as cost thereafter.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Focus on the two trigger events: loss of significant influence and severe long-term restrictions. Mention that carrying amount on discontinuation becomes cost under AS 13.

Examiner’s Observation Many students write situations where equity method is not applicable instead of conditions for discontinuation.

Answer 7 (i) Carrying amount of investment in Separate Financial Statement of Bright Ltd. as on 31.03.20X2

Particulars Rs. Amount paid for investment in Associate (on 1.06.20X1) 2,00,000 Less: Pre-acquisition dividend (Rs. 50,000×30%) (15,000) Carrying amount as on 31.3.20X2 as per AS 13 1,85,000 Carrying amount of investment in Consolidated Financial Statements of Bright Ltd. as on 31.3.20X2 as per AS 23

Particulars Rs. Carrying amount as per separate financial statements 1,85,000 Add: Proportionate share of 10-month profit of investee as per equity method 75,000 (30% of Rs.3,00,000 × 10/12) Carrying amount as on 31.3.20X2 2,60,000 Carrying amount of investment in Consolidated Financial Statement of Bright Ltd. as on 30.6.20X2 as per AS 23

Question 8. A Ltd. invested Rs. 1,00,000 to acquire 10% stake (Investment I) in B Ltd. and later invested Rs. 3,00,000 to acquire additional 20% (Investment II). The net asset value of the B ltd. at the respective investment dates was Rs. 7,50,000 and Rs. 12,50,000 respectively. Determine whether B Ltd. is an associate of A Ltd. Also, calculate goodwill arising on the acquisition of the associate.

[4 Marks | 6 Minute | ICAI Fav. (RTP Sept.2025), Medium to High]

Answer 8. As per para 3 of AS 23 an associate is an enterprise in which the investor has significant influence and which is neither a subsidiary nor a joint venture of the investor. Significant influence may be gained by share © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 793

ownership, statute or agreement. As regards share ownership, if an investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary (i.e.s), 20% or more of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor has significant influence, unless it can be clearly demonstrated that this is not the case. In this case, A Ltd. has invested 30 % in B Ltd. so B Ltd. is to be considered as an associate of A Ltd. The goodwill arising on the acquisition of the associate will be computed as follows:

Particulars Particulars Rs. Investment I 1,00,000 Share of net assets (10 percent of Rs. 7,50,000) (75,000) Goodwill (A) 25,000 Investment II 3,00,000 Share of net assets (20 percent of Rs. 12,50,000) (2,50,000) Goodwill (B) 50,000 Total goodwill (A + B) 75,000

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Determine significant influence based on cumulative holding (10% + 20% = 30%). Compute goodwill separately for each tranche of acquisition and then aggregate.

Examiner’s Observation Students generally calculate goodwill only on the second acquisition and ignore the first tranche.

Question 9. A Ltd. has a share capital of 50,000 shares @ Rs. 100 per share. H Ltd. acquired 15% shares in A Ltd. on 1.4.2024. It also acquired all the 5,000, 12% convertible debentures of Rs. 100 each of A Ltd. These debentures will be converted at par into equity shares of A Ltd. after 3 years. State whether, as per AS 23, A Ltd. is an Associate of H Ltd. or not with reasons?

[4 Marks | 5 Minute | ICAI Fav. (MTP May 2025), High Chance]

Answer 9. As per para 3 of AS 23 ‘Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements’, an associate is an enterprise in which the investor has significant influence and which is neither a subsidiary nor a joint venture of the investor. Standard further explains in para 4 that as regards share ownership, if an investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary (i.e.s), 20% or more of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor has significant influence, unless it can be clearly demonstrated that this is not the case. Conversely, if the investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary (i.e.s), less than 20% of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor does not have significant influence, unless such influence can be clearly demonstrated. Further as per an explanation to para 4 of the standard, for the purpose of classification of associate, the potential equity shares of the investee held by the investor will not be taken into account for determining the voting power of the investor. In other words, the voting power should be determined on the basis of the current outstanding securities with voting rights. As per the information given in the question, H Ltd. presently holds indirectly 22.7% shares (with and without voting rights) (Refer W.N.) in A Ltd. However, the current outstanding securities with voting rights in A Ltd. is only 15% and the remaining holding is on account of potential equity shares. Since potential equity shares do not have © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 794

voting rights they will not be taken into consideration while determining the significant influence of H Ltd. on A Ltd. Hence, A Ltd. is not an associate of H Ltd. Working Note: Calculation of percentage of holding of shares after conversion Current holding is 15% i.e. 7,500 shares of Rs. 100 each 7,50,000 Potential equity shares i.e. 5,000 shares of Rs. 100 each 5,00,000 12,50,000 Total share capital of A Ltd. after conversion of debentures into equity shares will be = Rs. 50,00,000 + Rs. 5,00,000 = Rs. 55,00,000 Percentage of holding = Rs. (12,50,000/55,00,000) × 100 = 22.7% approx.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Remember that potential equity shares are ignored while determining voting power under AS 23. Only current voting rights are considered for assessing significant influence.

Examiner’s Observation Students frequently include convertible debentures while calculating voting power and incorrectly conclude that significant influence exists.

### PART B

### Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. A Ltd. is holding 90% share in B Ltd. and 10% shares in C Ltd., and B Ltd. is holding 11% shares in C Ltd. Identity which of the statements are incorrect. (i) In this case, A Ltd. is parent of B Ltd. (ii) As far as the relationship between A Ltd. and C Ltd. is concerned; A Ltd. has a total nf direct and indirect holding of (10% + 90% of 11%) 19.9 %in C Ltd. (iii) C Ltd. is an associate of A Ltd. (a) Statement (ii) is incorrect. (b) Statement (iii) is incorrect. (c) Statement (ii) and (iii) both are incorrect. (d) All statements are incorrect.

(Study Material)

Ans: (a) Reason Let's break down the statements: Statement (i): "In this case, A Ltd. is parent of B Ltd." This statement is correct because A Ltd. holds 90% of the shares in B Ltd., which means A Ltd. has control over B Ltd. (usually defined as owning more than 50% of the voting shares), making A Ltd. the parent of B Ltd. Statement (ii): "As far as the relationship between A Ltd. and C Ltd. is concerned; A Ltd. has a total of direct and indirect holding of (10% + 90% of 11%) = 19.9% in C Ltd." This statement is incorrect. A Ltd. holds 10% directly in C Ltd. and 90% of 11% (i.e., 9.9%) indirectly through its 90% holding in B Ltd. This would give A Ltd. a total holding of 19.9% in C Ltd. However, this statement overlooks the fact that in consolidated financial statements, A Ltd.'s effective control over C Ltd. through its indirect holding should be carefully considered. But, the exact interpretation of the relationship (whether it constitutes control, significant influence, or joint control) will depend on the legal definitions, thresholds, and other details of ownership and governance structures. But, the confusion lies in how control or influence is calculated. Indirect holdings are considered in the context of significant influence (which typically starts at 20% or more), not necessarily control. A Ltd. would not necessarily have significant influence over C Ltd., but it does have an indirect shareholding of 19.9%. This is the critical point where the wording of the statement causes it to be incorrect in the given context. Statement (iii): "C Ltd. is an associate of A Ltd." This statement is incorrect because an associate is typically defined as a company where the investor holds 20% to 50% of the voting power and has significant influence. A Ltd. holds only 19.9% in C Ltd. (including indirect holdings). This does not meet the threshold for significant influence, so C Ltd. is not an associate of A Ltd. Conclusion: Statement (ii) is incorrect because the indirect holding percentage might lead to confusion about the level of control or influence. Statement (iii) is incorrect because A Ltd.'s effective holding does not meet the criteria for an associate relationship (typically 20% or more). Therefore, (a) Statement (ii) is incorrect is the correct answer.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 796

Question 2. Capital Reserve = Rs. 20,000. 4. A Ltd. acquired 10% stake of B Ltd. on April 01 and further 15% on October 01 during the same year. Other information is as follow: Cost of Investment for 10% Rs. 1,00,000 and for 15% Rs. 1,45,000 Net asset on April 01 Rs. 8,50,000 and on October 01 Rs. 10,00,000. What is the amount of goodwill or capital reserve arising on significant influence? (a) Goodwill = Rs. 10,000. (b) Goodwill = Rs. 20,000. (c) Capital Reserve = Rs. 10,000. (d) Capital Reserve = Rs. 20,000.

(Study Material)

Ans: (a) Reason To calculate goodwill or capital reserve arising from the acquisition of significant influence (when the investor holds between 20% and 50% of the equity share capital), we need to follow the Purchase Method for accounting for investments. This involves comparing the cost of investment with the share of the net assets acquired. Step-by-Step Calculation: Investment in B Ltd.: A Ltd. acquires 10% of B Ltd. on April 01 for Rs. 1,00,000. A Ltd. acquires an additional 15% on October 01 for Rs. 1,45,000. So, the total investment is: 1,00,000 \\, (\\text{for 10%}) + 1,45,000 \\, (\\text{for 15%}) = 2,45,000 Net Asset Value of B Ltd.: On April 01, the net asset value of B Ltd. is Rs. 8,50,000. On October 01, the net asset value of B Ltd. is Rs. 10,00,000. Total percentage acquired = 10% + 15% = 25%. Share of Net Assets Acquired: On April 01, when A Ltd. acquires 10%, the share of net assets acquired is: 10%×8,50,000=85,000 10%×8,50,000=85,000 On October 01, when A Ltd. acquires 15%, the share of net assets acquired is: 15%×10,00,000=1,50,000 15%×10,00,000=1,50,000 So, the total share of net assets acquired is: 85,000+1,50,000=2,35,000 85,000+1,50,000=2,35,000 Goodwill Calculation: Now, we compare the total cost of investment to the share of net assets acquired. Total investment = Rs. 2,45,000 Total share of net assets = Rs. 2,35,000 The difference between the cost of the investment and the share of net assets acquired represents goodwill: 2,45,000−2,35,000=10,000 2,45,000−2,35,000=10,000 Thus, the amount of goodwill arising on significant influence is Rs. 10,000. Conclusion

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 797

The correct answer is (a) Goodwill = Rs. 10,000 because the investment exceeds the share of net assets acquired, indicating the presence of goodwill.

Question 3. Identity which of the statements are correct. An enterprise can influence the significant economic decision making by many ways like: (i) Representation on the board of directors or governing body of the investee. (ii) Participation in policy-making processes. (iii) Interchange of managerial personnel. (iv) Provision of essential technical information. (a) Statement (i) and (ii) are correct. (b) Statement (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct. (c) Statement (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) are correct. (d) Statement (ii) and (iii) are correct.

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason All the statements listed are valid ways in which an enterprise can exercise significant influence over another entity. Significant influence is defined as the power to participate in the financial and operating policy decisions of an investee without having control or joint control. This can be achieved through various mechanisms that allow an entity to affect the investee’s decision-making. Let’s break down each statement: (i) Representation on the board of directors or governing body of the investee: Correct: Having representation on the board of directors or the governing body allows an enterprise to directly influence the strategic and operational decisions of the investee. This is a clear example of exercising significant influence. (ii) Participation in policy-making processes: Correct: Being involved in policy-making processes means the enterprise can contribute to the direction in which the investee is moving. This could include input on major decisions, such as strategic goals, financial policies, or operational methods, which indicates significant influence. (iii) Interchange of managerial personnel: Correct: The interchange of managerial personnel between the investee and the investor company helps establish a closer relationship, aligning the operational practices of both entities. The sharing of key personnel can affect decision-making and policy formation, thereby exerting significant influence. (iv) Provision of essential technical information: Correct: Providing essential technical information (such as proprietary knowledge, expertise, or intellectual property) helps the investee make informed decisions, particularly in areas that require technical know-how. This can also lead to a significant influence over the business operations and strategy. Conclusion: Since all four statements accurately describe the ways an enterprise can exert significant influence over another, (c) Statement (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) are correct is the right answer.

Question 4. Identity which of the statements are correct. (i) In case an associate has made a provision for proposed dividend (i.e. dividend declared after the reporting period but it pertains to that reporting year) in its financial statements, the investor’s share of the results of operations of the associate should be computed without taking into consideration the proposed dividend.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 798

(ii) In case an associate has made a provision for proposed dividend (i.e. dividend declared after the reporting period but it pertains to that reporting year) in its financial statements, the investor’s share of the results of operations of the associate should be computed after taking into consideration the proposed dividend. (iii) The potential equity shares of the investee held by the investor should not be taken into account for determining the voting power of the investor. (iv) The potential equity shares of the investee held by the investor should be taken into account for determining the voting power of the investor. (a) Statement (i) and (iii). (b) Statement (ii) and (iv). (c) Statement (i) only. (d) Statement (iii) only.

(Study Material)

Ans: (a) Reason Let's analyse each statement in detail: (i) In case an associate has made a provision for proposed dividend (i.e. dividend declared after the reporting period but it pertains to that reporting year) in its financial statements, the investor’s share of the results of operations of the associate should be computed without taking into consideration the proposed dividend. Correct: When computing the investor's share of the associate's results, the provision for proposed dividends (which is an appropriation of profits) should not be considered in the profit/loss calculation. The investor’s share of the results is typically based on the associate’s net profit or loss from operations, excluding any effects of proposed dividends. The proposed dividend is not part of the income statement's operating results and is instead dealt with in the equity section of the balance sheet. (ii) In case an associate has made a provision for proposed dividend (i.e. dividend declared after the reporting period but it pertains to that reporting year) in its financial statements, the investor’s share of the results of operations of the associate should be computed after taking into consideration the proposed dividend. Incorrect: This statement is incorrect because the proposed dividend is considered an appropriation of profits and does not form part of the operational results of the associate. Therefore, it should not be included in the investor’s share of the associate's results. (iii) The potential equity shares of the investee held by the investor should not be taken into account for determining the voting power of the investor. Correct: When determining significant influence or control in an associate, the investor’s voting power is typically calculated based on the actual equity shares held, not potential equity shares (like stock options or convertible securities). The potential shares that can be converted into equity do not count towards voting power unless they are already exercised or converted into actual shares. (iv) The potential equity shares of the investee held by the investor should be taken into account for determining the voting power of the investor. Incorrect: As mentioned above, potential shares (such as those arising from convertible securities or options) are not counted in determining voting power unless converted into actual shares. This statement is incorrect because voting power is based on actual, not potential, equity shares. Conclusion: The correct answer is (a) Statement (i) and (iii) because both these statements are consistent with the principles of equity method accounting and voting power determination.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 799

Question 5. A Ltd. acquired 10% stake of B Ltd. on April 01 and further 15% on October 01 of the same year. Other information is as follows: Cost of Investment for 10% Rs. 1,00,000 and for 15% Rs. 1,55,000 Net asset on April 01 Rs. 8,50,000 and on October 01 Rs. 10,00,000. What is the amount of goodwill or capital reserve arising on significant influence? (a) Goodwill = Rs. 10,000. (b) Goodwill = Rs. 20,000. (c) Capital Reserve = Rs. 10,000.

(Study Material)

Ans: (b) Reason To calculate goodwill or capital reserve arising on significant influence, we need to use the purchase method for accounting for investments. This method compares the cost of investment to the share of the net assets acquired by the investor. Let’s break it down: Step-by-Step Calculation:

1. Cost of Investment:

A Ltd. acquires 10% of B Ltd. on April 01 for Rs. 1,00,000. A Ltd. acquires an additional 15% of B Ltd. on October 01 for Rs. 1,55,000. So, the total investment is: 1,00,000+1,55,000=2,55,000

2. Net Asset Value of B Ltd.:

On April 01, the net asset value of B Ltd. is Rs. 8,50,000. On October 01, the net asset value of B Ltd. is Rs. 10,00,000.

3. Share of Net Assets Acquired:

On April 01, when A Ltd. acquires 10%, the share of net assets acquired is: 10%×8,50,000=85,000 On October 01, when A Ltd. acquires 15%, the share of net assets acquired is: 15%×10,00,000=1,50,000 So, the total share of net assets acquired by A Ltd. is: 85,000+1,50,000=2,35,000

4. Goodwill Calculation:

The difference between the cost of investment and the share of net assets acquired represents goodwill (if the investment is greater than the share of net assets). Total investment = Rs. 2,55,000 Total share of net assets = Rs. 2,35,000 The difference (representing goodwill) is: 2,55,000−2,35,000=20,000 Conclusion: The goodwill arising on the acquisition of significant influence by A Ltd. is Rs. 20,000, so the correct answer is (b) Goodwill = Rs. 20,000.

### Chapter-10

### Unit 3

### AS 27- FINANCIAL REPORTING OF INTERESTS IN JOINT VENTURES

### PART A

Question 1. Describe the cases when AS 27 does not allow the use of Proportionate consolidation method of accounting?

[3 Marks | 3 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 1. Proportionate consolidation method of accounting is to be followed except in the following cases: a) Investment is intended to be temporary because the investment is acquired and held exclusively with a view to its subsequent disposal in the near future. The term ‘Near Future’ is explained with AS 21.

Or b) Joint venture operates under severe long-term restrictions, which significantly impair its ability to transfer funds to the venture’s. In both the above cases, investment of venture in the share of the investee is treated as investment according to AS 13.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Focus on the two exceptions given in AS 27. Memorize them exactly as they are repeatedly tested in theory questions. Link both exceptions with treatment under AS 13. No calculations are involved.

Examiner’s Observation Students generally remember only one exception and forget the second. Many also fail to mention that investment should thereafter be accounted for under AS 13. Complete provision fetches full marks.

Question 2. When is a venture required to discontinue the use of the proportionate consolidation method?

[4 Marks | 4 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 2. A venture should discontinue the use of the proportionate consolidation method from the date that: a) It ceases to have joint control in the joint venture but retains, either in whole or in part, its investment. b) The use of the proportionate consolidation method is no longer appropriate because the joint venture operates under severe long- term restrictions that significantly impair its ability to transfer funds to the ventures. From the date of discontinuing the use of the proportionate consolidation method, a) If interest in entity is more than 50%, investments in such joint ventures should be accounted for in accordance with AS 21, Consolidated Financial Statement. b) If interest is 20% or more but up to 50%, investments are to be accounted for in accordance with AS 23, Accounting for Investment in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statement. c) For all other cases investment in joint venture is treated as per AS 13, Accounting for Investment. d) For this purpose, the carrying amount of the investment at the date on which joint venture relationship ceases to exist should be regarded as cost thereafter.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 801

Remember the trigger point: loss of joint control or severe long-term restrictions. Then write the subsequent accounting treatment under AS 21, AS 23, or AS 13 depending upon the level of holding.

Examiner’s Observation Many students stop after writing the reasons for discontinuance and miss the consequential accounting treatment. The standard specifically requires mentioning subsequent accounting treatment.

Question 3. JVR Limited has made investments of Rs. 97.84 crores in equity shares of QSR Limited in pursuance of Joint Venture agreement till 20X1-X2 (i.e., more than 12 months). The investment has been made at par. QSR Limited has been in continuous losses for the last 2 years. JVR Limited is willing to reassess the carrying amount of its investment in QSR Limited and wish to provide for diminution in value of investments. However, QSR Limited has a futuristic and profitable business plans and projection for the coming years. Discuss whether the contention of JVR Limited to bring down the carrying amount of investment in QSR Limited is in accordance with the Accounting Standard.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium to High]

Answer 3. As per para 26 of AS 27 “Financial Reporting of Interests in Joint Ventures”, in a venture’s separate financial statements, interest in a jointly controlled entity should be accounted for as an investment in accordance with AS 13 ‘Accounting for Investments’. As per para 17 of AS 13 “Accounting for Investments”, long-term investments are usually carried at cost. However, when there is a decline, other than temporary, in the value of a long-term investment, the carrying amount is reduced to recognize the decline. Indicators of the value of an investment are obtained by reference to its market value, the investee’s assets and results and the expected cash flows from the investment. The type and extent of the investor’s stake in the investee are also taken into account. However, where there is a decline, other than temporary, in the carrying amounts of long- term investments, the resultant reduction in the carrying amount is charged to the profit and loss statement. Since the investment was made in the year 20X1-20X2 i.e., more than a year, it is a long-term investment. In the given case, though the QSR Ltd. is in continuous losses for past 2 years, yet it has a futuristic and profitable business plans and projections for the coming years. Here, one of the indicators i.e. ‘losses incurred to the company’ may lead to diminution in the value of the shares while the other indicator that ‘the company has positive expected cash flows from its business plans’ does not lead to decline in the value of shares. Considering both the facts, in case the expectation of profitable business plans and positive cash flows is based reliable presumptions (such as tender in favour of QSR Ltd., strong order book etc.), the decline will be regarded as temporary in nature and the investment in equity shares will continue to be carried at cost only. However, should the aforesaid presumptions be based on projections without reasonable evidence backing the claims, the decline could be regarded as non-temporary in nature in which case the write down of the carrying amount become necessary in line with AS 13, thereby implying the contention of QSR Ltd. to be correct.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Identify that the investment is a long-term investment and apply AS 13. Analyze whether decline is temporary or other than temporary. Quote both positive and negative indicators before concluding.

Examiner’s Observation

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 802

Students often conclude immediately based on losses of the investee. ICAI expects evaluation of all indicators, including future profitability and expected cash flows.

Question 4. Mr. A, Mr. B and Mr. C entered into a joint venture to purchase a land, construct and sell flats. Mr. A purchased a land for Rs. 60,00,000 on 01.01.20X1 and for the purpose he took loan from a bank for Rs. 50,00,000 @ 8% interest p.a. He also paid registering fees Rs. 60,000 on the same day. Mr. B supplied the materials for Rs. 4,50,000 from his godown and further he purchased the materials for Rs. 5,00,000 for the joint venture. Mr. C met all other expenses of advertising, labour and other incidental expenses which turnout to be Rs. 9,00,000. On 30.06.20X1 each of the venture agreed to take away one flat each to be valued at Rs. 10,00,000 each flat and rest were sold by them as follow: Mr. A for Rs. 40,00,000; Mr. B for Rs. 20,00,000 and Mr. C for Rs. 10,00,000. Loan was repaid on the same day by Mr. A along with the interest and net proceeds were shared by the partners equally. You are required to prepare the draft Consolidated Profit & Loss Account and Joint Venture Account in the books of each venture.

[10 Marks | 18 Minutes | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]
