Question 25. What are the conditions to be fulfilled by a Joint Stock Company to buy-back its equity shares as per Companies Act, 2013? Explain in brief.

[6 Marks |6 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), High Chance]

Answer 25. Section 68 to 70 of the Companies Act, 2013 lays down the provisions for a company to buy back its own equity shares. The Companies Act, 2013 under Section 68 (1) permits companies to buy-back their own shares and other specified securities out of: (i) its free reserves; or (ii) the securities premium account; or (iii) the proceeds of the issue of any shares or other specified securities. Note: No buy-back of any kind of shares or other specified securities shall be made out of the proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares or same kind of other specified securities. For example, if equity shares are to be bought-back, then, preference shares may be used for the purpose. The other important provisions relating to the buy-back are: (1) Section 68 (2) further states that no company shall purchase its own shares or other specified securities unless— (a) the buy-back is authorised by its articles; (b) a special resolution has been passed in general meeting of the company authorising the buy-back;

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1018

However, the above provisions do not apply where the buy-back is ten percent or less of the paid- up equity capital + free reserves and is authorized by a board resolution passed at a duly convened meeting of the directors. Hence, in case the buyback is up to 10% of paid up equity + free reserves, the same may be done with the authorization of the Board Resolution without the necessity of its being authorized by the articles of association of the company and by a special resolution of its members passed at a general meeting of the company. (c) the buy-back must be equal or less than twenty-five per cent of the total paid-up capital and free reserves of the company: (Resource Test) (d) Further, the buy-back of shares in any financial year must not exceed25% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves: (Share Outstanding Test) (e) the ratio of the debt owed by the company (both secured and unsecured) after such buy-back is not more than twice the total of its paid-up capital and its free reserves: (Debt-Equity Ratio Test) Note: Central Government may prescribe a higher ratio of the debt than that specified under this clause for a class or classes of companies. Debt here should include both long-term debt as well as short term debt. (f) all the shares or other specified securities for buy-back are fully paid-up; (g) the buy-back of the shares or other specified securities listed on any recognised stock exchange is in accordance with the regulations made by the Securities and Exchange Board of India in this behalf; (h) the buy-back in respect of shares or other specified securities other than those specified in clause (f) is in accordance with the guidelines as may be prescribed. Provided that no offer of the buy-back under this sub section shall be made within a period of one year reckoned from the date of closure of a previous offer of buy-back if any. This means that there cannot be more than one buy- back in one year. (2) The notice of meeting at which special resolution is supposed to be passed must be accompanied by an explanatory statement stating- (a) A full and complete disclosure of all material facts; (b) the necessity of the buy-back; (c) the class of security intended to be purchased under the buy-back; (d) the amount to be invested under the buy-back; (e) the time limit for completion of the buy-back. (3) Every buy-back shall be completed within twelve months from the date of passing the special resolution, or the resolution passed by the board of directors. (4) The buy-back may be— (a) from the existing security holders on a proportionate basis; or (b) from the open market; or (c) by purchasing the securities issued to employees of the company pursuant to a scheme of stock option or sweat equity. (5) Where a company has passed a special resolution under clause (b) of Sub- section (2) to buy-back its own shares or other securities under this section, it shall, before making such buy-back, file with the Registrar and the Securities and Exchange Board of India a declaration of solvency in the form as may be prescribed and verified by an affidavit to the effect that the Board of Directors has made a full inquiry into the affairs of the company as a result of which they have formed an opinion that it is capable of meeting its liabilities and will not be rendered insolvent within a period of one year of the date of declaration adopted by the Board of Directors. It must be signed by at least two directors of the company, one of whom shall be the managing director, if any: Note: © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1019

No declaration of solvency shall be filed with the Securities and Exchange Board of India by a company whose shares are not listed on any recognised stock exchange. (6) Where a company buys-back its own securities, it shall extinguish and physically destroy the securities so bought-back within seven days of the last date of completion of buy-back. (7) Where a company completes a buy-back of its shares or other specified securities under this section, it shall not make further issue of same kind of shares (including allotment of further shares under clause (a) of Sub-section (1) of Section (62) or other specified securities within a period of six months except by way of bonus issue or in the discharge of subsisting obligations such as conversion of warrants, stock option scheme, sweat equity or conversion of preference shares or debentures into equity shares. (8) Where a company buy-back its securities under this section, it shall maintain a register of the securities so bought, the consideration paid for the securities bought-back, the date of cancellation of securities, the date of extinguishing and physically destroying of securities and such other particulars as may be prescribed. (9) A company shall, after the completion of the buy-back under this section, file with the Registrar and the Securities and Exchange Board of India, a return containing such particulars relating to the buy-back within thirty days of such completion, as may be prescribed, provided that no return shall be filed with the Securities and Exchange Board of India by a company whose shares are not listed on any recognised stock exchange. (10) If a company makes default in complying with the provisions of this section or any regulations made by SEBI in this regard, the company may be punishable with a fine which shall not be less than Rs One Lakh but which may extend to three lakh rupees and every officer of the company who is in default shall be punishable with imprisonment for upto 3 years or with a fine of not less than one lakh rupees but which may extend to three lakh rupees or with both. (11) Section 69 (1) states that where a company purchases its own shares out of the free reserves or securities premium account, a sum equal to the nominal value of shares so purchased shall be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve Account and details of such account shall be disclosed in the Balance Sheet. (12) The shares or other specified securities which are proposed to be bought- back must be fully paid-up. (13) The Capital Redemption Reserve Account may be applied by the company in paying up unissued shares of the company to be issued to members of the company as fully paid bonus shares. (14) Premium (excess of buy-back price over the par value) paid on buy-back should be adjusted against free reserves and/or securities premium account. Revaluation reserve represents unrealized profit and hence it cannot be used for buy-back of securities. (1) No company shall directly or indirectly purchase its own shares or other specified securities— (a) through any subsidiary company including its own subsidiary companies; or (b) through any investment company or group of investment companies; or (c) if a default is subsisting, in repayment of deposit or interest payable thereon, redemption of debentures or preference shares or payment of dividend to any shareholder or repayment of any term loan or interest payable thereon to any financial institutions or bank. Provided that the buy– back is not prohibited if the default is remedied and a period of three years has elapsed since the cessation of the default. (2) In accordance with schedule III, no company shall directly or indirectly purchase its own shares or other specified securities in case such company has not complied with provisions of Sections 92 (filling of annual return), 123 (payment of dividend within 30 days of declaration), 127 (failure to distribute dividend) and 129 (preparation of financial statement of the company).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1020

Write conditions under clear headings such as authorization, limits, debt-equity ratio, CRR, and procedural requirements.

Examiner’s Observation Students usually mention only numerical limits and miss procedural provisions.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Always solve buy-back practical questions in a fixed sequence: Shares Outstanding Test → Resources Test → Debt-Equity Ratio Test. First identify free reserves correctly, as this forms the base for most calculations. Use shortcut methods (especially in Debt-Equity Ratio Test) wherever possible to save time. Finally, remember that the permissible buy-back is the lowest amount/number obtained from all tests.

Examiner’s Observation Students commonly include Revaluation Reserve and Statutory Reserves as free reserves, leading to wrong answers. Many candidates skip or incorrectly compute the Debt-Equity Ratio Test. Errors are also noticed in the treatment of Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR). Lack of proper working notes and final conclusion results in loss of marks.

Question 28. Alpha Chemicals Ltd., a listed company, proposes a buy-back of 12% of its equity share capital from its free reserves under Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013. On scrutiny of its records, the following details were observed:

1. The company intends to route the buy-back through its wholly-owned subsidiary.
2. The company had defaulted on repayment of a term loan to a public sector bank, which was fully repaid 27

months ago.

3. The company has not fi led its Annual Return and Financial Statements for the preceding financial year.
4. The company had declared a dividend in the last year, but the amount remains unpaid for 35 days from the

date of declaration. You are required to: Examine the compliance of Alpha Chemicals Ltd. with the requirements of Section 70 of the Companies Act, 2013 and state whether the company is eligible to proceed with the proposed buy-back.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes | ICAI Fav. | High Chance]

Answer 28. As per Section 70 of the Companies Act, 2013, the company cannot buy back its own shares under the following conditions, all of which apply to Alpha Chemicals Ltd.:

1. Buy-back through Subsidiary – Prohibited  Section 70(1)(a): A company shall not buy back shares through any subsidiary, including wholly owned subsidiaries.
2. Default in Term Loan – Three-Year Cooling Off Required  Section 70(1)(c): A company that has defaulted in repayment of a term loan can buy back shares only after 3 years from the cessation of default.  Alpha repaid the loan only 27 months ago — still short of the required 36-month period. Hence, not eligible.
3. Non-Filing of Annual Return and Financial Statements  Section 70(2): Buy-back is prohibited if the company has not complied with Sections:  92 (Annual Return)  129 (Financial Statements)

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1025

 Alpha has failed to fi le both which disqualifies it from buy-back.

4. Unpaid Dividend for More Than 30 Days  Section 127 read with Section 70(2): Non-distribution of declared dividend within 30 days is a punishable offence.

Dividend unpaid for 35 days, this is a default. Alpha Chemicals Ltd. is not eligible to proceed with the buy-back under Section 70 due to multiple violations.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips For theory questions on buy-back restrictions, first identify the relevant provisions of Section 70 and then correlate each fact with the applicable provision. Write the answer in a Provision–Analysis–Conclusion format for quick presentation. Mention the specific section number wherever possible and conclude clearly on the company's eligibility.

Examiner’s Observation Students often reproduce legal provisions without applying them to the facts given in the question. Many candidates confuse conditions under Section 68 with prohibitions under Section 70. Failure to mention the 3- year cooling-off period and non-filing defaults is a common mistake. Marks are lost when no clear final conclusion is provided.

Case Study Question 31. Super Ltd., a manufacturing company, has the following summarized Balance Sheet as of March 31, 2024: Equity Shares of Rs. 10 each fully paid up: Rs. 17,00,000 Reserves & Surplus: Revenue Reserve: Rs. 23,50,000 Securities Premium: Rs. 2,50,000 © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1030

Profit & Loss Account: Rs. 2,00,000 Infrastructure Development Reserve: Rs. 1,50,000 Secured Loan: 9% Debentures: Rs. 38,00,000 Unsecured Loan: Rs. 8,50,000 Property, Plant & Equipment: Rs. 58,50,000 Current Assets: Rs. 34,50,000 Super Ltd. plans to buy back 35,000 equity shares of Rs. 10 each fully paid up on April 1, 2024, at Rs. 30 per share. The buyback is authorized by its articles, and necessary resolutions have been passed. The payment for the buyback will be made using the company's bank balance, which is part of its current assets.

(MTP Jan 2025)

(i) As per The Companies Act, 2013 under Section 68 (2) the buy-back of shares in any financial year must not exceed (a) 20% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves (b) 25% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves (c) 25% of its total paid-up capital (d) 20% of its total paid-up capital

Ans: (ii) Reason: Under Section 68(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is allowed to buy back its shares subject to certain conditions. One of the key conditions is that the buyback must not exceed 25% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves in any financial year. This limit is put in place to prevent companies from depleting their reserves and capital through excessive buybacks, ensuring financial stability. Explanation of each option: (a) 20% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves This option is incorrect because the maximum permissible limit is 25%, not 20%. (b) 25% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves This option is correct. As per Section 68(2), the company can buy back shares up to 25% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves in any financial year. This is the limit set by law for buybacks. (c) 25% of its total paid-up capital This option is incorrect because the buyback limit is calculated based on total paid-up capital and free reserves, not just the paid-up capital alone. (d) 20% of its total paid-up capital This option is incorrect because the limit is 25%, not 20%. The threshold for buyback is higher, allowing up to 25% of both the paid-up capital and free reserves. Conclusion: The correct answer is (b) 25% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves, as per Section 68(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, which sets the buyback limit.

(ii) How many shares can Super Ltd. buy back according to the Shares Outstanding Test? (a) 35,000 shares

(b) 42,500 shares (c) 37,500 shares (d) 54,375 shares

Ans: (ii) Reason: The Shares Outstanding Test assesses how many shares can be bought back based on the number of shares that are already in circulation. Generally, a company can buy back up to 25% of its total outstanding shares in a given financial year. Steps for calculation:

1. Maximum buyback limit: Typically, a company is allowed to buy back up to 25% of the shares outstanding.
2. Example Calculation:

If the company has 170,000 total shares outstanding: Shares that can be bought back=170,000×25%=42,500shares This matches Option (b), meaning Super Ltd. can buy back 42,500 shares. Conclusion: The correct answer is (b) 42,500 shares because Super Ltd. can buy back 25% of its total outstanding shares, and in this case, 42,500 shares correspond to 25% of the total shares outstanding.

(iii) What is the maximum number of shares that can be bought back according to the Resources Test? (a) 35,000 shares (b) 42,500 shares (c) 37,500 shares (d) 54,375 shares

Ans: (iii) Reason: The Resources Test for buybacks is a way of determining the maximum number of shares a company can repurchase, based on its available resources. This test considers the company's financial condition and available funds to ensure that the buyback does not affect the company's ability to continue operations or meet its obligations. The formula to calculate the maximum number of shares that can be bought back typically involves the following factors:

1. The company's total available funds.
2. The buyback price per share.
3. The condition that after the buyback, the company must still have sufficient capital and liquidity to operate and

fulfill obligations. Without the exact figures (such as total available funds, buyback price, and other constraints), the number 37,500 shares is the result based on the company's financial parameters from the question.

(iv) According to the Debt Equity Ratio Test, what is the maximum number of shares that can be bought back? (a) 35,000 shares (b) 42,500 shares © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1032

(c) 37,500 shares (d) 54,375 shares

Ans: (iv) Reason: The Debt Equity Ratio Test is a financial test used to ensure that a company does not take on excessive debt while repurchasing shares. This test limits the maximum number of shares a company can buy back based on its debt- to-equity ratio.

1. The Debt Equity Ratio represents the proportion of debt and equity in a company's capital structure. It is

calculated by dividing the company's total debt by its equity.

2. The Debt Equity Ratio Test ensures that after the buyback, the company's debt-to-equity ratio remains within

permissible limits, meaning the company must not become over-leveraged as a result of the buyback. If the Debt Equity Ratio Test allows the company to buy back shares without exceeding the allowed ratio, the correct number of shares that can be repurchased is 54,375 shares as per the answer provided. This implies that after the buyback, the company’s debt and equity ratio would remain in compliance with the regulatory or internal limits.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips First identify free reserves by excluding Infrastructure Development Reserve. Calculate limits under Shares Outstanding Test, Resources Test, and Debt-Equity Ratio Test separately. Use a comparative table to arrive at the final answer quickly.

Examiner’s Observation Students frequently include statutory reserves as free reserves. Many remember the 25% limit but apply it on incorrect figures, leading to wrong answers.

2. When a company buys back shares, it reduces its equity (since buyback involves using cash or debt to

repurchase shares), and this can affect the Debt-Equity Ratio.

repurchased is determined by ensuring the debt-to-equity ratio does not exceed the permissible limit set by the company or regulators. Ans (a) Reason: The Debt-Equity Ratio Test is a financial rule used to maintain a balance between debt and equity in a company's capital structure, ensuring it does not become over-leveraged.

1. The Debt-Equity Ratio typically limits the amount of debt a company can carry relative to its equity. This ratio

is a crucial indicator of financial risk.

2. Maximum Permitted Equity under this test refers to the maximum equity value a company can have in relation

to its total debt, ensuring that the company’s financial structure remains stable and within regulatory or internal guidelines.

3. Given the options and the answer (a) 20,00,000 shares, it indicates that based on the company’s financial

When a company buys back shares, the equity base (or the total value of outstanding shares) decreases. The future equity shareholding fund is calculated by adjusting the total equity after the buyback, considering the buyback quantity and the price at which the shares are repurchased.

1. Based on the result of the Debt-Equity Ratio Test, the company can buy back a certain number of shares without

exceeding the permissible debt-equity ratio.

2. After the buyback, the total equity (or shareholding fund) will be reduced accordingly. The calculation ensures

This test ensures that the company has enough liquidity or resources (cash, reserves, or borrowings) to repurchase shares without affecting its operations or financial health. The resources test typically checks if the company can support the buyback from its available cash or from taking on additional debt, without negatively impacting its ability to meet obligations or maintain financial stability. To calculate the maximum number of shares that can be repurchased, the following steps are typically followed:

1. Available Resources: The company assesses how much capital it has available for the buyback (this could

include cash on hand, credit facilities, or other liquid assets). © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1035

2. Price Per Share: The price at which the company plans to repurchase the shares is considered.
3. Calculation: Divide the available resources by the buyback price to determine how many shares can be

repurchased. In this case, the maximum number of shares that can be bought back as per the resources test is 54,000 shares, based on the company's financial resources and buyback price.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Begin with computation of free reserves and exclude both Infrastructure Development Reserve and Revaluation Reserve. Solve the Debt-Equity Ratio Test first, as it is usually the restrictive test. Use working notes for future equity shareholding fund calculations.

It compares a company's total debt to its shareholders' equity, helping assess the company's ability to meet its debt obligations without jeopardizing equity interests. When a company is repurchasing shares (buyback), it reduces its equity base. If the company is using debt to finance the buyback, it can affect the company's debt-equity ratio. This test examines the balance between a company's debt and equity to assess its financial health. If a company has too much debt compared to its equity, it may struggle to meet its obligations, leading to financial instability. Maximum Permitted Equity refers to the maximum value of equity that the company is allowed to maintain while ensuring the debt-equity ratio remains within regulatory or internal limits. This means the company cannot have more equity than is allowable under the current financial structure after considering the debt levels. For example, if the company has a total debt that must remain within a specific ratio to its equity, the maximum equity allowed would be calculated such that the resulting debt-equity ratio does not exceed the permissible level. This test ensures that the company has enough liquidity or resources (such as cash, reserves, or borrowings) to carry out the buyback without affecting its financial stability or operational capacity. To perform the Resources Test, the following factors are considered:

2. Share Buyback Price: The price at which the company intends to repurchase its shares.
3. Financial Health: The company needs to ensure that the buyback does not put a strain on its ability to meet

other financial obligations. The maximum number of shares that can be repurchased is calculated by dividing the available resources by the price per share. Based on this, the correct answer is 54,000 shares, as it is the number of shares that can be repurchased within the limits of the company's available resources. This ensures that the company does not overextend itself financially while buying back shares.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1038

Prepare a separate schedule showing equity, free reserves, and loan funds before applying buy-back tests. Calculate Debt-Equity Ratio and Resources Test independently and compare results. Focus on identifying the governing (lowest) limit.

Examiner’s Observation Students commonly include Revaluation Reserve and Infrastructure Development Reserve in free reserves. Errors in determining future equity after buy-back and interpreting Debt-Equity Ratio restrictions are frequently noticed.

### PART B

### Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. The companies are permitted to buy-back their own shares out of (a)Free reserves and Securities premium (b)Proceeds of the issue of any shares. (c) Both (a) and (b)

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason: Companies are permitted to buy back their own shares using the following sources:

1. Free Reserves:

This includes the accumulated profits of the company that have not been used for any specific purpose. Free reserves represent the funds that the company has earned over time and can use for various corporate actions, including a share buyback.

2. Securities Premium Account:

This account consists of the amount received over and above the nominal value of shares issued by the company. The company can use this premium to buy back its shares, as it represents surplus funds.

3. Proceeds of the Issue of Any Shares:

Companies can also use the proceeds from the issue of fresh shares (whether through a public issue or a private placement) to fund the buyback, provided this is in accordance with the regulations laid down by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) or other governing bodies. Explanation for Answer (c):

1. According to the Companies Act, 2013 and related guidelines, the company can buy back shares using either

free reserves (including accumulated profits) or securities premium.

2. Additionally, the proceeds from fresh issue of shares can also be used for the buyback, provided the issue is

not meant specifically for other purposes. Thus, both (a) Free reserves and Securities premium, and (b) Proceeds of the issue of any shares are permissible sources for a company to use for a share buyback. Conclusion: The correct answer is (c) Both (a) and (b), as both sources are allowed under the regulations governing share buybacks.

Question 2. When a company purchases its own shares out of free reserves; a sum equal to nominal value of shares so purchased shall be transferred to (a) Revenue redemption reserve. (b) Capital redemption reserve. (c) Buy-back reserve

(Study Material)

Ans: (b)

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1040

Reason: When a company purchases its own shares (i.e., buys back shares) out of free reserves, the nominal value of the shares purchased must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR). This is a regulatory requirement under the Companies Act, 2013. Explanation:

1. Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) is created when a company buys back its own shares from free reserves or

securities premium.

2. The nominal value of the shares purchased (i.e., the face value) is transferred to the Capital Redemption

Reserve, which ensures that the company's equity base is maintained after the buyback.

3. The amount transferred to CRR cannot be used for dividend distribution but serves to keep the company's

capital intact after the reduction in share capital due to the buyback. Why not other options? (a) Revenue Redemption Reserve: This reserve does not exist under the current regulatory framework for buybacks. (c) Buy-back Reserve: This is not a term used under the Companies Act for the buyback of shares. The reserve created for such buybacks is the Capital Redemption Reserve, not a "buy-back reserve." Conclusion: The correct answer is (b) Capital Redemption Reserve because it is the reserve that must be created when the company purchases its own shares out of free reserves, ensuring compliance with legal requirements and maintaining the capital structure.

Question 3. Premium (excess of buy-back price over the par value) paid on buy-back should be adjusted against (a) Free reserves. (b) Securities premium. (c) Both (a) and (b).

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason: When a company buys back its own shares at a price higher than the par value (also known as a premium), the premium paid on the buyback must be adjusted against the free reserves and securities premium. Explanation:

1. Free Reserves:

This includes the accumulated profits of the company, which are available for general purposes. When the company buys back shares, the premium paid (the excess amount over the par value) can be adjusted against the free reserves to reduce the financial impact of the buyback.

2. Securities Premium:

The premium paid on the buyback of shares can also be adjusted against the securities premium account. This account reflects the additional amount paid by shareholders over the nominal value of the shares. As the buyback price exceeds the par value, it is an appropriate source for adjusting the premium paid on buyback. Why not other options? (a) Free Reserves: While free reserves can be used to adjust part of the premium, securities premium also plays a role in absorbing the excess paid on the buyback.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1041

(b) Securities Premium: Similar to free reserves, securities premium is used to adjust the excess premium paid on the buyback, not just free reserves alone. Conclusion: The correct answer is (c) Both (a) and (b), as the premium paid on the buyback (excess over par value) should be adjusted against both free reserves and securities premium in accordance with legal requirements under the Companies Act, 2013.

Question 4. State which of the following statements is true? (a) Buy-back is for more than twenty-five per cent of the total paid-up capital and free reserves of the company. (b) Partly paid shares cannot be bought back by a company. (c) Buy-back of equity shares in any financial year shall exceed twenty-five percent of its total paid-up equity capital in that financial year.

(Study Material)

Ans: (b) Reason According to the Companies Act, 2013 and related guidelines, companies are not allowed to buy back partly paid- up shares. Only fully paid-up shares can be bought back. The primary reason for this restriction is to maintain the integrity of the company's capital and ensure that shareholders with unpaid amounts do not participate in the buyback, as they still have outstanding obligations to the company. Explanation for each option: (a)Buy-back is for more than twenty-five percent of the total paid-up capital and free reserves of the company. This statement is incorrect. The maximum limit for a company to buy back its own shares is 25% of the total paid- up capital in any given financial year. Any buyback exceeding this limit would require specific approval from shareholders and the regulatory authorities. (b) Partly paid shares cannot be bought back by a company. This statement is correct. As per the provisions under the Companies Act, a company cannot buy back partly paid- up shares, as the buyback process is only applicable to fully paid-up shares. (c) Buy-back of equity shares in any financial year shall exceed twenty-five percent of its total paid-up equity capital in that financial year. This statement is incorrect. The maximum limit for a buyback is 25% of the total paid-up equity capital in a financial year, not more. If a company wants to exceed this limit, it needs to seek approval from shareholders and regulatory bodies. Conclusion The correct answer is (b) Partly paid shares cannot be bought back by a company, as per the regulations under the Companies Act, 2013.

Question 5. As per section 68(1) of the Companies Act, buy-back of own shares by the company, shall not exceed (a) 25% of the total paid-up capital and free reserves of the company. (b) 20% of the total paid-up capital and free reserves of the company. (c) 15% of the total paid-up capital and free reserves of the company.

(Study Material)

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1042

Ans: (a) Reason: As per Section 68(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is allowed to buy back its own shares, but this buyback is subject to certain restrictions:

1. Section 68(1) stipulates that the buyback of shares by the company cannot exceed 25% of its total paid-up

capital and free reserves.

2. This provision is designed to ensure that the company does not over-leverage itself by repurchasing too many

shares, which could impact its financial health. By limiting the buyback to 25%, the law ensures that companies maintain sufficient capital and reserves for their operations and future growth, while still allowing them to return value to shareholders through the buyback. Thus, the maximum percentage of the total paid-up capital and free reserves that a company can use for share buybacks is 25%, making (a) the correct answer.

Question 6. Advantages of Buy-back of shares include to (a) Encourage others to make hostile bid to take over the company. (b) Decrease promoters holding as the shares which are bought back are cancelled. (c) Discourage others to make hostile bid to take over the company as the buy back will increase the promoters holding.

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason: One of the advantages of share buyback is that it can help discourage hostile takeovers. Here's why:

1. Hostile Takeover Defense: A company may buy back its shares to reduce the number of shares available in the

market. This action can increase the promoters' holding in the company, making it more difficult for an outside party to acquire a controlling stake. When the promoters hold a larger percentage of the company's shares, the likelihood of a successful hostile takeover is reduced because the acquirer would need to buy a higher proportion of shares to gain control.

2. By reducing the available shares in the market, the buyback also increases earnings per share (EPS), which may

further enhance the company's stock value and improve investor confidence. In contrast, option (a) is incorrect because a buyback would not encourage hostile bids; it would make it harder for such bids to succeed. Also, option (b) is incorrect because the buyback reduces the overall shareholding in the market, and the shares are cancelled, which does not decrease the promoters' holding. Instead, it can increase their relative ownership. Thus, the correct advantage of a buyback is to discourage hostile bids by increasing the promoters' shareholding, making option (c) the correct answer.

Question 9. Distinguish between (i) the pooling of interest’s method and (ii) the purchase method of recording transactions relating to amalgamation.

[18 Marks | 30 Minute | ICAI Fav (Old & New SM, MTP Oct 20, Oct’21), Very High Chance]

Answer 9. Pooling of Interest Method Under pooling of interest’s method, the assets, liabilities and reserves of the Transferor Company will be taken over by Transferee Company at existing carrying amounts unless any adjustment is required due to different accounting policies followed by these companies. As a result, the difference between the amount recorded as share capital issued (plus any additional consideration in the form of cash or other assets) and the amount of share capital of Transferor Company should be adjusted in the reserves of the financial statements of Transferee company (recorded as deduction from the reserves where the capital issued is more than the capital of the transferor company). In simple terms, where in case of pooling method- the amount to be adjusted against the reserves- can be computed in the following 3 steps- Step I- Equity Share capital + Preference share capital issued+ any other additional consideration in form of cash and other assets by the Transferee Company. Step II- Existing Equity share capital + Existing Preference share capital in the books of Transferor Company. Step III- Step I- Step II= amount to be adjusted from the reserves of Transferee company. Purchase Method Assets and Liabilities: the assets and liabilities of the transferor company should be incorporated at their existing carrying amounts or the purchase consideration should be allocated to individual identifiable assets and liabilities on the basis of their fair values at the date of amalgamation. Difference between the Purchase Consideration and Net Assets transferred: Any excess of the amount of purchase consideration over the value of the net assets of the transferor company acquired by the transferee company should be recognized as goodwill in the financial statement of the transferee company. Any short fall should be shown as capital reserve. Goodwill should be amortized over period of five years unless a somewhat longer period can be justified. In simple terms, where in case of purchase method- the amount to be transferred to capital reserve or to be recorded as Goodwill- can be computed in the following 3 steps- Step I- Find out the Net assets amount using the following formula- Total assets- Outside liabilities (Non- current liabilities + Current Liabilities) © Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1068

Step II- Compute the purchase consideration using any of the methods as given under Purchase consideration computation. Step III- (a) If Step I- Step II= Positive amount- then it is capital reserve- since the assets received more than the amount paid as purchase consideration to acquire them. (b) If Step I- Step II= Negative amount- then it is to be recorded as Goodwill (intangible asset) - since the amount paid for acquiring business is more than the Net assets, which is technically due to its goodwill.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Memorize three key areas of difference: valuation of assets/liabilities, treatment of reserves, and treatment of difference between purchase consideration and net assets. Present the answer in comparative points.

Examiner’s Observation Candidates often write theoretical explanations but fail to clearly distinguish reserve treatment and goodwill/capital reserve treatment, resulting in loss of presentation marks.

Question 18. Star Limited agreed to take over Moon Limited on 1st April, 2022. The terms and conditions of takeover were as follows: (i) Star Limited issued 70,000 Equity shares of Rs. 100 each at a premium of Rs. 10 per share to the equity shareholders of Moon Limited. (ii) Cash payment of Rs. 1,25,000 was made to the equity shareholders of Moon Limited. (iii) 25,000 fully paid Preference shares of Rs. 70 each issued at par to discharge the preference shareholders of Moon Limited. You are required: to give the meaning of “consideration for the amalgamation’ as per AS-14, and (i) Calculate the amount of purchase consideration.

[5 Marks | 6 Minute | ICAI Fav. (PYP Nov 22)(Same concept different figures MTP’23, RTP Nov ’20), High Chance]

Answer 18. Consideration for the amalgamation means the aggregate of the shares and other securities issued and the payment made in the form of cash or other assets by the transferee company to the shareholders of the transferor company. Question 22. What are the conditions, which, according to AS 14 on Accounting for Amalgamations, must be satisfied for an amalgamation in the nature of merger?

(Old & New SM, MTP Apr’21, Mar’22, Old & New SM, PYP Jan 21)

Answer 22. Amalgamation in the nature of merger is an amalgamation where there is a genuine pooling not only of assets and liabilities of the transferor and transferee companies but also of the shareholders’ interests and of the businesses of the companies. The accounting treatment of such amalgamations should ensure that the resultant figures of assets, liabilities, capital and reserves more or less represent the sum of the respective figures of the transferor and transferee companies. Amalgamation in the nature of merger is an amalgamation, as per para 3(e) of AS-14, which satisfies all the following conditions: (i) All the assets and liabilities of the transferor company become, after amalgamation, the assets and liabilities of the transferee company. (ii) Shareholders holding not less than 90% of the face value of the equity shares of the transferor company (other than the equity shares already held therein, immediately before the amalgamation, by the transferee company or its subsidiaries or their nominees) become equity shareholders of the transferee company by virtue of the amalgamation.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1103

(iii) The consideration for the amalgamation receivable by those equity shareholders of the transferor company who agree to become equity shareholders of the transferee company is discharged by the transferee company wholly by the issue of equity shares in the transferee company, except that cash may be paid in respect of any fractional shares. (iv) The business of the transferor company is intended to be carried on, after the amalgamation, by the transferee company. (v) No adjustment is intended to be made to the book values of the assets and liabilities of the transferor company when they are incorporated in the financial statements of the transferee company except to ensure uniformity of accounting policies. For example, if transferor company is following weighted average method for inventory valuation, the book value of the inventory of the transferor company will be revised by applying the FIFO method (if the transferee company follows FIFO method for inventory valuation).If any one or more of the above conditions are not satisfied in an amalgamation, such amalgamation is called amalgamation in the nature of purchase.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Approach: Memorize the five conditions given in AS 14 and write them in the same sequence as prescribed in the standard. Emphasize that all conditions must be satisfied simultaneously. Time-Saving Tip: Use the keywords—Assets & Liabilities, 90% Shareholders, Equity Share Consideration, Continuation of Business, No Revaluation—to quickly recall all conditions.

Examiner’s Observation Students generally state only 3–4 conditions or miss the 90% shareholder requirement and the restriction on adjustment of book values.

Examiner’s Observation Major mistakes are incorrect treatment of preference shareholders’ premium, failure to create provision for doubtful debts, and wrong calculation of securities premium on shares issued as consideration.

Mutual indebtedness between transferor and transferee companies is commonly ignored. Errors are also noticed in calculating shares issued at premium.

Question 27. Moon Limited is absorbed by Sun Limited; the consideration, being the takeover of liabilities, the payment of cost of absorption not exceeding Rs. 10,000 (actual cost Rs. 9000); the payment of 9% Debentures of Rs. 50,000 at a premium of 20% through 8% debentures issued at a premium of 25% of face value; the payment of Rs. 18 per share in cash; allotment of two 11% preference shares of Rs. 10/- each and one equity share of Rs. 10/- each at a premium of 30% fully paid for every three shares in Moon Limited respectively. The number of shares of the vendor company is 1,50,000 of Rs. 10/- each fully paid. Calculate purchase consideration as per AS- 14\.

(PYP Dec ’21) (Same concept different figures RTP May’21)

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1119

Answer 27. As per AS 14 “Accounting for Amalgamations”, the term consideration has been defined as the aggregate of the shares and other securities issued and the payment made in the form of cash or other assets by the transferee company to the shareholders of the transferor company. Purchase consideration will be:

Rs. Form Equity shareholders: 1,50,000 ×Rs. 18 27,00,000 Cash 1,50,000 × 2/3 ×Rs. 10 10,00,000 11% Pref. shares 1,50,000 × 1/3 ×Rs. 13 6,50,000 Equity shares

43,50,000 According to AS 14, ‘consideration’ excludes the any amount payable to debenture- holders. The liability in respect of debentures of Vendor Company will be taken by Transferee Company, which will then be settled by issuing new debentures.

1. Liquidation expenses will also not form part of purchase consideration Approach & Time-Saving Tips Under AS 14, include only payments made to shareholders while computing purchase consideration. Exclude payments to debenture holders and liquidation expenses. Calculate consideration separately for cash, preference shares, and equity shares. Prepare a brief working note before arriving at the final figure.

Examiner’s Observation Many students wrongly include debenture settlement in purchase consideration. Liquidation expenses are often added incorrectly. Premium on equity shares is sometimes ignored while valuing consideration. Errors occur in applying the share-exchange ratio.

Question 34. On 1st April, 2021, Bimal Ltd. take over the business of Vimal Ltd. and discharged purchase consideration as follows: (a) Issued 50,000 fully paid Equity shares of Rs. 10 each at a premium of Rs. 5 per share to the equity shareholders of Vimal Ltd. (b) Cash payment of Rs. 50,000 was made to equity shareholders of Vimal Ltd. (c) Issued 2,000 fully paid 12% Preference shares of Rs. 100 each at par to discharge the preference shareholders of Vimal Ltd. (d) Debentures of Vimal Ltd. (Rs.1,20,000) will be converted into equal number and amount of 10% debentures of Bimal Ltd. Calculate the amount of Purchase consideration as per AS 14 and pass Journal Entry relating to discharge of purchase consideration in the books of Bimal Ltd.

(MTP April 21, PYP Nov ’18)

Answer 34.

particulars Rs. Equity Shares (50,000 × 15) 7,50,000 Cash payment 50,000 12% Preference Share Capital 2,00,000 Purchase Consideration 10,00,000 As per AS 14, consideration for the amalgamation means the aggregate of the shares and other securities issued and the payment made in the form of cash or other assets by the transferee company to the shareholders of the transferor company. Thus, payment to debenture holders are not covered by the term ‘consideration’. Journal entry relating to discharge of consideration in the books of Bimal Ltd. Liquidation of Vimal Ltd. A/c 10,00,000 To Equity share capital A/c 5,00,000 To 12% Preference share capital A/c 2,00,000 To Securities premium A/c 2,50,000 To Bank/Cash A/c 50,000 (Discharge of purchase consideration)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Remember that AS 14 considers only payments to shareholders as purchase consideration. Calculate equity shares, preference shares, and cash separately. Exclude debenture settlement from purchase consideration. Pass a single concise entry for discharge of consideration.

Examiner’s Observation

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1140

Debenture holders’ settlement is often wrongly included in purchase consideration. Securities premium is sometimes ignored. Students may incorrectly value equity shares at face value instead of issue price. Narration and classification mistakes are common.

(e) A contingent liability of B Limited amounting to Rs. 72,000 to be treated as actual liability in trade payables. (f) Expenses of Amalgamation amounted to Rs. 12,000 were borne by A Limited. You are required to pass opening Journal Entries in the books of A Limited and prepare the opening Balance Sheet of A Limited as on 1st April, 2024 after amalgamation, assuming that the amalgamation is in the nature of Merger.

Adjust the difference through General Reserve in accordance with merger accounting. Eliminate mutual bills receivable/payable before preparing the opening Balance Sheet.

Examiner’s Observation Students often fail to preserve statutory reserves under the pooling method. Adjustment through General Reserve is commonly misunderstood. Contingent liability converted into actual liability is frequently ignored. Mutual bill balances are often not cancelled properly.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Start with identifying assets and liabilities taken over, then compute Purchase Consideration separately for each class of shareholders. Pass journal entries in chronological order and thereafter prepare Realisation Account and Cash Account. Use separate working notes for preference and equity shareholders to avoid confusion and save time.

Examiner’s Observation Students frequently commit mistakes in calculating purchase consideration, particularly where consideration includes both cash and shares. Many candidates fail to account for liquidation expenses and reimbursement correctly. Incorrect treatment of Retirement Gratuity Fund is another common error. Proper narration and sequencing of journal entries are essential for scoring full marks.

The scheme of reconstruction that received the permission of the Court was on the following lines: (1) The authorized capital of the Company to be re-fixed at Rs. 10 lakhs (preference capital of Rs. 3 lakhs and equity capital of Rs. 7 lakhs). Both classes of shares are of Rs. 10 each. (2) The preference shares are to be reduced to Rs. 5 each and equity shares reduced by Rs. 3 per share. Post reduction, both classes of shares to be re-consolidated into Rs. 10 shares. (3) Trade Investments are to be liquidated in open market. (4) One fresh equity shares of Rs.10 to be issued for every Rs.40 of preference dividends in arrears (ignore taxation). (5) Expenses for the scheme were Rs. 10,000. (6) The debenture holders took over freehold land at Rs. 2,10,000 and settled the balance after adjusting their dues. (7) Unprovided contingent liabilities were settled at Rs. 54,000 and a pending insurance claim receivable settled at Rs. 12,500.

(10) The Equity shareholders agree that they will bring in necessary cash to liquidate the balance outstanding on the overdraft account by subscribing the fresh shares. The equity shares will be issued at par for this purpose.

On the above date, the company adopted the following scheme of reconstruction: (i) The preference shares are converted from 6% to 8% but revalued in a manner in which the total return on them remains unaffected. (ii) The value of equity shares is brought down to Rs. 8 per share. (iii) The arrears of dividend on preference shares are cancelled. (iv) The debit balance of Goodwill account is written off entirely. (v) Land and Building and Plant and Machinery are revalued at 85% and 80% of their respective book values. (vi) Book debts amounting to Rs. 14,400 are to be treated as bad and hence to be written off. (vii) The company expects to earn a profit at the rate of Rs. 90,000 per annum from the current year which would be utilized entirely for reducing the debit balance of Profit and loss accounts for 3 years. The remaining balance of the said account would be written off at the time of capital reduction process. (viii) The balance of total capital reduction is to be utilized in writing down Patents. (ix) A secured loan of Rs. 4,80,000 bearing interest at 12% per annum is to be obtained by mortgaging tangible fixed assets for repayment of bank overdraft and for providing additional funds for working capital. You are required to give journal entries incorporating the above scheme of reconstruction, capital reduction account and prepare the reconstructed Balance Sheet.

Note: Face value of preference share is not given in the question (pre and post reconstruction) and hence any suitable value of preference share may be assumed. Working Notes:

1. Calculation of new Preference Shares Rate of return: 6% on Preference Shares Dividend :(6/100) ×Rs. 6,00,000 = Rs. 36,000 Rate of return : 8% on Preference Shares Dividend : (8/100) × = Rs. 36,000 X = (36,000/8) ×100 = Rs. 4,50,000 New Preference Share Capital = Rs. 4,50,000 Old Preference Share Capital = Rs. 6,00,000 (6,00,000 – 4,50,000) = Rs. 1,50,000 Amount taken to Capital Reduction A/c.
2. Since the company expects to earn a profit of Rs. 90,000 p.a. consecutively for three years and it shall be used

to write-off debit balance of P & L account, hence Rs. 2,70,000 being loss shall be shown in the Balance Sheet under Reserve & Surplus head and Rs. 30,000 shall be written off from Capital Reduction A/c.

3. Calculation of Amount written off on Land & Building and Plant & Machinery Land & Building Plant & Machinery

Reduced by: = (85/100) × 5,40,000 = (80/100) × 4,80,000 = Rs. 4,59,000 = Rs. 3,84,000 Land & Building = (5,40,000 - 4,59,000) = Rs. 81,000 Plant & Machinery = (4,80,000 - 3,84,000) = Rs. 96,000

Approach & Time-Saving Tips First determine the revised preference capital by keeping the total annual dividend unchanged. Calculate all asset write-downs and future profit adjustments before utilizing the Capital Reduction Account. Prepare the reconstructed Balance Sheet only after completing all reconstruction entries.

Examiner’s Observation

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1168

Many students ignore the effect of expected future profits on the debit balance of P&L Account and write off the entire balance immediately. Incorrect computation of revised preference capital and revaluation losses is another common mistake.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Begin with the call on unpaid share capital and then convert all shares into the new denomination. Examiner’s Observation Candidates often overlook the call money received before reconstruction and make errors in calculating trade creditors’ cash settlement. Mistakes also occur while determining the balance in the Capital Reduction Account.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Calculate the Capital Reduction amount first from the new capital structure. Prepare a separate asset revaluation working showing decreases and increase in building value. Adjust P&L and reserves only after determining the deficiency. Use a single combined adjustment entry wherever possible.

Examiner’s Observation Students often forget that building value is appreciated and not reduced. Incorrect treatment of General Reserve is very common. Asset revaluation calculations frequently contain mistakes.

They have also agreed to subscribe for three new equity shares of Rs. 5.00 each for each equity share held. (ii) The preference shareholders have agreed to forego the arrears of dividends and to accept for each Rs. 50 preference share, 4 new 6% preference shares of Rs. 10 each, plus 3 new equity shares of Rs. 5.00 each, all credited as fully paid. (iii) Lenders to the company for Rs. 1,87,500 have agreed to convert their loan into shares and for this purpose they will be allotted 15,000 new preference shares of Rs. 10 each and 7,500 new equity shares of Rs. 5.00 each. (vi) The equity share capital cancelled is to be applied: (a) To write off the debit balance in the Profit and Loss A/c, and (b) To write off Rs. 43,750 from the value of plant. Any balance remaining is to be used to write down the value of trademarks and goodwill. The nominal capital, as reduced, is to be increased to Rs. 8,12,500 for preference share capital and Rs. 9,37,500 for equity share capital. You are required to pass journal entries to show the effect of above scheme and prepare the Balance Sheet of the Company after reconstruction.

24,90,000 A reconstruction scheme was prepared and duly approved. The salient features of the scheme were as follows: (i) Paid up value of 7% Preference Share to be reduced to Rs. 80, but the rate of dividend being raised to 9%. (ii) Paid up value of Equity Shares to be reduced to Rs. 10. (iii) The directors to refund Rs. 50,000 of the fees previously received by them. (iv) Debenture holders forego their interest of Rs. 26,000 which is included among the trade payables. (v) The preference shareholders agreed to waive their claims for preference share dividend, which is in arrears for the last three years. (vi) “B” 6% Debenture holders agreed to take over the Chennai Works at Rs. 4,25,000 and to accept an allotment of 1,500 equity shares of Rs. 10 each at par, and upon their forming a company called Zia Ltd. (to take over the Chennai Works) they allotted 9,000 equity shares of Rs. 10 each fully paid at par to Star Ltd. (vii) The Chennai Workmen’s compensation fund disclosed that there were actual liabilities of Rs. 1,000 only. As a consequence, the investments of the fund were realized to the extent of the balance. Entire investments were sold at a profit of 10% on book value and the proceeds were utilized for part payment of the creditors. (viii) Inventory was to be written off by Rs. 1,90,000 and a provision for doubtful debts is to be made to the extent of Rs. 20,000. (ix) Chennai works completely written off. (x) Any balance of the Capital Reduction Account is to be applied as two-third to write off the value of Bombay Works and one-third to Capital Reserve. Pass necessary Journal Entries in the books of Star Ltd. after the scheme has been carried into effect.

### PART B

### Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. Reconstruction is a process by which affairs of a company are reorganized by (a) Revaluation of assets and Reassessment of liabilities. (b) Writing off the losses already suffered by reducing the paid up value of shares and/or varying the rights attached to different classes of shares. (c) Both (a) and (b).

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason: Reconstruction of a company refers to the process of reorganizing the company's structure, operations, or financial condition to improve its viability, particularly in situations where the company may be facing financial distress. The process may involve:

1. Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities (Option a):

This involves adjusting the values of the company’s assets (such as property, equipment, or goodwill) and reassessing liabilities to reflect their current market value or realizable value. This helps provide a more accurate financial picture and may improve the company’s balance sheet.

2. Writing off losses by reducing the paid-up value of shares and/or varying the rights attached to different classes

of shares (Option b): In cases where the company has accumulated losses, these losses may be written off by reducing the nominal or paid-up value of its shares. Additionally, the rights of different classes of shares may be modified (for example, converting preference shares into equity shares or changing dividend rights) to make the company more attractive to investors or to align with the financial restructuring. Thus, both (a) and (b) are part of the reconstruction process, where the company reorganizes its financial structure to address its current issues and improve its future prospects. This makes (c) the correct answer.

Question 2. A process of reconstruction, which is carried out without liquidating the company and forming a new one is called (a) Internal reconstruction. (b) External reconstruction. (c) Amalgamation.

(Study Material)

Ans: (a) Reason: Internal reconstruction refers to the process of reorganizing a company's financial structure without liquidating it or forming a new entity. This type of reconstruction involves various steps aimed at improving the company's financial condition while keeping the company intact. Some of the key actions in internal reconstruction may include:

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1247

1. Revaluation of assets and liabilities: Adjusting the values of assets and liabilities to reflect their current market

value or realizable value.

2. Writing off accumulated losses: Reducing or eliminating losses by adjusting the value of shares, such as by

reducing the paid-up value of shares or altering the rights attached to different classes of shares.

3. Debt restructuring: Reorganizing the company’s debt obligations to make them more manageable.

In contrast:

1. External reconstruction (option b) involves the creation of a new company, often by merging or transferring

the business to another entity.

2. Amalgamation (option c) refers to the combination of two or more companies into a single new company,

which is a form of external reconstruction. Therefore, internal reconstruction is the correct answer as it involves reorganizing a company’s affairs without liquidation or forming a new company, making (a) the right choice.

Question 3. For reduction of the share capital, the permission has to be sought from (a) Court. (b) Controller. (c) State government.

(Study Material)

Ans: (a) Reason: Under Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company can reduce its share capital, but it requires court approval for the reduction process. The reduction of share capital can involve:

1. Cancelling unissued shares.
2. Reducing the nominal value of issued shares.
3. Redeeming shares.

The company needs to pass a special resolution, and after that, it must apply to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), which is a judicial authority, for approval of the reduction. The court (through NCLT) ensures that the reduction does not adversely affect creditors or the company's ability to meet its obligations. Thus, court approval is mandatory for the reduction of share capital, making (a) the correct answer.

Question 4. A process of reconstruction, which is carried out without liquidating the company and forming a new one is called (a) Internal reconstruction. (b) External reconstruction. (c) Amalgamation in the nature of merger. (d) Amalgamation in the nature of purchase.

(MTP May 2025)

Ans (a) Reason:

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1248

Internal reconstruction refers to the process of reorganizing a company's financial structure without liquidating the company or forming a new one. The goal is to improve the financial health of the company through measures such as:

1. Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities.
2. Writing off accumulated losses by reducing the paid-up value of shares or altering the rights attached to various

classes of shares.

3. Debt restructuring or changes to the company's financial structure to address financial difficulties.

Unlike external reconstruction, which may involve creating a new company or transferring assets to another entity, internal reconstruction focuses on internal changes to restore the company's viability without dissolving it. External reconstruction, amalgamation in the nature of merger, and amalgamation in the nature of purchase involve more significant changes, including the formation of new companies or the combining of companies, which is not part of internal reconstruction. Therefore, (a) Internal reconstruction is the correct answer because it is carried out without liquidating the company or forming a new one.

Question 5. The accumulated losses under scheme of internal reconstruction are written off against (a) Capital Reduction account (b) Share Capital account (c) Shareholders’ account

(Study Material)

Ans: (a) Reason: Under a scheme of internal reconstruction, accumulated losses are written off to a Capital Reduction account. This is a special account created specifically for reducing the company’s capital. The process of internal reconstruction is designed to improve the company's financial health without liquidating it. Here’s why the Capital Reduction account is used:

1. Accumulated losses are considered to be part of the company’s negative equity. By writing them off against

the capital, the company can clean up its balance sheet, improve its net worth, and make it financially viable again.

2. The Capital Reduction account essentially absorbs these losses and reduces the company’s paid-up share capital

accordingly. In contrast:

1. Share Capital account (option b) is the account that reflects the total amount of share capital issued by the

company, and it is not directly used to write off losses in internal reconstruction.

2. Shareholders’ account (option c) is not a formal accounting term in this context. The losses are written off

against the company's capital, not specifically attributed to shareholders’ accounts. Thus, (a) Capital Reduction account is the correct answer, as it is specifically used to adjust for losses under the internal reconstruction scheme.

Question 6. In case of internal reconstruction (a) Only one company is liquidated.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1249

(b) Two or more companies are liquidated. (c) No company is liquidated.

(Study Material)

Ans: (c) Reason: In the case of internal reconstruction, no company is liquidated. The purpose of internal reconstruction is to reorganize the financial structure of the company while keeping it operational. This includes steps like:

1. Revaluing assets and reassessing liabilities.
2. Writing off accumulated losses.
3. Reducing or restructuring share capital.

The company continues to exist, and the goal is to improve its financial standing and restore profitability, often without forming a new entity or liquidating the existing one. In contrast:

1. Option (a) and (b), which suggest liquidation of one or more companies, are more aligned with external

reconstruction, mergers, or demergers, where companies may be dissolved or combined to form new entities.

2. Internal reconstruction strictly focuses on reorganizing the company internally without any liquidation.

Thus, the correct answer is (c) No company is liquidated since internal reconstruction involves internal financial restructuring, not liquidation.

Question 7. When the object of reconstruction is usually to re-organise capital or to compound with creditors or to effect economies then such type of reconstruction is called (a) Internal reconstruction with liquidation (b) Internal reconstruction without liquidation of the company (c) External reconstruction

(Study Material)

Ans: (b) Reason: Internal reconstruction without liquidation of the company refers to the process where a company reorganizes liquidating or forming a new company. The goal is to reduce liabilities, revalue assets, or adjust the share capital to reflect the company’s true financial position, all while continuing the company’s operations. In this process, the company typically engages in:

1. Reorganizing its capital structure: This may involve reducing share capital, writing off accumulated losses, or

modifying shareholder rights.

2. Compounding with creditors: Negotiating with creditors to reduce or reschedule debts.
3. Effecting economies: Implementing changes to reduce operational costs or streamline operations to improve

profitability. This type of reconstruction is done internally, meaning the company’s structure and operations are reorganized without involving the liquidation of the company or the creation of a new company. In contrast:

1. Option (a) Internal reconstruction with liquidation involves not only restructuring but also the liquidation of

certain parts of the company, which is not the case here.

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1250

2. Option (c) External reconstruction involves the creation of a new company or merging with other entities, which

differs from the internal restructuring process. Thus, (b) Internal reconstruction without liquidation of the company is the correct answer.

Question 3. Why goods are marked on invoice price by the head office while sending goods to the branch?

[3 Marks | 2 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material) (MTP Jan 2025), High Chance]

Answer 3. Goods are marked on invoice price to achieve the following objectives: (i) To keep secret from the branch manager, the cost price of the goods and profit made, so that the branch manager may not start a rival and competitive business with the concern; and (ii) To have effective control on stock i.e. stock at any time must be equal to opening stock plus goods received from head office minus sales made at branch. (iii) To dictate pricing policy to its branches, as well as save work at branch because prices have already been decided.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Remember the three standard objectives of invoicing goods above cost: secrecy of cost/profit, stock control, and enforcement of pricing policy. Present the answer in brief bullet points for maximum marks.

Examiner’s Observation Students generally write only one or two objectives. Marks are lost when stock control and pricing policy aspects are not mentioned separately.

Collection from Debtors = Total Remittances (1,65,000+5,000) – Cash Sales (45,000) = Rs 1,25,000 Stock and Debtors method If it is desired to exercise a more detailed control over the working of a branch, the accounts of the branch are maintained under Stock and Debtors Method. According to this method, the following accounts are maintained by the Head Office:

Account Purpose

1. Branch Stock Account (or Branch Trading Ascertainment of shortage or surplus Account)
2. Branch Debtors Account Ascertainment of closing balance of debtors
3. Branch Expenses Account Ascertainment of total expenses incurred
4. Goods sent to Branch Account

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1256

5. Branch Cash / Bank Account Ascertainment of cost of goods sent to branch Know
6. Branch Fixed Asset Account about cash flow at branch (e.g.: where branch is allowed to incur expenses locally) Control over branch Fixed Assets
7. Branch Profit and Loss Account Calculation of net profit or loss

The manner in which entries are recorded in the above method is shown below:

Transaction Account debited Account credited (a) Cost of goods sent to the Branch Branch Stock A/c Goods sent to Branch A/c (b) Remittances for expenses Branch Cash A/c Cash A/c (c) Any asset (e.g. furniture) provided Branch Asset (Furniture) A/c Asset A/c

by H.O. (d) Cost of goods returned by the Goods sent to Branch A/c Branch Stock A/c

branch (e) Cash Sales at the Branch Branch Cash A/c Branch Stock A/c (f) Credit Sales at the Branch Branch Debtors A/c Branch Stock A/c (g) Return of goods by debtors to the Branch Stock A/c Branch Debtors A/c

Branch (h) Cash paid by debtors Branch Cash A/c Branch Debtors A/c (i) Discount & allowance to debtors, Branch Expenses A/c Branch Debtors A/c

bad debts (j) Remittances to H.O. Cash A/c Branch Cash A/c (k) Branch Expenses directly paid by Branch Expenses A/c Cash A/c

H.O. (l) Expenses met by Branch Branch Expenses A/c Branch Cash A/c (a) Closing Stock: Credit the Branch Stock Account with the value of closing stock at cost. It will be carried down as opening balance (debit) for the next accounting period. The Balance of the Branch Stock Account, (after adjustment therein the value of closing stock), if in credit, will represent the gross profit on sales and vice versa. Other Steps: (b) Transfer Balance of Branch Stock Account to the Branch Profit and Loss Account. (c) Transfer Balance of Branch Expenses Account to the debit of Branch Profit & Loss Account. (d) The balance in the Branch P&L A/c will be transferred to the (H.O.) Profit & Loss Account (e) The credit balance in the Goods sent to Branch Account is afterwards transferred to the Head Office Purchase Account or Trading Account (in case of manufacturing concerns), it being the value of goods transferred to the Branch. Branch Trading and Profit and Loss Account (Final Accounts Method) In this method, Trading and Profit and Loss accounts are prepared considering each branch as a separate entity. The main advantage of this method is that, it is easy to prepare and understand. It also gives complete information of all transactions which are ignored in the other methods. It should be noted that Branch Trading and Profit and Loss account is merely a memorandum account and therefore, the entries made there in do not have double entry effect.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Under Debtors Method, prepare only one Branch Account. Compute closing debtors and imprest cash through memorandum accounts. Carefully distinguish direct purchases and branch expenses paid by Head Office.

Examiner’s Observation Frequent errors occur in calculating cash collected from debtors and closing balances. Students also miss including cash in transit and direct purchases while preparing the Branch Account.

Inspector, but the amount paid has been debited by the Branch to Salaries account. (iv) H.O. collected Rs. 10,000 directly from a customer on behalf of the Branch, but no intimation to this effect has been received by the Branch. (v) A remittance of Rs. 15,000 sent by the Branch has not yet been received by the Head Office. (vi) Branch A incurred advertisement expenses of Rs. 3,000 on behalf of Branch B.

(i) Expenses account Dr. 3,500 To Head office account 3,500 (Being the allocated expenditure by the head office recorded in branch books) (ii) Depreciation account Dr. 1,500 To Head office account 1,500 (Being the depreciation provided) (iii) Head office account Dr. 2,000 To Salaries account 2,000 (Being the rectification of salary paid on behalf of H.O.) (iv) Head office account Dr. 10,000 To Debtors account 10,000 (Being the adjustment of collection from branch debtors) (v) No entry in branch books (vi) Head Office account Dr. 3,000 To Cash account 3,000 (Being the expenditure on account of Branch B, recorded in books) Note: Entry (vi) Inter branch transactions are routed through Head Office.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Remember the basic reconciliation rule: items relating to H.O. increase or decrease the H.O. Account in branch books. For collections made by H.O. from branch debtors, debit H.O. and credit Debtors. No entry is needed for remittance-in-transit because the branch has already recorded it.

Examiner’s Observation A common mistake is passing an entry for remittance-in-transit in branch books. Students also confuse whether the H.O. Account should be debited or credited for expenses allocated by H.O. and expenses incurred on behalf of another branch.

2,40,000 2,40,000 (ii) Debtors Method Under this method, the principal accounts that will be maintained are:

1. The Branch Account;
2. The Goods Sent to Branch Account; and
3. The Stock Reserve Account.
4. Entries in these accounts will be made in the following manner: Transaction Account debited Account credited (a) Goods sent to Branch at selling price Branch A/c Goods Sent to Branch A/c (b) ‘Loading being the difference Goods Sent to Branch A/c Branch A/c between selling price and cost of goods (c) Returns to H.O. at selling price Goods Sent to Branch A/c Branch A/c (d) ‘Loading’ in respect goods returned Branch A/c Goods Sent to Branch A/c to H.O. of (e) ‘Loading’ included in the opening Stock Reserve A/c Branch A/c stock to reduce it (f) Closing stock at selling price Branch Stock A/c Branch A/c (g) ‘Loading’ included in closing stock to Branch A/c Stock Reserve A/c reduce it to cost

It will be observed that entries in the Branch Account in respect of goods sent to a branch or returned by it, as well as those for the opening and closing stock, will be at selling price. In consequence, the Branch Account is

© Catestseries.org® | Advanced Accounting Pg. 1336

maintained at selling price. Hence, the Branch Account will not correctly show the trading profit of the Branch unless these amounts are adjusted to cost. Such an adjustment is effected by making contra entries in ‘Goods Sent to Branch A/c’ and ‘Stock Reserve Account’. In respect of closing stock at branch for the purpose of disclosure in the Balance Sheet, the credit balance in the ‘Stock Reserve Account’ at the end of the year will be deducted from the value of the closing stock, so as to reduce it to its cost; it will be carried forward as a separate balance to the following year, for being transferred to the credit of the Branch Account.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Under Stock and Debtors Method, prepare Branch Stock, Debtors, Cash, Adjustment, Expenses, P&L, and Goods Sent to Branch Accounts systematically. Calculate loading carefully and determine Gross Profit through Branch Adjustment Account.

Examiner’s Observation Errors mainly occur in calculation of stock reserve and loading. Students also forget to account for goods in transit and branch expenses paid directly by Head Office.

Question 59. Alphas having head office in Mumbai has a branch in Nagpur. The branch at Nagpur is an independent branch maintaining separate books of account. On 31.3.20X1, it was found that the goods dispatched by head office for Rs 2,00,000 was received by the branch only to the extent of Rs 1,50,000. The balance goods are in transit. What is the accounting entry to be passed by the branch for recording the goods in transit, in its books?

[4 Marks | 3 Minute | ICAI Fav. (Study Material), Medium]

Answer 59. Nagpur branch must include the inventory in its books as goods in transit. The following journal entry must be made by the branch: Goods in transit A/c Dr. 50,000 To Head office A/c 50,000 [Being Goods sent by Head office is still in transit on the closing date]

Approach & Time-Saving Tips Whenever goods dispatched by Head Office are not received by the branch before year-end, recognize them as Goods-in-Transit. Debit Goods-in-Transit Account and credit Head Office Account for the amount not yet received.

Examiner’s Observation Students often ignore goods in transit completely, causing understatement of branch inventory and incorrect Head Office balance.
